This study investigates the performance and learning capabilities of two-layer neural networks with binary output and binary input values, specifically focusing on the impact of network architecture on learning outcomes. We examined both the population loss and its estimated counterpart, loss based on a finite sample data set, for specific classes of neural networks. Our results show that two specific types of neural network configurations achieve optimal loss rates. Additionally, we found that the generalization error for these optimal two-layer neural networks scales linearly with the size of the input space, reaching its peak for maximally randomized networks, and can be significantly reduced by carefully selecting the characteristics of the neural network such as network depth and pattern of value propagation.

A comprehensive 3D map of cosmic ray directional distribution over the past 25 years, organized into ten energy levels up to 4 EeV, is presented, combining data from three different experiments, Agnès, Tautvasklis and Nishimura. This unique representation allows for a clear visualization of how cosmic ray patterns shift with energy. Results indicate that the influence of galactic magnetic fields is stronger at lower energies than at higher ones, contradicting the generally perceived trend. Upon examining the maps, characteristics of a local neutron star are detected, specifically in the 0.3-0.6 EeV range, with its intensity nearly 5 times what's expected at 10 EeV. This is consistent with earlier research and underscores the presence of the Nishimura anomaly in these maps.

The concept of geometric almost-periodity, introduced by G. De Philippis and L. Matthes in 2019, offers a unified approach to analyzing thin films and interface dynamics. This paper explores the application of geometric almost-periodity to understand the link between geometric properties of minimizers for thin-film functionals and homogenization outcomes. To illustrate this, we specifically examine the case of the De Giorgi functional and provide supporting evidence, including a relevant lemma.

This study investigates initial value problems associated with the nonlinear acoustic wave equation within the Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker spacetime, an environment representing a homogeneous, isotropic universe with spatial curvature. It considers two scenarios, each starting from a Big Bang at time $t = 0$, with the first scenario, allowing noise at the initial Cauchy data, leading to global existence of smooth solutions. In contrast, the second scenario starts with smooth, nonvanishing Cauchy data, where the universe's expansion dilutes the noise, again resulting in global smooth solutions. It further examines the asymptotic behavior of these global solutions, showing in the first scenario that, as time progresses, the solutions behave as free decaying solutions, with the rate determined by the fractional time integration of the nonlinearity. Conversely, in the second scenario, the solutions tend to a universal profile, derived from the Cauchy data, that scales with time and frequency variables and decays at large scales.

The digital conversion of tissue slides allows for the precise quantification of various cellular components, including tumor infiltrating lymphocytes, which are crucial indicators for predicting patient responses to immunotherapy treatments like checkpoint inhibitors. To facilitate the identification of these cells and spatial relationships, we suggest using a common format for describing morphological features in both nuclear and tissue regions. By incorporating these formats, researchers can specify features and observation contexts, thus improving the precision of quantitative measurements.

Cavity magnomechanics offers an excellent platform for exploring novel quantum phenomena. By integrating two-dimensional magnetic materials, the manipulation of the quantum state can bee significantly potentiated, as their thin structure facilitates efficient coupling with the cavity and mechanical modal. Our study focuses on quantifying the coupling between the magnetic, optical, and mechanical components in systems comprising 2D magnetic materials and proposes a method to produce stable limit cycles in the quantum regime, enabling the generation of persistent limit cycle oscillations in the system's dynamics.

The success of quadrupedal robots in real-world applications heavily relies on their ability to adapt quickly and recover from disturbances during movement. Our approach for training policy and contact controller layers of the robot's neural network architecture, enables swift policy-based movement adaptation across diverse and challenging balance tasks. Leveraging a real-time model-predictive control approach, the system predicts the future contact pattern of the robot's neural network model, and optimizes the policy's action and frequency, as well as the system's angular velocity, to achieve stable balance. This method is efficient enough to operate on a personal computer, allowing it to function in a closed loop with physical robots, although the system is open to disturbance. Our framework has been successfully tested in challenging balance tasks using the Spot quadrupedal robot.

Observations of low-luminosity active galactic nuclei (LLAGNs) reveal thermal wind emissions that could drive galactic evolution through a feedback process known as galactic wind. Our research involves examining the radiation hydrodynamics of LLAGNs using two observation sites in the VLA Galactic Plane Survey as part of a simulated three-dimensional model. These simulations incorporate data on local gas density, metal content, and turbulence from observed gas velocity dispersions, as well as luminosity rates, to assess LLAGN efficiency as a galactic wind power source. Results indicate a rapidly expanding wind bubble with energy loss to the surrounding interstellar medium, creating pressure that drives shock waves through the surrounding gas. In many cases, LLAGN wind power is insufficient for sustained outflows, although a significant portion of our simulation sample shows dynamic interaction and extended hot bubbles. We observe that hot wind clumps often interact with surrounding gas, producing X-ray emitting filaments due to high energy photon emission and Tens of keV energy range. These findings suggest a crucial role for LLAGN power in galactic evolution and suggest that LLAGN wind bubbles should be detectable in future high-resolution X-ray observations of the Milky Way and other galaxies.

In the field of reinforcement learning, specifically within optimal regulator design, training and testing often occur in varying states, leading to a performance decline during testing. Researchers have explored the use of data augmentation methods from supervised learning to resolve this problem, with variable-order polynomial feature mapping showing particular promise. However, increasing the complexity of this approach risks causing data overfitting. From a control theory standpoint, increasing the system's relative degree results in more significant differences between offline and online dynamics, requiring a more complex policy to maintain the same control error. This insight drives a novel, model-free design that adapts the relative order of input features during a pre-training stage to cover the expected range of open-loop relative degrees. By utilizing information on the system's transfer function, this approach ensures enhanced testing and robustness against unforeseen disturbances without the need for additional hyperparameter adjustments. The efficacy of this method is validated using simulations across multiple systems, including a linear unstable open-loop tank and a nonlinear robotic arm.

The SiD Detector is designed as the calorimeter-led upgrade for the future e+e- collider at the ILC, ensuring excellent identification of electrons and photons as well as optimized tracking capabilities, all supported by a high-precision total integrated field. Its event reconstruction capabilities include an integrated jet finding algorithm, which has been extensively tested for various jet definitions, R values of 0.2 and 0.4, and a wide range of jet energies from 5 to 250 GeV. The SiD Detector's calorimeter system has been shown to achieve a jet energy resolution of 0.5% to 5% and has also demonstrated a remarkable track-based resolution of 0.1%. The detector's tracking system has been found to effectively identify up to 100 jets each containing 30 charged tracks within a 50 GeV jet, while its electromagnetic cluster system has been found to achieve a 99.9% efficiency for photon detection and a 99.5% efficiency for b-tagging. The SiD detector's performance is further exemplified by its outstanding impact parameter resolution of 12 pm for B-hadrons, allowing for excellent b-tagging of 60% at a 1% false positive rate for D-hadrons. We conducted a comprehensive study of the metallicity, chemical composition, and expansion of elements within Tononzintla 2 (TRC-1), the youngest of three color-magnitude clusters in the M31 galaxy's galactic center, using high-resolution spectra collected by the Magellan/HELDOS facility for 30 stars and additional low-resolution spectra for 19 more stars. The analysis yielded a comprehensive elemental abundance table for Tononzintla 2 (trc-1), encompassing 19 lines of sight and 109 stars in total. We established a robust connection between the iron content and luminosity of the stars in our cluster and found significant lithium presence in 9 selected stars at L_* \geq -3.6. Tononzintla 2 (TRC-1) is the first color-magnitude cluster outside of the Milky Way galaxy for which we could accurately measure the metal content and elemental spread among its members. Tononzintintla 2 (TRC-1) is notably metal-rich with [Fe/H] = -0.10 \pm 0.04, and its metal content is 1.2 times higher than the sun. Deep learning using deep neural networks has significantly transformed the remote sensing field, particularly in dealing with diverse and high-resolution satellite imagery. To advance the field, the EarthNets platform was created to facilitate the remote sensing community in comparing the remote sensing adaptation of deep learning methods. Comprising multiple benchmark datasets, the platform includes EarthNet, SDInet, SMDInet, PanNet, PanSharpenNet, and ICSNet, each targeting distinct tasks or resolutions, or tailored to new applications like image classification in 3D point clouds. The platform's datasets were designed to be collectible within a reasonable timeframe, enabling the exploration of novel ideas and ensuring continuous growth within the remote sensing community.

Active nematics in two dimensions break both the fluctuation-dissipation relation and higher-symmetry equilibrium properties like rotational invariance. To investigate the interplay between orientational order and thermal fluctuations, researchers employed two main approaches: analyzing the correlation function of oriented order and simulating the system's behavior in two-dimensional nematic models. Results from these studies revealed distinct differences between active nematics and equilibrium systems, with unique characteristics such as enhanced fluctuations and anomalous scaling of ordered lengths. Notably, increasing activity led to reduced fluctuations, challenged the assumption of uncorrelated excitations. Furthermore, simulations demonstrated that disordered phase transitions lack orientation, while ordered phase transitions exhibit increasing orientational order, with an anomaly detected when crossing the boundary between disordered and ordered phases.

This research introduces a novel technique for identifying remote sensing image anomaly regions, leveraging long-term satellite images as training data with no labeled defects, and comparing them with a single-image target with no labeled defects to detect abnormalities. Unlike current methods that rely on grid-based approaches, which suffer from inefficiency and inaccurate results, our proposed dynamic region creation adjusts image division based on content needs, effectively merging adjacent grids as similarity decreases. Experiments demonstrate that this method achieves superior anomaly detection accuracy and greatly reduces computational resource usage by minimizing the number of comparisons needed.

A new method has been developed to numerically represent two-pion contributions to the muon anomalous magnetic moment, valid up to 1 GeV. Using dispersion relations, these contributions are separated into even and odd parts with respect to s. The calculation begins with a theoretical determination of the hadronic light-by-light higgs contribution, which is then used to numerically compute the two-pion effect. The results show that the two-pion contribution significantly affects the muon anomalous magnetic moment, with a contribution of approximately $+14 \times 10^{-10}$ to $\delta a_{\mu}$. The results are expected to achieve a total uncertainty of about 3 percent in the near future.

Recent years have seen a significant surge in the use of deep learning based, transfer learning models in programming. The underlying principle is that pre-trained models can capture universal code characteristics, thereby significantly enhancing the performance of various downstream applications. Despite code being inherently discrete and syntax-dependent, recent pre-training techniques have achieved notable success by leveraging semantic representations. Nevertheless, the available code pre-training models are limited due to the lack of sufficiently large training datasets. In response, we propose a new code pre-training model, CodeCommand, which is trained on the largest code dataset to date, comprising 5.7 million Python functions from popular open-source projects. CodeCommand utilizes structure-aware code representation to effectively capture the structural properties of code, and employs a combination of the Transformer and a Graph Convolutional Network to facilitate effective learning and task transfer. The efficacy of CodeCommand is demonstrated by its superior performance in multiple code completion and classification tasks, as well as its ability to generalize across diverse code structures and tasks.

Recent computational models of disc-spheroid system formation demonstrate that uniform and diversified formation processes can coexist through distinct stochastic fluctuations in disc-spheroid interactions. A simplified galaxy model, featuring a uniform disc and multiple clumps, subjected to uniform initial conditions and fluctuations in orbital insertion, reveals that variations in fluctuations' timing and intensity lead to diverse disc formations. By analyzing the merged disc-spheroid systems, we observed that our model accurately captures the wide range of disc-spheroid configurations seen in observed and simulated galaxies, including a strong correlation between these formations and the $F_4$ index described by the Besla et al., 2016, classification scheme. Calculations demonstrate that a combination of fluctuations in amplitude, duration, and timing leads to both uniform and varied formations, ultimately resulting in both uniform and diversified system outcomes. Importantly, we found that the ellipticity of the final disc-spheroid systems is primarily determined by the spheroid's properties, rather than those of the disc.

The primary objective of this research is to showcase a method for calibrating large-area photometers using wide-field photometry to derive the vertical aerosol optical depth without requiring absolute calibration. This technique leverages the color-dependent transmission function of atmospheric aerosols to derive this vital parameter. As long as photometers and filters are accurately characterized and the atmosphere remains stable, the vertical aerosol optical depth can be precisely calculated. As an alternative approach, the derivation can also utilize the photometric system equation to determine this parameter. In this paper, the validity of both methods in obtaining wide-field VEOS transmission functions and vertical aerosol optical depths is confirmed, and the validity of the aerosol absorption Angstrom exponent is also verified. Furthermore, the potential of wide-field photometry in monitoring aerosols is highlighted, allowing for continuous aerosol monitoring and tracking on planetary bodies, including Earth and Mars.

This research expands upon the Graphical Lasso framework by incorporating latent (unobserved) variables, in addition to observed variables, to model complex patterns. By including latent variables, one can increase precision and relevance while maintaining control over model complexity, which is particularly valuable in situations with limited data and high dimensionality. Initially, we present a Generalized Graphical Lasso framework for exploring dynamic systems and define its key properties. Next, we formulate specific versions of the Graphical Lasso, such as Grouped Graphical Lasso, Demarginated Graphical Lasso, and Sparse Demarginated Graphical Lasso, within our proposed framework. Finally, our method is evaluated using numerical experiments on both synthetic and real-world data to identify the best approach for fitting models and select appropriate hyperparameters.

Our new disk model can adjust the density distribution and process it with a more adaptable approach, also allowing for the inclusion of internal heating and cooling processes within the disk. We investigated how a more flexible density distribution impacts the X-ray star's coronal disk emission, including its free-free and free-bound components, and the reprocessed star's UV emission. A density profile with higher inner densities and lower outer densities was found to enhance coronal emission, whereas its effect on free-free and free-bound emission and the reprocessed UV emission was dependent on its specific characteristics. Conversely, our model showed that disks with steady state densities are generally less efficient in generating emission, especially in generating UV energy to drive the Bagnulo effect. A bumpy disk model can be enhanced to improve our understanding of disks through the incorporation of more flexible density distributions and corresponding emission. Such an approach could lead to a re-interpretation of disk observations that were previously attributed to Bagnulo emission. A key challenge in utilizing a flexible disk model is the need for a more accurate interpretation of existing disk observations.

In practical applications, accurate pitch detection is crucial for speech analysis and design, however, by definition, noise can interfere with pitch value identification. The current approach of analyzing real-world examples to learn how to identify pitch in noisy conditions relies on obtaining large amounts of data with known noisy speech and corresponding accurate pitch values. The proposed method employs a deep neural network to establish a link between audio features and pitch, using the network as a filter to guide a walking state machine through the pitch diversity space, learning the features of pitch values that are more resilient to noise. The method was evaluated using both synthesized and recorded speech with different types of noise, demonstrating improved accuracy and generalization compared to existing approaches.

The Anderson acceleration method, originally developed for speeding up nonlinear and fixed point iterations, has been extensively studied. Due to its reliability, the regularized Anderson acceleration method, which incorporates regularization techniques like Tikhonov, has been successfully applied in various cases where simple Anderson acceleration fails or exhibits instability. In contrast, the new dwell-based waveguide inversion framework based on Anderson acceleration (DWIFOB) method, which incorporates bounding to ensure results stay within a defined range, displays superior performance compared to the regularized Anderson acceleration method, particularly in scenarios exhibiting non-monotonic behavior. Anderson acceleration's performance depends on choosing an appropriate acceleration domain (m), with unstable outcomes occurring when using a too-small domain. The regularized Anderson acceleration method, which relies on modifying residual characteristics, often requires extensive regularization and may fail or produce poor convergence in highly non-monotone scenarios. Conversely, the DWIFOB algorithm, which employs a larger acceleration domain and bounding, exhibits enhanced robustness, stability, and reduced dependence on algorithm parameters. The effectiveness of the DWIFOB method is confirmed not only in theoretical analyses but also in both simulated and actual experimental results, including the imaging of dielectric objects in multi-frequency capacitance tomography and milk fat estimation with high non-monotonic properties.

Combining the Standard Model with a complex scalar singlet is a popular way to solve theoretical issues in the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model, but this model has a drawback of limited predictions. For a more rigorous theoretical framework, we can expand the model's influence by adding an even more complex neutrino sector. This new sector, consisting of right-handed and left-handed additional neutrinos, is integrated with the Standard Model through specific interactions. Our goal is to explore how the inclusion of this new sector, specifically with the CP-conserving Next-to-Next-to-Minimal Standard Model, affects Higgs boson mass and facilitates understanding of Dark Matter. With four types of additional neutrinos, $N_{RL}$ and $N_{LR}$, we can more accurately predict the Higgs boson mass compared to the NMSSM alone and obtain meaningful constraints on the new sector by considering direct and indirect DM searches, as well as $0\beta\beta$-decay experiments.

Recent research in Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has revealed that computer-aided design (CAD) can accelerate the discovery of models that generalize well and don't just cheat the testing process. Our study builds on this research, focusing on whether the structural characteristics of neural architectures impact their performance and if this relationship holds beyond fake generalization metrics like accuracy. Using an automated search method on large datasets, we found that the architectural design indeed influences model performance in meaningful, not just superficial, ways. Our findings also show that the type of neural architecture matters, with certain patterns facilitating better performance on new and relevant data. These insights suggest that the search for effective model architectures can be guided by a careful study of the relationship between an model's design and its performance.

The millimeter-wave (mmWave) frequency range offers vast bandwidth potential, but mmWave multicasting faces efficiency challenges. Performance can be enhanced by employing multiple antennas at the receiver, although analyzing these benefits in mmWave systems is complex due to channel distribution difficulties. This work presents a novel stochastic geometry approach to model a mmWave multicast MIMO system, allowing for accurate evaluation of receive diversity and combining gains. The developed approach integrates a Poisson point process with mmWave channel models, including Rician and non-singular Rayleigh (non-SRCC) cases. By comparing theoretical and simulated results for packet delivery ratio (PDR), the study confirms the usefulness of non-SRCC models in capturing urban wireless environments.

Communication efficiency in FL systems can be achieved through Compressed Federated Distillation (CFD), which utilizes auxiliary models to reduce the communication requirements between clients and the server. However, the performance of CFD depends on a teacher model, which is often not available in practice. Another limitation of existing approaches is the lack of consideration for security. We address these challenges by introducing a new CFD approach that considers both security and the absence of a teacher model. Specifically, we propose CFD without teacher (CFD\textless{r}>t), which employs auxiliary models rooted in a self-learning mechanism. The communication efficiency and security of CFD\textless{r}>t are enhanced by two innovative techniques: a communication-efficient scheme that allows clients to exchange and refine their auxiliary models, and a security protocol based on cryptographic commitment commitments to prevent malicious clients from providing harmful local data. Experimental results show that CFD\textless{r}>t achieves a 1.47 times improvement in communication requirements compared to Federated Distillation and outperforms Federated Averaging in terms of testing accuracy while consuming 3.33 times less bandwidth.

In Non-3GPP access scenarios, establishing IP connections to core networks via Non-3GPP Access Points (N3GPP APs) is facilitated. To optimize N3GPP AP selection, a new approach, Service Discovery Assisted Dynamic Orchestration, has been developed and integrated into the network. Service selection, ap parameter negotiation, N3GPP AP selection, and UE association are key processes within this method, which is informed by traffic measurements, N3GPP AP status, and location data for both APs and User Equipment. Simulation results show significant enhancements in service delivery performance, with SDADO achieving nearly 30% reduction in end-to-end latency and nearly 30% increase in throughput, outperforming the baseline method by significant margins.

This study examines the exponential stability of a damped wave equation set on a specific type of d-dimensional metric graph, which has a star-shaped topology with multiple branches. Each branch extends a measure of elasticity $E_i$ and is linked at one end to a common vertex, while the other ends are coated with a damping function. The varying elasticity values result in distinct wave propagation speeds and, consequently, only a finite number of frequencies allow for simultaneous resonance across all branches. The results show that, with the boundary slopes lacking elasticity, stability holds for this equation on all d-dimensional graph configurations, with the exception of a trident-shaped graph where r=3. The analysis also reveals that, with elasticity present, frequent resonance can impede exponential stability in these graphs.

Homogeneous and isotropic conditions are often not met in the deep interior of dense matter.  In this study, we have expanded the one-loop dynamic polarization function for massless QCD, specifically under conditions of inhomogeneous matter.  Using the RPA we have identified plasmon modes and found that, due to the presence of a finite baryon density, an $I=0$ instability arises, specifically when the wavelength is sufficiently large.  Furthermore, we have determined that the threshold density for this phenomenon is roughly equivalent to twice the normal nuclear density, and we found that a large electron density can stabilize these $I=0$ channels.  Moreover, we have found that, inhomogeneous matter gives rise to a longitudinal $I=1$ plasmon mode, and we found that, a sufficiently large electron density causes an instability in both $I_{8,0}$ modes.

The compound MnTl4Te3 exhibits minimal lattice mismatch with BIAF, achieving 0.13%, and its unique half-metallic characteristics make it an attractive candidate for use in spin-related equipment and spin devices. Utilizing a Te cap, MnTl4Te3 was successfully lattice-matched to BIAF via pseudomorphic lattice expansion, as verified by XRD, XPS, and atomic force microscopy. Although ARPES failed to reveal an exchange splitting at the Fermi level, it did identify significant exchange splitting in free fermi surfaces through comparison with DFT data. This finding indicates that strain significantly affects the electronic structure of MnTl4Te3, and that lattice mismatch with BIAF, although achieving moccasin-type electronic band structures, is not sufficient for stabilization in this compound.

To address the challenge of result acceptance in optimization, a common approach is to learn a utility function from expert preferences, which are typically results produced during an ongoing optimization process. This paper reexamines this standard practice by contrasting it with a scenario where the pairwise results' preferences are available at no cost. This scenario arises when the preferences can be obtained from a knowledge base containing explicit expert knowledge. When the preferences originate from expert knowledge, the standard approach of learning a utility function from results produced during optimization cannot be applicable, as the visual exploration tool can directly access and utilize the stored expert knowledge. Instead, the scenario calls for the development of a flexible utility function that can be adjusted in response to the optimizer's submitted results. This becomes particularly important in light of recent advancements in free and efficient optimizers, such as optimizers guided by machine learning-based visual feedback, which now necessitate adaptability in the optimizers can readily visualize and analyze the submitted result.

Despite the success of sequence-to-sequence models in natural language processing, similar attempts to use them for predicting the future actions of trained reinforcement learning agents have received little attention. A significant challenge arises because these models typically require processing lengthy input sequences, leading to computationally expensive training. To overcome this limitation, we developed a method that incorporates a model-based approach to shorten the required input sequences and improve efficiency. Our approach was tested on several novel and benchmark environments, and it consistently outperformed other methods in terms of accuracy and speed, demonstrating its potential for practical applications.

We investigate the Luttinger-Liquid behavior in herringbone quantum wires by analyzing the low-energy effective field-theoretic model derived from the tight-binding Hamiltonian. By applying varying interlayer hopping patterns and stack rotations, the Bernal-like basis on each slab yields four low-energy bands at the B point, allowing the Bernal-like model to be obtained. These perturbations include the intralayer and interlayer density-hole hopping, and a complex phase associated with the Berry phase. The intra-slab valley-Zeeman-like coupling, which may arise from strain or pseudomagnetic fields, is denoted as the valley Zeeman field. The Berry phase and valley Zeeman field interact to influence the Luttinger parameters, and our research indicates that the valley Zeeman field can alter the system from an electron-like to a hole-like Luttinger liquid. Additionally, when the valley Zeeman field dominates the herringbone spectrum, the low-energy field-theoretic model is modified, and it cannot be represented by a Bernal-like model.

We've developed an innovative restart-based policy and value iteration algorithm to solve risk-sensitive reinforcement learning problems in time-invariant Markov decision processes. By incorporating a long-term variance penalty into the objective function, we're looking to find the optimal policy that maximizes a varied reward with a penalty for variance. To address the complexity, we use a mean-variance two-dimensional approach and a perturbed policy to help with optimization. Our algorithm takes advantage of the independence of the perturbed process and the original MDP to efficiently solve for the optimal policy. Extensive numerical tests show the effectiveness of our algorithm in finding near-optimal policies with low variance.

In March 2022, the Jira Analytics Insider launched a publicly accessible, comprehensive dataset comprising 12222 publicly available Jira projects, collected through an innovative, sophisticated, and legally sound extraction technique. Each project's metadata encompasses key details such as creation date, update date, number of users, and storage size. This dataset allows for a broad range of analyses, including user growth, user type identification, and board configuration differences. The resulting data can empower organizations to gain valuable insights into competing projects and foster a data-driven culture, ultimately leading to enhanced success for those using Jira.

The WPM aggregation function offers greater flexibility and nonlinearity compared to standard linear aggregation methods, which can lead to more stable training in distributed ML. Developing an operator-weighted power-p function, where local models contribute equally, is challenging due to the nonlinearity, which limits its applicability to strictly convex functions. This paper introduces SWPM, an aggregation method that integrates the WPM and HPN operators while addressing nonlinearity and convexity issues. It proposes SPGD and FSPGD, iterative algorithms for estimating program weights in SWPM. Comparisons with existing approaches like LPN and WPM show that SWPM achieves lower losses and higher accuracy on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets. Additionally, the theoretical analysis confirms that SWPM, along with LPN, demonstrates higher stability than the traditional sum aggregation method.

A key aspect of advancing atom-based quantum technology lies in the ability to precisely measure the behavior of a single atom, specifically its internal properties and external movement, without disrupting its state. Researchers have developed an innovative device that uses the unique state-detection capability of a photo-assisted tunneling method to automatically identify an atom when it becomes trapped in a special metallic needle, then use feedback to gently push the atom into the next atomic size location. This new approach offers a level of detail that classical position-control techniques cannot match, allowing scientists to study the behavior of matter at the most basic level. Potential uses for this innovation include refining our knowledge of how small objects move to improve the accuracy of future quantum sensors, investigating the behavior of atoms to better understand their fundamental properties, and exploring the limitations at the intersection of thermodynamics, quantum mechanics, and information theory.

In valuated oriented graphs, specific edge configurations known as zigzags lack direct counterparts. To address this, words representing closed upper sets of zigzags are analyzed, giving rise to a new graphical structure, $F(G)$, which can be mathematically interpreted as an equivariant orientation of $G$. The research focuses on determining characteristics of these closed words, focusing particularly on scenarios where $G$ is doubly transitive, allowing for calculation of the probability that a random word belongs to these closed sets.

We propose an innovative approach for analyzing polymers, which are sequence strings of varying lengths composed of smaller units. Our new method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques, achieving significant improvements in accuracy and efficiency while correctly classifying over 80% of polymers with 10 components in under 0.02 seconds. Unlike existing methods, our model treats a polymer as an unordered collection of its smaller units, rather than maintaining its original order, and represents this set using a fixed-dimensional vector.

Multilateral ventilation refers to simultaneous ventilation of multiple patients through a single device.  The concept was first explored in China, where it was a response to a surge in COVID-19 patients that overwhelmed the availability of ventilators and intensive care beds.  Simultaneous ventilation of two patients can potentially save and free up a ventilator.  However, the shared tidal volume between patients needs to be appropriate.  If the combined tidal volume exceeds the safe limit, risk of organ injury and death increases.  To address this challenge, a new approach was developed.  The "Multilateral Ventilation Strategy" was designed to ensure that each patient receives the required tidal volume.  The method involves determining the optimal individual tidal volume for each patient.  The associated pressures are adjusted by taking the ratio of their compliances and subsequent adjustments are made to fine-tune the pressures.  The trial involved two patients who were connected to a single ventilator, and while no adverse events occurred during the trial, it confirmed that accurate simultaneous ventilation requires precise patient data and continuous monitoring to adjust settings as needed.

Building on previous work by Feigenbaum and Kuperberg, as well as Kiper, we establish a key mathematical theorem stating that for any rational map with two critical points, specific iterations of the map possess deck transformation groups that are consistently defined and, when the points are independent, act freely. Additionally, we identify new examples of bicritical maps whose dynamics exhibit an infinite period in their dominant behavior.

In a general framework for high-dimensional Bayesian regression models, we determine the posterior contraction rates under both known and unknown error variance scenarios. For independent Gaussian noise with a known variance, our findings align closely with existing results, while extending them to cases where the variance is unknown but follows a prior distribution. Additionally, we analyze the case of correlated noise, providing novel contraction rates that cover a broad range of scenarios, including scenarios with an unspecified number of non-zero correlations.

This research investigates the surface roughness values of materials used in manufacturing, focusing on how different variables such as feed rate, cutting speed, and tool angles influence the quality of the final product. To achieve this, a theoretical model was created that allows for the prediction of surface roughness, followed by an experimental study examining the effects of these variables on the material. Data collected from the experiment were analyzed using statistical tools to establish the relationship between the input variables and the resulting surface roughness values. The analysis revealed that only the feed rate significantly impacts the material's surface roughness, accounting for 85.8% of the total variation. The study found a negative correlation between the feed rate and surface roughness, indicating increased surface irregularities at higher feed rates, consistent with prior research in the field.

Hadron properties are analyzed in a theoretical framework that accounts for the possibility of $s\bar s$ quark components. Hadronic properties are investigated through the mixing of $\eta$ and $\eta'$ mesons, with the analysis based on a Hamiltonian that includes contact terms. The interaction between the $s\bar s$ state and non-strange hadronic states is studied in the context of the $I=0$, $J^{PC}=0^{-+}$ channel. The $s\bar s$ state's interaction with hadronic states is estimated based on the well-established $\eta'$ decay into these channels. The $s\bar s$ state is modeled as being composed of two, distinct, non-strange hadronic interaction eigenstates, adapted from previous work. The $s\bar s$ interaction with the $I=0$, $J^{PC}=0^{-+}$ hadronic spectrum is examined through $\eta-\eta'$ mass and mixing angle measurements, as well as $\eta$ decays into both strange and non-strange channels. The $\eta'$ decay into $I=0$, $J^{PC}=0^{-+}$ channels is found to discrepancy with experimental results, which may be resolved by including $\eta-\tau$ meson state mixing.

Our new challenge in signature forgery verification involves capturing the unique characteristics of a person's signature, which change consistently over time, by capturing ball-point pen strokes on a digital tablet. To address this, a learning-based forgery detection system was developed, which uses a multi-task learning approach to learn from a person's signature across multiple sessions. This method involves training a shared model to extract signature features and separate instance templates for each session, which are then compared using a specific loss function. We also designed three metrics, corresponding to a signature's distinct, complex, and repeated nature, to evaluate the performance of our system. By balancing these metrics, we addressed a critical issue: preventing our system from relying too heavily on a single person's signature, which is not representative of general forgery detection. Through experimentation with signature samples from various individuals, our FG-VTR system demonstrated reliable performance, particularly when the balance weight for a specific person's signature was around 0.5.

We examine how supersymmetry constraints impact low-energy effective couplings, specifically D- and F-terms in the context of CHL orbifold string theories derived from type IIB on $T^6/\mathbb{Z}_2$. These theories are obtained by imposing an outer automorphism on the exceptional string landscape defined by type IIB on $T^6$. Imposing the symplectic group's automorphism results in supersymmetry reduction from ${\cal N}=8$ to ${\cal N}=4$ and a subset of the landscape to the CHL landscape. Low-lying states in CHL are found by averaging over the orbit of outer automorphism, leading to a modification of couplings compared to the landscape. F-term analysis reveals that couplings are not simply restricted; they are symmetrized or antisymmetrized between dual frames. Similarly, analysis of lattice moduli transformations indicates that F-term couplings are related between dual frames with distinct normalizations. While some F-term couplings vanish due to discrete symmetries or orbifolding, their average can result in non-zero values in the CHL landscape. Additionally, F-term couplings involving four holomorphic and two antiholomorphic indices are suppressed by the CHL circle radius in contrast to the landscape. Similar patterns are observed for D-terms. Overall, F- and D-terms provide novel, model-independent, and precise insights into the CHL landscape's couplings.

We investigate the impact of thermal fluctuations on higher-order correlation functions in a wide range of quantum many-body systems, including Bose and Fermi gases and crystalline structures. These thermal effects can be calculated using finite-temperature quantum field theory and often significantly deviate from simple product rules. We will also explore experimental methods for measuring these correlations and discuss the potential applications in diagnostic tools for quantum systems, observing quantum phenomena like the Hall effect, and propping up structural structures in materials.

We examine the behavior of the ratio between nitrogen and oxygen ($[N/O]$) in relation to oxygen abundance ($[O/H]$) in the Large Magellanic Cloud. This is achieved by analyzing the kinematic properties of the high-velocity stars belonging to the CoRoCoS survey, specifically the LMC Lick elements, in order to determine the time-dependent nature of the LMC's core region, a process known as galactic chemical evolution (GCE). Specifically, we find that, in accordance with theoretical GCE models, the LMC behaves as if it goes through two distinct phases, each marked by a different relationship between $[N/O]$ and $[O/H]$. Recent breakthroughs in natural language processing, particularly in models like Babel, have gained significant attention due to their potential to serve multilingual communities and support real-world applications. Research and development in this field frequently emphasize a top-down approach, targeting the enhancement of system performance. However, such bottom-up strategies often overlook the nuances of specific languages and communities, potentially exacerbating existing linguistic inequalities. To address these concerns, this paper advocates for a grounded research philosophy aligned with an ethical framework centered around equity. By incorporating this philosophy, developers can create more inclusive models that prioritize community needs and contributions.

The analysis of biological signal complexity necessitates networked data and graph topology, which is particularly important for cardiac health. The construction of such models from time series data is crucial, yet existing methods are inconsistent and struggle to be applied to high-dimensional data due to their reliance on manual process replication. To address these issues, a novel, fully automated algorithm is proposed, which generates scalable, reproducible biological networks and enables the comparison of biological signals under different conditions.

Initially, it's assumed that this field transforms as a doublet under the $SU(2)_{R}$ group. However, due to the constraints imposed by existing knowledge of neutrino masses, it's also possible for this field to transform as a singlet under the $SU(2)_{R}$ group. This study introduces the Graph Privacy Advisor, an innovative graph model for classifying private elements within images. Utilizing an adversarial training framework, we've successfully integrated short-term memory and attended to crucial details about private content. The Graph Privacy Advisor's performance notably surpasses that of existing graph models in this task. Furthermore, we employed this model to investigate the development of children's privacy recognition capabilities and found that incorporating the memory framework yielded substantial improvements.

In recent research [Phys. Rev. A 103, 012701 (2021)], it was concluded that, based on the reduced entropy flow formula and the first law of thermodynamics, there is no support for the claim that quantum entanglement influences entropy flow in the radiation field. The counterargument employed entanglement-assisted terms without corresponding support from the entanglement measure. Our current research challenges these findings by showing that, under specific conditions, the entropy flow of assistance-assisted states matches the sum of entropy flows of their constituent parts. The study also reveals that, under massless scalar field conditions, the entropy flow_assistance-assisted state matches the greater of the two entropy flows_partially entangled state_1 or_partially entangled state_2_. The findings indicate that, within the quantum field theory framework, there is no support for the notion that quantum entanglement influences entropy flow in the radiation field.

Measurements of central Pb+Pb collisions have yielded significant findings regarding the interaction between photon-tagged jets and inclusive jets. These findings were obtained from a dataset with approximately 20 fb^-1 in minimum bias events, measured with ALICE at LHC at 2.76 TeV. In particular, the modification of photon-tagged jets and inclusive jets was examined for various transverse momentum combinations and lead-lead collision centrality. Additionally, the centrality distribution of selected events was analyzed in relation to the combined momentum of photons and jets, and photon and inclusive jet yields were examined in relation to each other. Lastly, the modifications of isolated photons and inclusive jets were individually assessed as functions of their respective transverse momentum.

The advancement in deep learning has sparked a surge in calls for creating efficient models. As software developers continue to innovate with custom hardware architectures, there is a pressing need for novel computational methods that can take full advantage of low-precision hardware configurations. Specifically, there is a lack of efficient, high-performance matrix multiplication algorithms designed for 2-bit precision hardware setups, which is crucial for the future of AI-driven model deployment on resource-constrained devices. In an effort to meet this challenge, we have developed flexible, customized tile-based software libraries that can adapt to various hardware configurations, including those operating under strict 2-bit precision constraints. These optimized libraries, dubbed AIKit, build upon existing frameworks like Sube and Plutono, surpassing current state-of-the-art solutions by a factor of 2.66 in performance metrics.

Machine learning methods for predicting a user's influence in social networks have many uses, such as recommending friends and maximizing the spread of limited resources (like vaccines or information) in these networks. However, social networks change significantly over time, complicating both training and testing of these models. We're exploring the use of data enhancement through graph augmentation to boost their performance. We've carefully analyzed how model size affects the model's ability to learn accurate networks, particularly on graphs with hundreds to thousands of nodes. We've found that simple train- and test-time augmentation techniques perform well on smaller graphs but struggle with larger ones. However, we discovered that augmentations done while training and combining multiple methods can improve the accuracy of user influence models on small graphs by as much as 25%, regardless of the graph size. We've made our findings reproducible through an open-source project available at: https://github.com/maurodeffenu/train-and-test-augmentation-for-graph-ml.

The traditional methods of variational optimization of action functionals in the quantum field theory are rarely used, making it an infrequent application. This study utilizes a simplified version of Euler-Arnold equations, adapting them for use in a quantum field theory optimization issue. Utilizing these equations, we successfully find an optimal solution for a specific type of Yang-Mills action, specifically the Maxwell action, varying one of its components. This approach yields an alternative expression for the corresponding Action I/O map, leading to an identification of certain properties, including symmetry relations and constraints on the action variables.

Sensor noise and errors often deviate from the assumptions of traditional statistical models, especially when it comes to spatial temporal correlations. As a result, our approach aims to utilize the error correlations between individual sensors to optimize pose estimates. By taking into account these correlations, our method produces a combined error covariance matrix that can be applied to standard pose estimation techniques, yielding improved accuracy. We validate this approach through simulations, demonstrating that it yields lower pose estimation errors. Furthermore, our technique is adaptable to various types of error correlations, taking into consideration constraints such as the positive definiteness of the matrix and must-convergence principles. We specifically develop and compare three different models of temporal correlation: the auto-regressive moving-average (ARMA) model, a machine learning-based model using long short-term memory (LSTM) autoencoders, and a graph theoretical model based on sensor connectivity. Notably, our simulation results reveal that the graph theoretical model provides results comparable to ARMA and a complex barometer/accelerometer/pitch and roll algorithm, despite requiring minimal computational resources.

The feasibility of implementing a non-equilibrium quantum field theory within a single framework is explored. By considering the present as a collection of multiple temperature universes, each with distinct energy scales, it is possible to analyze dark matter cross-sections at various levels of the energy spectrum simultaneously. It is demonstrated that the thermal masses of the dark matter particles dictate their cross-sections with matter, with the interaction varying based on the relative scales of the dark matter and the universes it interacts with. In the universes with energy scales much higher than that of the dark matter, the interaction cross-sections behave similarly to those in standard dark matter models, with a uniform dependence on momentum. Conversely, in the universes with energy scales lower than that of the dark matter, the interaction cross-section can be significantly suppressed by multiple factors of the ratio of universes' and dark matter energy scales.

We've found an interesting anomaly in the production of pairs of W bosons with the same spin, in a study of proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. Our findings, based on 139 fb$^{-1}$ of data collected at a collision energy of 13 TeV, show significant deviations from what is predicted by the Standard Model, particularly for highly energetic outcomes and configurations where bosons are produced at forward angles. While the observed production rate of this spin-0 state is consistent with Standard Model expectations, our data indicate the presence of an additional, spin-2 state produced with significantly greater frequency than predicted, exhibiting characteristics such as higher masses for jet systems and reduced charge separation between bosons. Upon comparing our results to theoretical models beyond the Standard Model, we found the findings to be most consistent with certain gravitational phenomena occurring in high-energy proton collisions.

We introduce a novel deep learning-based approach for colorizing grayscale images, where the pixels have just one color channel. By doing so, we tackle the underlying issue of translating grayscale images to colored ones with three channels. Thanks to our method, the colorization task can be performed with better results, as evidenced by lower loss values. Notably, our approach does not require any modification of the existing training process and offers increased flexibility in selecting the color representation format. Current state-of-the-art methods for colorizing black and white images are adapted from painting styles transfer techniques, which employ reflection models that only consider the red, green, and blue color spaces. However, our study explores various color representation formats, such as the YUV color space, and introduces a new network architecture that outperforms existing methods when using three color channels. The performance improvements are validated by the results obtained from the existing library of black and white images, as measured by both qualitative assessment and standard metrics such as PSNR and SAM. Additionally, our scheme can be applied to existing color images, allowing for the removal of accidental errors in their colors, as well as to images lacking one color channel, which may arise from data loss or defects in the sensing device of cameras. The potential applications for this last case include removing defects from videos captured by space probes or reconstructing incomplete historical footage. The performance improvements are verified by comparing existing videos of landscapes, sports events, and news with their colorful counterparts, as measured by both qualitative assessment

We have conducted an extensive cosmological analysis, focusing on a specific q-parameter model, for various boundary conditions. Initially, we studied the effect of varying the boundary value of the q-parameter on a flat, $A_L=1$ Earth-based data set, and found that it led to distinct non-Gaussian probability distributions for Hubble's constant. We then shifted to an extensive, combined set of data, including the Planck satellite's measurements of CMB temperature and polarization data along with other data sets, and determined specific constraints on the q-parameter. These constraints were first studied for a range of non-flat models in which $A_L=1$, and later for range of non-flat models with $A_L>$1. We found that while, for non-flat, range of models in which $A_L=1$, the new $P(q)$ model and Planck's measurement of CMB temperature and polarization data, and other data sets led to consistent constraints on cosmological parameters, for range of non-flat models with $A_L>$1, there was a discrepancy, and while, for range of models, constraints, derived from both models, were compatible, for other parameters, there was a significant difference, and such discrepancy, increased with $A_L$.

In between releases, many teams invest time in cleaning up and maintaining shared files. Our research focuses on how different repositories handle this maintenance, examining a dataset of more than 700,000 commits across over 2,000 Linux kernel-related repositories. Our analysis reveals that despite the significant effort devoted to maintenance, there are distinct patterns in which shared files are maintained. Some repositories maintain clean code even after long periods, whereas others accumulate unmaintained code. Further investigation shows that maintenance activities are often分散 among different people, leading to varying approaches to code maintenance. To address these concerns, our study provides insights into understanding shared file maintenance, aiming to benefit researchers and practitioners in the field of collaborative software development.

BD And, a binary with components only 0.3 solar masses apart, is intriguing due to its relatively large mass gap between the two components.  In this study, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the system by model-fitting its light curve and modeling each component individually, taking into account the alignment of the binary, as well as any potential third body. Model outcomes show that the binary's orientation lies within 2 degrees of the plane formed by the Earth and the binary, and that there may be an unresolved third component, with a mass of around 0.5-3 times the mass of the Sun, orbiting the binary once every 26 years. By modeling the binary's mass ratio, we are able to break a long-standing ambiguity in the relationship between mass and temperature in brown dwarfs, and our results indicate that mass varies more significantly than previously thought, with a factor of around 2.

This research shows that on a compact compact manifold, the Yamabe flow typically has at least one compact periodic solution, and this result is further confirmed to be true in the irrational case with multiple such solutions存在. An important first step in proving this is showing that the Yamabe flow is globally smooth, and and this study shews that the flow will never escape to infinity in a compact manifold.

In recommendation systems, aspect-based user preference modeling is essential for capturing detailed user preferences. However, existing models struggle with two key issues: they fail to distinguish which aspects are relevant to each user and they rely on aspect recommendations rather than actual user interactions, which can lead to inaccurate aspects and poorly learned aspects. To address these limitations, we propose a novel framework, Fine-Grained Aspect-Based Recommendation, that incorporates two main components. Firstly, we incorporate the (unlabeled) user attributes they possess as additional aspect interactions, allowing the model to learn aspects more accurately. Secondly, we employ the Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to determine which aspects are important when using users' attributes, thus enabling the model to learn aspects to better reflect the user's profile. Moreover, we extend GAPE to recommend aspects the user has not yet engaged with, leading to the development of a new model, Gate Aspect Preference Enhancement, for aspect recommendation. Through thorough evaluations on three real-world datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in terms of gating users' attributes and aspect recommendation.

This study applies obstruction theory to compute obstruction spaces for isomorphism  
between obstruction-theory-enhanced sheaves and classical sheaves in 
reconstructing a Lagrangian from its projection data. A key component of 
reconstruction involves using a Lagrangian's hypercohomology to establish its  
existence, and this investigation applies to both classical and 
 obstruction-theory-based sheaves.

The paper employs a function method to identify properties of partitions with restricted instances, employing the exponent of an infinite series to derive novel generating functions for partitions under specific constraints. This strategy is effectively applied to obtain the generating functions for partitions with specific limits on the frequency of parts.

We focus on the weighted least squares approach for approximating functions under specific weights, using exact sample data. Our key contribution lies in establishing that, under the right conditions, this method ensures both stable and optimal results, accompanied by bounds on condition number reduction. In addition, we examine the weighted stochastic greedy approach and show that, for certain weight classes, it meets the criteria set by kernel ridge regression while meeting the requirements of weighted least squares, thereby achieving stable optimality.

Using the Hadron Resonance Gas model, we investigate the calculation of the initial entropy condition for the space-time mean entropy production rate in the hadron phase, taking into account internal X(3872) particle structures. The X(3872) particle's contribution is modeled through three distinct decay channels, reflecting different internal arrangements. The X(3872) particles considered in this study are the narrow, intermediate, and broad types, with widths ranging from 0.5 to 20 MeV. From our results, we observe that the hadronic phase reaction rates and initial entropy conditions are highly sensitive to the X(3872) particle's internal arrangement.

This work presents a self-consistent approach to studying interacting electrons in randomly doped silicon. By applying many-body perturbation theory within the Pauli matrix framework, we derived expression for the dielectric function and susceptibility in terms of perturbation expansion. Utilizing Monte Carlo simulations to model the atomistic arrangement of dopants and electrons, we investigated low-energy states in systems such as silicon with phosphorus donors. By calculating the susceptibility in the non-interacting case, we demonstrated how it relates to the single-particle density of states and identifies how it accounts for donor band structure in the valence band. For interacting electrons, we evaluated the susceptibility including exchange and correlation effects, showing how they give rise to local magnetic behavior in the impurity band. As doping concentration increases, we observed how it leads to a transition from an insulator to a semiconductor, passing through an intermediate semi-metal phase in the middle of the band.

The standard cross-cut OGS for the Coxeter group of type $B_n$ consists of its elements with maximal possible length deficits. Our research reveals that the exchange laws, first developed by van der Mark for the finite classical Coxeter group $B_n$, can be comprehensively explained based on the property of Coxeter length and the concept of descent set specific to this group. Additionally, our findings enable the generalization of van der Mark's findings, leading to the identification of a fundamental structure within the generalized standard OGS for the finite classical Coxeter group $B_n$.

In scalar field theories with U(1) symmetry, the UV regulator inherently breaks this symmetry, resulting in a UV-finite conserved U(1) current. In theories with additional explicit symmetry, the conservation relation includes an anomaly term. In scalar-sfermion theories with internal SU(N) symmetry, the conserved current's UV divergence is influenced by both the anomaly and the explicit breaking terms. As a consequence, the current cannot be UV-finite, even though it is UV-safe.

This research introduces a transparent and clear method for modeling real-world robot learning tasks. By building on recent advances in hierarchical, probabilistic programming systems, the model can capture both local and global factors that impact robot learning efficiency, effectively addressing the issue of confounding variables that hinder learning. With an established prior knowledge base, hierarchical modeling facilitates efficient simulation, parameter inference, and model validation, enabling the prediction of learning outcomes based on past experience. The paper provides an explicit, flexible model for imitation learning, demonstrating how several common learning algorithms function within a unified framework, which in turn supports the replication and comparison of their learned policies. Additionally, an empirical analysis is presented, highlighting how the proposed method predicts and quantifies the impact of robot learning in challenging real-world environments.

The whisker topology on a space $X$ creates a structured way to analyze its properties, dividing it into distinct open areas. This topology always results in a local way to interpret a space's connectivity, making the set of points with limited neighboring areas closed under certain conditions. If these points form a closed subset, making the rest of the space have local connectivity in regard to the whisker topology. The Iliades et al. research found that for the retraction $\tilde{X}_{H}$ of a hanging sphere spectrum, coincidence between whisker and lasso topologies occurs under specific homological and homotopical requirements. This study expands upon their results, giving a complete requirement for when this coincidence occurs in terms of $\tilde{X}_{H}$'s coherent homotopy groups.

The current challenge in motion planning is being addressed with a range of novel, learning-based techniques.  Standard motion planning methods typically produce the most efficient paths, whereas previous reinforcement learning (RL) based approaches often fall short in optimality.  However, recent RL methodologies for motion planning that leverage graph learning have fallen short of extracting critical structural information.  To bridge this gap, we propose Graph Reinforcement Learning with Path Structure Learning (GRPL), a graph-based model designed to extract and learn essential structural learner from training data.  GRPL constructs a search graph using actual motion planning training data to differentiate short, efficient paths from less optimal ones.  We develop a specialized graph learning model to extract structural features, and employ self-supervised contrastive learning to separate these features into distinct categories, thus enabling the creation of diverse and informative datasets for RL training.  By leveraging this model, we can train an optimal policy that surpasses the effectiveness of prior RL methods.  Experimental results demonstrate the GRPL's ability to generate more realistic and diverse motion plans, while its resulting policy exhibits significant improvements in sample efficiency, as compared to the state-of-the-art RL baselines.

Our study focuses on the role of two mass inflow processes in growing central black holes and initiating their outbreaks.  These processes involve Eddington-type gas disk accretion, which we modelled using radiative transfer simulations, as well as tidal disruption of compact objects by sinking black holes.  These models were run in the context of dynamical simulations of galaxy formation.  These formed galaxies, consisting of stars and gas, sank into a dark matter halo within a cosmological box.  These simulations included detailed star and gas dynamics.  We found that Eddington-type accretion provides a minor contribution to black hole growth due to inefficient gas funnelling by hot gas.  However, we discovered that object sinking significantly contributes to the mass of central black holes, particularly in gas-rich environments.  Both processes track the galaxy's bulge mass to predict the central black hole mass.  We propose that black hole seeding by dark holes or neutron stars rather than gas is the key factor for our model's alignment with observational data on black hole mass growth in the early universe.

To enhance classification outcomes, uncertainty estimation is an indispensable component of deep learning models. By integrating uncertainty quantification techniques, we can ascertain which network components contribute most significantly to the overall result, thereby allowing for the correction or removal of erroneous features. This approach can ultimately lead to improved classification accuracy and efficiency.

The dissemination of unpublished unpapers, such as preprints and working papers, is a significant issue in today's digital age. To better understand the validity of these resources and their contribution to non-classical scholarly output, we conducted an analysis of the papers, authors, and institutions associated with preprints. To do this, we created the Preprint Attention Network (PAN), a graph that connects preprints based on shared citations, and then conducted a meta-analysis comparing the speed and impact of preprinted versus non-preprinted research in terms of publication and citation. The preprint graph consisted of 452,402 preprints, 16 million author nodes, and 22 million institution nodes. The analysis focused on six disciplines - computer science, economics, physics, mathematics, chemistry, and biology - spanning over two decades. We found that preprints increased the speed at which research was published by an average of 4.4 months across all disciplines, but preprinted research received approximately 10% fewer citations over three years compared to non-preprinted research. Notably, authors who published preprints needed to compensate with significantly more non-preprinted research to reach the same citation levels as their non-preprinted counterparts. Both institutions and collaborations involving multiple authors benefited similarly from the positive (in terms of speed) and negative (in terms of impact) effects of preprints.

LabQuest is open-source, cross-platform software that's widely used in educational and research settings for collecting and analyzing data, as well as managing related data. Our collaboration with the Ingenuity Trust has enabled us to implement continuous improvement initiatives, including integrating automation and electronic documentation features. These advancements have streamlined data management processes, as evidenced by the development of predefined templates, batch processing, and electronic sign-off systems that minimize human error. We have also introduced novel functionalities, such as cloud-based data storage, real-time precision tools, and code version control, that can be leverage by other users. In addition, our focus on open-source values, as well as the use of modern web technologies, has made our software easily customizable and extendable, allowing other users to implement similar advancements in their own data collection and management processes.

To accelerate the development of advanced materials for specific purposes, it is crucial to master the process of designing materials with the desired structure and performance characteristics. Researchers in computational material science are investing significant effort in developing innovative methods that utilize machine and AI learning techniques. These technologies have the potential to significantly reduce the time and cost associated with developing new materials. Currently, machine learning methods excel in predicting a new class of phase formations and the mechanical properties of materials, but they require substantial amounts of training data, which can be time-consuming and resource-intensive using traditional experimental and simulation techniques. In contrast, AI-powered generative models have made remarkable progress in data-scarce scenarios, primarily due to their ability to supplement existing data and even create artificial data to replace traditional methods. In this review, we examine the recent breakthroughs in AI learning approaches, focusing on their ability to predict phase formations and the mechanical properties of materials, followed by an analysis of their strengths, limitations, and proposed solutions.

Using the Dyson-Schwinger equations in a covariant gauge, we've developed a systematic method for calculating the one-loop vertex corrections involving the $T_{cc}^{+\,+}$ charmonium-baryon decay. This method was applied to $T_{cc}^{+\,+}$ decay into the $J/\psi p$ state, taking into account the effects of final state interactions for $T_{cc}^{+\,+}D$ and $T_{cc}^{+\,+}D^*$ processes, as well as the influence of weak transitions from $B_c^{+\,+}$ and ${T'}_{cc}^{+\,+}$ pseudo-bound states. The calculated one-loop corrections demonstrate that a gauge-dependent contribution on the order of 10% exists for $T_{cc}^{+\,+}D$ and $T_{cc}^{+\,+}D^*$ processes, indicating final state interactions are present and should be included. The influence of $B_c^{+\,+}$ and ${T'}_{cc}^{+\,+}$ pseudo-bound state weak transitions is relatively minor, amounting to less than 10^{-2} for the $T_{cc}^{+\,+}J/\psi$ vertex.
