In a novel fusion of networking and machine learning, researchers employ vehicle-based network emulation to collect realistic data and share it, fostering a federated learning environment for privacy-preserving collaboration. This paper investigates the potential benefits and limitations of using federated learning for distributed learning of network intrusion detection in a secure and privacy-preserving manner. By utilizing a dataset within a vehicle simulation environment, the authors compare the performance of a traditional network intrusion detection machine learning model with one developed under a federated learning framework. The study demonstrates that federated learning offers a dependable method for sharing data securely, enabling multiple organizations to contribute data without exchanging or combining their datasets. Furthermore, the authors highlight areas for improvement in collecting and managing data under a federated learning approach.

In robotic systems, real-time execution of various tasks is crucial for seamless operation, particularly when dealing with resource constraints and unpredictable environments. Developments in parallel processing technology have provided the foundation for innovative approaches to optimize task scheduling, scheduling which determines the optimal sequence of tasks and schedules which assigns specific tasks to threads for real-time execution. This research introduces an advanced method that modifies existing research suggestions and incorporates an optimization strategy to automate task scheduling with superior results. The proposed strategy Task Execution at Optimal Rate (TEOR) assumes access to all task information, including dependencies, real-time execution performance, and current system status, and seeks to assign specific tasks to free system resources for real-time completion without violating system constraints. TEOR employs a hierarchical tree structure, where root nodes are assigned to free resources, and subsequent levels contain unassigned tasks connected to completed tasks, with uncompleted tasks as inner nodes. Inner nodes' completion times are estimated using previously determined parent nodes' completion times and updated execution times. Based on this information, the method identifies the most promising tree root for assignment to free resources. By considering task workload and system status during scheduling, the approach successfully reduces missing task real-time execution rates and enhances overall system performance and efficiency. The methodology has been implemented in LabVIEW and simulated using the Framework for Simulation of Real-Time Systems time model. Results demonstrate reduced task delays and improved system efficiency and throughput for simulated and actual testing of the LabVIEW time model.

To optimize the performance of KSeTe2 semiconductor devices, it is crucial to minimize interface defects and select gate materials with comparable mobility. This study investigates the electrical properties of thin KSeTe2 layers sandwiched between different gate materials, which are compared to a reference device made of SiO2 and Ta2O5. Notably, a SiO2 substrate yielded higher mobility than a Si substrate due to differences in defect density and the mobility of charge carriers in the native region. Furthermore, the investigation into devices with Al and Au gates revealed significant improvements in mobility when SiO2 was used as a gate, likely due to improved quality of the KSeTe2 layer and its incorporation into the bulk material. This research provides valuable insights into the potential applications of KSeTe2 in semiconductor devices and p-n junctions.

The study investigates the stability of time-dependent synchronization patterns in networks consisting of diverse oscillators with arbitrary connections. Although existing methods can identify stable synchronous states, they fail to account for numerous simultaneous perturbations in cluster parameters. In contrast, a newly developed approach evaluates the impact of these overlapping perturbuations on the overall stability of the synchronization pattern. Specifically, this approach derives critical thresholds for parameter deviations that ensure stability and demonstrates through numerical simulations and theoretical examples that these bounds are achievable in practice.

This research examines the search results generated by a diverse group of popular search engines across Western nations, accessing a total of 22 engines by conducting 10 million searches on three distinct topics. Analyzing the top 10 links produced in each search was performed using both manual analysis and machine learning, aiming to detect instances of Russian interference. Our analysis discovered a conspicuous pattern: one of the major search engines consistently included YouTube in its output results. Furthermore, the content uploaded by a single Russian entity - "Caspian Center" - was present in nearly all search outcomes, often ranking second only to established media outlets. Our data suggests that this entity's content is structured for search engine optimization, significantly outperforming other content in search rankings. Crucially, our analysis demonstrates that this entity's content often presents more extreme narratives than that of reputable news sources, diverging from previously observed patterns of interference that favored more moderate viewpoints.

We've investigated higher-dimensional renormalization group properties of mass-type defects with various monodromy characteristics, using a non-linear renormalization equation for the Beta-function. The results show that with monodromy defects, the Beta-function requires a separate scaling equation, unlike system-wide renormalization. Scaling transformations for momentum and mass must also adjust the defect scale independently. With monodromy defects, the Beta-system remains independent from the mass-system, whereas mass-type defects create an interaction between the two.

We consider an elliptic curve $E$ possessing a $K$-rational point of order 13, where $K$ is the Galois extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ defined by the minimal polynomial of a cubic irrationality. The elliptic curve $E$ is defined over $L$, a field that results from the splitting of the point of order 13 on $E$. As a consequence, $E$ admits a significant structure with respect to both $K$ and $L$, namely, it has points of order 13 defined over $L$ and a point of order 4 defined over $K$. We then investigate the possibilities for the reduction types of such an elliptic curve, leading to the discovery of its Weierstrass equation, which in turn, enables us to find all prime numbers that can be fully covered by the good reduction of these curves.

We examine OpAMP, a distributed variant of subgradient methods, to analyze its convergence in amplitude networks with time-delay. Our prior work, delay-tuned OpAMP, investigated its asymptotic behavior and defined three operational regimes based on local delay: slow, static, and fast. This paper builds on "OpAMP on Potential Networks," which ensured linear convergence for sufficiently small local delay and explored the slow and static regimes' asymptotic behavior. Focusing on the static regime, we demonstrate that, beyond a critical delay threshold, OpAMP converges to its target at a linear rate. Additionally, we explore the impact of inexact gradient evaluation and asymptotically analyze OpAMP's static regime, especially on the boundary where the local delay and stepsize approach zero.

This paper presents a new semi-supervised node classification method based on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) with pseudo-labels. It addresses the limitations of existing GNN semi-supervised methods that utilize pseudo-labels, which can lead to several problems. First, they rely on per-node optimization, hindering parallel processing on large graphs. Second, they expand the training dataset with poorly-labeled nodes, reducing model accuracy. Third, they fail to account for the interdependence of nodes during the pseudo-labeling process. To tackle these issues, we have developed a new approach that integrates these components into a single optimization framework. We introduce the Constrained Dual Decomposition (CDD) algorithm, which relies on two key mechanisms: the first ensures that nodes with high-confidence labels are added to the dataset. The CDD algorithm also employs Lagrange multipliers as soft labels for nodes, with the ability to capture node interdependence when predicting hyper-Lagrange multipliers. The method can run in parallel across tasks and datasets, and has demonstrated improved accuracy over competing methods in the node classification benchmarks.

This research introduces a novel deep learning architecture, "PatchNet", which is both lightweight and accurate for video object detection tasks. By integrating "strongly-supervised semantic segmentation with loose spatial constraints", PatchNet relaxes the strict requirement for precise spatial location in object detection, allowing a network with significantly fewer parameters and operations than MobileNetV2 to achieve the task effectively. Our approach involves using a patch-cropping technique during training and a range of evaluation metrics, and the resulting architecture outperforms models like MobileNetV2 computational-wise while yielding better or comparable results on multiple datasets and conditions.

The discrete time totally asymmetric exclusion process (TASEP) with a finite lattice of size $L$ employs time-dependent boundary occupation probabilities $\alpha$ and $\beta$ at the ends of the lattice. Due to the exclusion principle, the system's global configuration depends entirely on its initial state, which is uncommonly explored experimentally but crucial theoretically. While analyzing equilibrium configurations has been investigated extensively, non-equilibrium scenarios remain under-explored. Our research delves into the tendency of the system's configuration at specific points, given known occupancies at earlier points, which also provides a pathway to study the system's configuration at later points. Our study reveals that for $\alpha = \beta$, equidistant known points converge towards an error pattern consistent with a Gaussian distribution as point count increases, a pattern that applies to various initial conditions and non-equal probabilities cases. Moreover, we demonstrate that the standard deviation in point count grows linearly with distance for equal probabilities but follows a complex, non-easy formula for unequal probabilities.

This study introduces a new model for improving energy systems in networks that combine SWIPT and backhaul communication. The proposed model is based on generalized antenna switching, which uses the same antennas for both data transmission and reception to reduce energy consumption. General antenna switching offers greater flexibility compared to other techniques like beam switching and partial beam switching, making it a valuable contribution to the field. We employ the E-rate of return (ERoR) approach to balance energy consumption and system performance. Two optimization methods are developed to maximize energy efficiency in the access and backhaul links. Numerical results show that the general antenna switching technique outperforms other methods in energy efficiency and can achieve a significant improvement (26%, 40%, and 50%) in the OA, OA-E, and EA cases, respectively.

We present a detailed analytical framework to evaluate SU(N) fermion phases influenced by random transverse fields, encompassing all possible nearest-neighbor fermion interactions up to a specified order of perturbation. Notably, our approach yields second-order findings aligning with prior research and reveals discrepancies with first-order results, also derives fermion interaction coefficients. Furthermore, we demonstrate alignment between our analytical predictions and numerical results via the transfer matrix approach.

To better comprehend and model optomechanical systems, it is essential to establish a basis of widely accepted classical circuit equations, which are frequently used when the optomechanical interaction is intense and the occupation numbers are considerable. This paper delves into the derivation of these fundamental classical model equations, which are typically employed to simulate and model optomechanical experiments. Additionally, it bridges the gap between the classical circuit models and the standard quantum treatment by demonstrating how the circuit models are implicitly quantum-mechanically founded when the optomechanical interaction is intense. Furthermore, it offers a method for constructing classical models from a quantum-mechanical foundation, which also reveals limitations in the applicability of these models, important for the interpretation of experiment results.

The orthogonal polynomials of generalised Freud type for the sextic weight are derived as a specialised case of the graded frustrated q-Jack polynomials, particularly by modifying the generalised Airy weight in sextic form by integrating a potential generalised sextic Freud factor. The resulting formulas for the norm squared and recurrence coefficients are presented in closed form. The outcomes for the recurrence coefficients align with the predicted values derived from the asymptotic relations of the generalised Airy weight, while providing non-zero values for the recurrence coefficient $a_{2n,0}^{(6)}$.

This study examines the influence of distance sensor field of view on the movement of a robotics device that follows walls, specifically looking at how the field of view impacts the robot's track, distance from obstacles, and its movement stability. Data was collected using multiple fields of view, and the movement patterns are analyzed with metrics such as variance, standard deviation, and power spectral density. Results show that increasing the field of view leads to longer cycles and a more consistent distance from walls, with most distance samples falling within the 95% confidence limit, indicating a statistically significant difference and field of view's influence on the robot's movement.

In the context of perturbative algebraistic quantum field theory, a causal disjointness relation is established between algebras tied to spacetime regions, underpinning the framework. The interaction's properties are defined in a way that maintains the causality principle, thus aligning with the causality principle itself. The compatibility of this approach with unitary automorphisms, specifically those representing plane waves, is analyzed, highlighting that while some level of compatibility is achievable, others result in a complete breakdown. A similar tension arises with regard to the reliance on a specific Cauchy surface to define the subalgebras, with this dependency potentially undermining the causality principle in certain scenarios.

Smoke detection during laparoscopic surgery can be challenging, but smoke images are frequently encountered, which can hinder the surgeon's visibility. A key factor in distinguishing smoke from non-smoke images is the low contrast, as smoke causes a gradual reduction in contrast as light passes through smoke particles. Our research proposes an image degradation approach that LapARNet can utilize to learn the mapping between non-smoke and smoke images, leveraging the low contrast feature to facilitate this process. Unlike previous methods, this low contrast feature can be easily extracted without prior knowledge of a smoke source's location. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of the proposed method, demonstrating significant improvement in smoke image classification. Additionally, low contrast laparoscopic images contain sufficient information for the low contrast component of a model to learn from. Through the low contrast feature, low contrast images can be restored to a cleaner state, as if the smoke had not been present.

A new approach to creating robust Molmer-Sorensen gates is developed to improve their resistance against variations in ion position within the chain. The revised pulse sequences maintain the necessary magnetic field strength but distribute Rabi frequencies more evenly across the frequency spectrum. This design significantly minimizes unwanted entanglement buildup with neighboring ions and can be applied to any ion mix by choosing an optimal Rabi frequency scaling and including an extra pulse on the outer edges of the band. The effectiveness of these gates is demonstrated to have very low error rates, including technical, magnetic, and two-photon excitation errors, when using 11 ions. Furthermore, the gates are combined to explore their impact on quantum error correction, particularly the surface code, with the goal of achieving higher survival rates and reduced noise in block codes.

Non-centrosymmetric distortions in perovskites exhibit non-trivial properties.
This research explores the mechanisms behind cation off-centering distortions,
equilibrium sizes, and non-centrosymmetric structures using first-principles calculations on
BaTiO3 and KBaTiO3. Equilibrium volumes and larger A cations promote B cations
off-centering. Both KBaTiO3 and BaTiO3 show B cations displaced from the center,
with origins in non-centrosymmetric local energy profiles. Despite similarities,
restoring B cation off-centering poses an impossible task through hydrostatic pressure, while it might be achievable via strain engineering.

We introduce a new class of conditional independent processes that can be used to build a detailed model of data, with time varying parameters and dependencies. These processes can be used build independent scalar times series, multivariate times series and functional data models, with flexible structure and dependency. We derive analytical marginal distributions and show the method can be applied to markov processes, making it suitable for use in Bayesian analysis and providing efficient convergence. We apply this method, utilizing the PyMC3 platform, to create a dependent model for multiple times series, predicting future values and demonstrating its effectiveness on synthetic and real data.

We analyze the capacity of short-range 1D variational quantum algorithms to accurately compute the ground state properties of 1D harmonic oscillators and Mason's model. By combining these variational quantum algorithms with short-range cluster transformations, our results reveal that recurrent patterns in quantum circuits can efficiently enhance the ground state representation, allowing quantum processors to achieve high computation precision, regardless of system size. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that a moderate number of variational parameters, coupled with a well-optimized initial state, may be sufficient to obtain precise results, potentially lowering the quantum resource requirements. Crucially, our research suggests that these cluster-transformed algorithms could achieve comparable accuracy to state-of-the-art techniques, like the variational quantum eigensolver and tensor network methods, suggesting a notable gain from the utilization of similar circuit patterns to complex tensor network structures.

The Generalized Chebyshev method, first described by Spall in 2014, is a robust direct search approach for both unconstrained and constrained singly-constrained problems. This study delves into the average-case performance of its unconstrained variant, utilizing Wedin's framework from 1971. By doing so, it reveals that GC outperforms classical optimization algorithms such as gradient descent and conjugate gradient in average-case scenarios. Furthermore, an improved estimate of the average condition number is obtained, which is better than the standard estimate found in Ipolyvi-Zelkovitz's research from 2019.

Moiré heterostructures exhibit exciting optical properties due to their unique ability to form coherent layers and manipulate light. Research has focused on understanding the light-matter interaction, particularly the role of excitons, in these structures. Studies have shown that interlayer excitons can be bound and their binding energy can significantly impact the light absorption and emission in moiré superlattices. To explore this, we investigated the light-matter interaction in twisted double heterostructures and found that studying the density functional theory of interlayer excitons is crucial for accurate predictions. Our results indicate that considering interlayer exciton binding is necessary for accurate light-matter interaction simulations and that the light absorption and emission in moiré superlattices can be significantly affected by the interlayer exciton binding energy.

We propose an innovative adaptive probabilistic data association (PDA) estimator for mobile agencies utilizing range-based measurements of a target object. This algorithm is designed to effectively handle outlying measurements, enhancing position estimation in varying dynamic conditions. By evaluating measurement reliability, it admits or rejects data points, thereby improving accuracy. The proposed algorithm can operate independently of traffic signals, as it assesses the validity of measurements before use. Its effectiveness is demonstrated through simulations, which show enhanced target object localization and adaptability to varying signal reliability.

The LHCb collaboration, in combination with ATLAS, CMS, and LHCb, has performed a detailed analysis of the production of heavy vector bosons WW, WZ, ZZ, and their corresponding backgrounds. Using 150 fb^-1 of data collected at 13 TeV, the researchers studied WW and WZ decays into lepton-plus-neutrino systems, and then analyzed the joint helicity fractions of the W and Z bosons. The findings for WW decays showed a minor discrepancy with the Standard Model predictions, while the WZ data aligned with expected values. Additionally, the study obtained the first joint angular distributions of WW and WZ decays into pairs of electrons or muons, and found that the observed distributions matched expected patterns. Furthermore, the analysis allowed for the derivation of new constraints on anomalous trilinear gauge couplings, specifically a combination of two specific couplings. The results revealed that this particular combination of anomalous couplings is significantly smaller than individually assessed in previous studies.

We develop a first-order formalism for three-dimensional Yang-Mills theory, demonstrating that the theory's equations can be interpreted as constraints on spin connection and gauge field when gauge and Lorentz gauge are satisfied. The theory's dynamical variable is identified as the dual of the spin connection, with spin as the sole source. Notably, the theory has no propagating degrees of freedom in the absence of matter, as indicated by the vanishing of the Cotton tensor, with the condition $F_{\mu\nu}=0$ representing the theory's vacuum in the first-order framework.

A new concept, called an orthomodular space, is proposed, establishing a one-to-one correspondence with orthomodular lattices and many-body quantum physics' algebraic framework. Originating from the idea of orthomodular frames, this equivalence enables a topological representation of orthomodular lattices. Additionally, it facilitates a method for approximating quantum systems by one that can be fully observed, concurring with a suggestion by Malicet and Ruviloš. Furthermore, it is found that irreducible equivalence relations yield simple topological spaces.

In this paper, we explore the application of neural network-based synthesized proof formats, such as those from the Lean theorem prover, in streamlining the code review process. While currently, reviewing generated code is the primary method, our approach leverages the theorems and lemmas proven as side effects to achieve several objectives. Firstly, we demonstrate the theoretical benefits of using generated code in reviews, covering side effects, logical dependencies, and potential reviewer strategies. Secondly, we employ these side effects to automatically validate changes, effectively reversing the impact of code modifications and nullifying insertions. Thirdly, we utilize these side effects to facilitate interactive review and enhance understanding of the underlying proofs.

We apply Watson's formula, as well as previous developments by Soundararajan and Harper, to calculate higher moments, specifically the 4k-th moment, across a sparse family of L-functions. Their work expressed the (k=1) moment as the average of known zeta function values, but for higher orders (k>1), the problem is more complex due to the lack of a clear interpretation for $(L(\tfrac{1}{2},f))^{4k}$ as a product of simpler terms. By factorizing $(L(\tfrac{1}{2},f))^{4k}$ into more manageable components, including the original k=1 case, we establish a pathway to understanding this moment. Building upon this pathway, we construct a zeta function-based expression for the 4k-th moment, contingent on specific properties of the sparse family in question. Our work also identifies an obstruction to achieving the largest possible moment magnitude. Examples, including the family of Genus curves, sound out the possibility of achieving this obstruction. Furthermore, we explore how their work addresses palindromic and anti-palindromic local polynomial coefficients, extending this exploration to palindromic coefficients and examining its implications on numerical computations.

Interior point methods are a widely accepted class of algorithms used to solve complex optimization problems, including those that are convex or can be reformulated as such.  To enhance computational efficiency, our proposed variant of the interior point method, its distributed form and a specific application in optimizing communication costs, incorporates an innovative feature - early termination of inner iterations.  This is done by initially applying a simpler, Newton-based method until certain criteria are met, thus reducing computational time without compromising final accuracy.  The benefits of this approach are confirmed through tests and also seen in an application involving the decentralization of communication during Q-factorization using an interior point method.

We calculate the three-jet transition function, $A_{g \rightarrow J}^{(3)}(N)$, used in the variable flavor number scheme, and involve the nonperturbive parameter $\langle \bar{q} q \rangle$. This function is essential for determining nonperturbive corrections to three-jet events in $e^+ e^-$ collisions to the order $1/Q^2$. This transition function is related to other processes, including the charge-algebraic moment, $M_{[3]}^{(8)}(N)$$, and the pseudoscalar moment, $M_{5}^{(1)}(N)$, and we examine its connection to these moments.

We have created the AI Incident Database, a comprehensive online resource that aggregates any intelligent system-related error, flaw, or failure identified in literature or publications. This online repository, currently housed at ai-incidents.com and integrated with GitHub, serves as a catalyst for AI development by learning from past mistakes to avoid reproducing similar pitfalls in the future. The database aggregates a broad spectrum of incidents spanning diverse technical architectures, applications, and underlying technologies. This resource is intended for AI developers and is slated for ongoing expansion with the addition of a wealth of information about failures and lessons from history. Our goal is to engage the AI community in identifying new incidents for replication and, by doing so, contribute meaningfully to the field. For insights into how the database can help prevent recurring issues, refer to our related research.

A proposed differential equation, specifically a Ward-Takahashi identity for differentiators, has been thoroughly examined in Yang-Mills theory. It's been shown that the RTD can be explicitly implemented while preserving gauge symmetry for the fundamental representation, specifically for Yang-Mills theory. Furthermore, a successful check has been conducted for the SU(2) group at tree level, supporting the possibility of an all-order implementation. By leveraging RTD, a method to determine Yang-Mills coupling constants is developed, including an derivation of the beta function, and a surprising finding is that the theory exhibits asymptotic freedom, with a positive beta function.

We develop a monitoring approach that can handle scenarios where multiple process requirements must be met simultaneously, even when discrepancies arise during runtime. Our monitoring algorithm ALPO-YMW follows the combined process models of the E-PROBES toolset and adheres to all specifications that haven't been violated thus far. Unlike previous methods which use approximation or ignore potential violations, our algorithm ensures that the monitoring model YMW exactly matches the remaining valid behaviors when no violations have occurred. Additionally, we create a closed-form expression for the combined process models and devise an efficient closed approximation for its inverse, addressing the challenge of generating a model that includes the group of behaviors remaining after a violation has occurred. We implement and test our algorithm on a range of scenarios from the literature.

This text describes a formal system, Proto-Quipper-M, designed for reasoning about quantum circuits within the context of higher-order classical programming. To guarantee compliance with quantum physics principles, such as preventing the duplication of quantum states, Proto-Quipper-M incorporates sophisticated features like recursive functions, randomness generation, and control flow. Proto-Quipper-M achieves this by integrating with the Sequent Calculus for bunched implications and leveraging an indexed monad system based on work by Jacobs and Leinster. This strategic design draws on prior research in quantum circuit verification to streamline the proof process for complex quantum programs.

Investigating random-matrix models offering a clear analytical understanding of the convergence of eigenvalues, we explore how a matrix's finite size impacts their convergence, revealing how these effects scale with the size. Our study examines three specific models—centered, spin-coated, and droved eigenvalue matrices, and evaluates their eigenpositions and spacings, along with the associated level number distribution. Utilizing the percolation threshold's scaled coordinates, we demonstrate the consistency of our results with the universal Gaussian orthogonal and distributed ensemble predictions for standard spacing distributions. Furthermore, we assess the validity of the three models by comparing the standard spacing distributions across different system sizes, with a focus on their finite-size effects. Our research also highlights how these varying degrees of order within the eigenvalue matrix influence and map onto the standard spacing distributions, with an emphasis on the complexity of the droved ensemble, and its correlation with the complex web of interactions within these systems.

Two-mode squeezing can be seen as the most efficient known method for quantum-enhanced sensing of an optical phase, but the benefits gained from this method are limited to a specific type of coupler when using conventional light sources, ultimately canceling out at high levels of squeezing. However, the cancellation can be prevented if the coupling non-reciprocity is introduced. Our research shows that the benefits of two-mode squeezing can be improved to beyond the standard quantum limit when the coupling non-reciprocity is introduced, and the level of non-reciprocity is independent of the level of squeezing. Ultimately, we believe that the coupling non-reciprocity is a viable property for improving the quantum-limited sensitivity of optical phase measurements using two-mode squeezing.

Supercomputers with massive amounts of memory can be better utilized through multiway number partitioning, which balances the workload across them. This is particularly relevant in the overlap-layout-consensus approach to genomic sequence assembly, involving over a trillion overlapping genomic sequences. We present an efficient method utilizing the shared memory architecture of CPU-GPU hybrid supercomputers like the Japanese Fugaku. This approach leverages the power of multiple CPUs and their corresponding GPUs to speed up the overlap graph's largest connected component detection. Additionally, we outline an optimal strategy for using multiple CPUs in sequence assembly.

This research proposes a framework for developing mathematical models of cell populations, centered around a novel version of the delayed logistic equation. This version includes a boundary that integrates past cell death, and we represent it as a partial integro-differential equation. Our work focuses on analyzing the equation with initial value distributions that may cross zero, across a range of spaces for functions of single and multiple variables. Our results show the solution remains non-negative, and it converges to a stable, positive cell density equilibrium. Our approach leverages the equation's boundary values past the boundary of non-negative functions. Our study encompasses relevant spaces of single- and multiple-variable functions and their boundaries, and it highlights the continuity between this framework and the standard delayed logistic equation. Our work also opens doors for high-order finite difference methods to solve the equation, outperforming the limited approach of reflecting past values from the boundary, as often done in models of individual cell dynamics. Our study aims to facilitate the development of numerical methods for the equation, while its boundary structure may find applications in other first-order hyperbolic problems with singular boundaries, such as certain forms of free-boundary problems and models of traffic.

Process monitoring, a critical aspect of controlling point processes, significantly ensures the timely detection of anomalies in various fields such as network diagnostics and medical surveillance. The maximum likelihood ratio and Bayes procedures are commonly employed for process monitoring, though they often fail to maintain a consistent type I error rate due to the dependent nature of posterior and likelihood ratios in point processes. Following Karlin and Rubin's (1955) work, researchers have proposed transforming post-LRT and B procedures based on Isometric Log-Ratio (ILR) transformation, drawing from Normal distribution properties. The transformed methods (T-LRT and T-Bayes) offer a more reliable alternative, guaranteeing a consistent type I error rate. The T-LRT and T-Bayes methods outperform traditional approaches in maintaining type I error rates and exhibit only minor losses in power, while leveraging ILR transformation remains computationally efficient.

The increasing relevance of hybrid quantum devices has prompted a need to accurately model and identify entangled quantum states that drive these systems. Specifically, quantum circuits combining superconductors and ferromagnets may now facilitate the creation of entangled Cooper pairs due to the unique properties of antiferromagnetic exchange fields, which lead to the formation of spin-polarized Cooper pairs. Research into these hybrid quantum connectors has long been a source of controversy, but the introduction of the antiferromagnetic component makes them viable. The antiferromagnetic insulator surface naturally functions as a unique spacer that promotes the entanglement of Cooper pairs. The reduced spin-carrier interaction minimizes the entanglement degradation typically associated with the entangled Cooper pair's spin. The surface of the antiferromagnetic insulator functions as a coherent tunnel junction that couples to both superconductors, resulting in the entanglement of the Cooper pair and their entangled sons, which then drive the hybrid quantum connectors. The entangled Cooper pairs provide an enhanced source of entangled quantum states for the development of entangled quantum circuits and the implementation of the Bell inequality. The entangled Cooper pairs hold potential as a new and improved resource for the development of entangled quantum information and the realization of the Bell inequality.

Investigations into the nuclear shell structure of even-even nickel isotopes near neutron number 40 have yielded valuable insights. However, in the vicinity of neutron number 40, a distinct shift from spherical to deformed shapes is observed in zinc and germanium isotopes, a phenomenon unreported in nickel. To better understand this exception, we conducted a study using the self-consistent Hartree-Fock plus contact pairing model with the density-dependent Serber force, allowing for a comparative analysis of the deformation trends in nickel, zinc, and germanium isotopes. Our findings suggest that while even-even nickel, zinc, and germanium isotopes exhibit similar deformation patterns with varying neutron numbers, the rapid onset of deformation in zinc and germanium, a consequence of the shifted deformation island's boundary, is not present in nickel. Furthermore, we observed a pronounced shape coexistence of spherical and deformed shapes in Ni62 and Ge62, but not in the zinc and germanium isotopes examined.

Machine learning models that adapt to specific problem constraints, known as constrained training, are gaining attention, especially in the context of generating complex distributions. A notable method for this, known as normalizing flows, has seen significant applications in the field of physics. This study enhances the metropolis update algorithm, a standard technique in normalizing flows, by integrating gauge symmetries. We specifically adapt it for U(1) gauge theory, providing a general approach for building gauge-invariant normalizing flows. Our framework can be applied to various models, including U(1) gauge theory, lattice QED and lattice U(1) lattice gauge theory. We illustrate its effectiveness with experiments on the lattice U(1) gauge theory, recovering results consistent with established theories. A notable advantage of our work is the development of normalizing flows that respect gauge symmetries, enabling simplified simulations and more accurate approximations of complex models.

We test the theory that biased approaches are more effective at identifying text conforming to particular syntax. By using a simple character-based model with limited capacity to recognize formatted text with character-level bias, we observe the bias significantly increases the model's accuracy in this context. The bias also encourages the model to make more predictions and reduces random predictions. Moreover, this bias does not negatively impact the model's performance on other tasks, and we examine its effects on biasing during training.

This report presents an analysis of top quark production through the decay channel $t\bar{q}q'$, where $q$ represents a light quark or a gluon, by observing the subsequent breakdown into three jets and one lepton of charge $+\,$ (in combination with one or more additional jets) in ATLAS data. Data was collected at $\sqrt{s}=7$ TeV, totaling $45.1$ fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity. A cross-section measurement of $529 \pm 57$ (stat)$\pm 16$ (syst) pb was determined with an identification efficiency of $98.1\%$, finding consistency with predictions from perturbative quantum chromodynamics at next-to-next-to-leading order.

We utilize the Low Frequency Array Sky Survey (LoTSS) to conduct a study of galaxy angular clustering at an average redshift of 0.76, covering a 10 x 10 square degree area in the ecliptic coordinates. By creating tomographic bins, we investigate the inter-electronic baryon interaction within each of the seven bin sets. Nine estimates of the $w_0c$-cosmology parameters are derived from galaxy pairwise separation and tomographic bin set analysis, ranging from bin 1 to bin 7. We find that the Binned LoTSS estimates closely match the Clustering Large Scale Survey results, while showing increased sensitivity to cosmology due to higher contrast between sources. Our statistical analysis reveals no significant difference between the Binned LoTSS estimates and the standard $\Lambda$CDM cosmology, characterized by $E_{w0,0} = 0$ and $\sigma_8 = 0.81$.

The Lasso, a well-established technique for regularized linear modeling, significantly reduces dimension and improves interpretability. When dealing with high-dimensional binary outcomes, a specific application known as the canonical link Lasso, or Lasso, becomes crucial. Sparse canonical correlation, a related task, also faces challenges with high-dimensional data. In all these cases, a complex mathematical formulation called the high-dimensional rank Lasso arises. Notably, this problem requires solving a concave optimization issue involving many constraints, a computationally demanding task. Existing algorithms, such as those based on coordinate descent or iterative reweighted least squares, suffer from slow convergence or large memory requirements. A previously developed adaptive-sieving-based algorithm demonstrated significant improvements, allowing it to produce accurate results quickly. This paper builds on its success by extending it to address the general rank Lasso problem, a task involving various outcomes, whether continuous or mixed. A key challenge lies in its related dual problem, a task involving many constraints, a memory-intense optimization issue. To overcome this, a revised algorithm utilizes regularized dual decomposition with an adaptive sieving technique. Experiments on synthetic and real data sets indicate its capability to generate rapid solutions, even in the presence of high dimensionality and rank.

Building on a non-strict version of a previous result about the protocol that minimizes the rate of entropy production (with uniqueness up to specific points), we prove (with uniqueness of the optimal protocol) that when a Markovian thermal bath is involved and the protocol begins and ends at equilibrium, the protocol minimizing the rate of entropy production is not always a quasi-static process.

To effectively address climate change, it's crucial to understand and incorporate the environmental impact of various technologies. While research has explored the carbon footprint of AI algorithms, there's a lack of comprehensive methodology for evaluating the environmental impact of AI-driven services. This study presents a novel life cycle assessment framework for AI services, complemented by a mathematical model that relates machine learning training metrics to electricity consumption, derived from cluster sizing and energy density. Additionally, a unique energy consumption metric for dynamical systems, called orbit length, is introduced. Two applications demonstrating how to apply this framework are presented: one comparing different regularization techniques and their impact on the carbon footprint, and another exploring a server efficiency trade-off and its connection to over-parameterization.

Prescriptive Process Monitoring methodologically supports operational decision-making by identifying and analyzing deviations from planned data in real-time. To be effectively applicable to a specific industry, prescriptive process monitoring needs to be context-specific and thus requires verification in real-world environments. Due to the interdisciplinary nature of PPM, validating its four stages - detection, diagnosis, prediction, and suggestion - can be particularly challenging. To overcome these challenges, a comprehensive framework for evaluating PPM suggestions is presented, taking into consideration both its technical feasibility and practical benefits.

Graph packing problems, particularly those involving vertex-disjoint paths, are known for their computational complexity. Although a linear-time algorithm exists to find near-maximal graph packings, obtaining strict upper bounds remains difficult. This paper presents an algorithm with linear runtime that takes a path demand and produces a $(1-\epsilon)$-additive approximation of the maximum number of $k$-length disjoint paths in any given graph.

This study revisits the one-dimensional opinion formation model and explores its
expected final state. One-dimensional dynamics generate societal cliques, where
opinions cluster around fixed values based on the initial system configuration.
Clouds representing clusters expand or contract based on specific factors. In
this work, we demonstrate that these cloud growth and shrinkage patterns adhere
to the laws characteristic of a random walk.

We investigate a recently developed theory of an almost extremal Reissner-Nordstrom black hole that has developed scalar hair from a nearly extremal starting point, and compare it with observations of holographic superconductors. The addition of scalar hair on these black holes leads to unique modifications in their thermodynamic properties, as well as infall dynamics that differ from the standard case without hair. Notably, the standard general relativistic effects of geodesic infall are intensified in the presence of scalar hair, despite the extra scalar field creating an additional scalar potential barrier. We also explore the implications of this new scalar degree of freedom on geodesic instabilities near the black hole's horizon, and find that it actually contributes to stabilizing these instabilities.

Established methods for estimating uncertainty for gene expression levels based on single-cell RNA-sequencing data focus on creating a unified profile for each gene, disregarding information about individual transcript transcripts. In contrast, this paper proposes an approach that preserves nuanced information about each gene by recognizing the connection between different segments of the same transcript. We develop a model that separates the processes involved in transcription, splicing, and transport, to determine how variation in mature mRNA production is affected by underlying transcription dynamics. This new approach leads to a revised definition of gene expression that can be used for quantitative analysis.

High-energy excitation energy of 64Ni has been measured with increased precision, resolving discrepancies in previous studies. This measurement is essential for examining the composition of the neutron N = 40 subshell gap in 64Ni, and also enables a more accurate comparison of monopole interaction effects within the 62Ni nucleus and theoretical models. Additionally, this measurement allows a more precise comparison of the monopole interaction influence between the proton-rich 62Ni and the proton-stable 64Ni nuclei, facilitating a more thorough examination of the shell structure near the N = 40 subshell gap in the 62Ni and 64Ni nuclei and the development of the N = 40 gap. Furthermore, this measurement enables a more accurate comparison of the monopole interaction effect between the proton-rich 62Ni and the proton-stable 64Ni nuclei as well as other nuclei with varying neutron numbers.

A binary linear code's equivalence was previously defined by Brouwer and Neumaier in 1980. A new equivalence definition has been proposed which links codes in a meaningful way via their duals. This new definition is more restrictive than the traditional one and leads to a question: under what conditions are two codes equivalent if their duals are? While the answer is known for codes whose length is prime or 6, a general proof remains an open problem. Assuming a answer to this open question, it can be shown that the distribution of code distributions is stable. A number-theoretic formula was also found to confirm this result for codes with lengths that are prime or equal to 6.

We are exploring how to improve Bucket Elimination, a well-known algorithm used for processing intricate mathematical calculations, by applying principles of circuit complexity. Bounded Circuits are an established framework for restricting the size and complexity of computation, and our goal is to understand how this framework can be applied to BEE and benefit optimization and inference tasks.

Our analysis reveals that the most complex computation involving exponential values can be modeled as a circuit with a depth equivalent to the number of variables in the problem and width proportional to the largest group of variables analyzed by the algorithm. We show that by leveraging 'lax arithmetic', a circuit compiler can expand this computation into an equivalent but more efficient circuit, which may have wider widths but smaller depth.

This insight has two significant implications. Firstly, it allows us to establish a lower bound on the efficiency of each analysis performed by the algorithm. Secondly, it relates each analysis to the computational challenge of determining the existence of solutions in certain types of circuits, and our understanding of this challenge can help accelerate the computation. Based on this connection, we develop a simplified version of the algorithm that terminates earlier than the traditional method, and experimental results indicate that this simplified version achieves comparable performance.

To test the capabilities of different systems, we developed a complex task that requires integrating information from multiple sources: multiple cameras, sensors measuring air displacement, and a database of 3D object shapes. Essentially, we aim to track the path of moving objects that are out of view, using only the air flow data, to identify their current positions. This is combined with visual data from multiple sources, combined with a 3D shape database, under the assumption that we know the objects' initial positions. Ultimately, we aim to guide an agent to interact with and manipulate these objects that are moving out of sight.

We designed this task with varying levels of information availability to define a common framework for comparing different systems. Specifically, we compare systems with different sensor setups, and those that use different methods of information processing. 

In terms of system performance, we found that efficient interaction with out-of-sight objects is possible when the information and its processing are taken into account. However, direct observation significantly compromises this effect, which suggests that information integration is a crucial component of visual haptics.

Continuing our investigation into the universality of isotropic jamming, we contrasted jamming transitions in frictionless and friction-bearing systems, via compactified isotropic shear and monotonic compression, respectively. We found that the critical exponents for frictionless isotropic jamming (aw = 0.25 and aeta = 1/3) diverge from those in binary discs under shear (aw = 1/3 and aeta = 0.5). Additionally, the structural order parameter exponent gamma remains consistent across both types of systems, at 11/4. We also discovered that the frictional isotropic jamming transition yields the same critical exponents as its frictionless counterpart.

This study evaluates two advanced models designed to forecast electricity usage, specifically the transformed time series model MS(2)-AR(4) and the autoregressive model, utilizing data from the Eon, one of Germany's leading power consumption markets. We incorporate the Box-Pierce method of arc-sine sine transformation to stabilize the variance in hourly demand, then apply an autoregressive model to the transformed data. We find that the MS(2)-AR(4) model more effectively captures electricity demand dynamics, outperforming the simpler autoregressive model, which, when applied to the transformed series, yields comparable results. Given these findings, the autoregressive model can still provide useful, albeit less accurate than the MS(2)-AR(4) model, forecasts of electricity demand, which we measure using the RMSE, a standard error metric.

Public sector workers should be aware of web search result biases for the benefit of their respective organizations and community policy-making. To address this, we developed and tested a survey to evaluate how public sector professionals understand and use algorithmic bias when interacting with web search results. The study found that these professionals generally recognize search engine biases but their approaches to detecting and mitigating them vary. Although most rely on personal experience, a small fraction employs relevant analytical tools. The findings also reveal differences among professionals from different organizations, with a lack of shared best practices or standard procedures. Ultimately, there is a call for more research and standardization of search result bias detection methods within public sector organizations.

Our research focuses on developing a computer program automatically.
We introduce a novel framework that efficiently creates C functions to execute tasks within specified domains, given the function's header, required outputs, and sample input-output pairs.

The framework is built from a tree-structured program where individual nodes represent partial computations, generated rapidly using a novel 'skeleton construction' technique that incorporates 'wildcards' to fill in details based on user specifications and program constraints.

We've implemented a version of this framework in the system, which performs task selection, component addition, and wildcard refinement. The system successfully locates solutions to test cases, demonstrating its practical utility.

To evaluate our approach, we performed multiple runs on a laptop, comparing the system's output program to that of a human expert, and found our method to be both effective and efficient, producing on average 10 lines of code per second, with an average synthesis time of under a minute, while generating average program lengths of around 20 lines of code, with a small number of parameters, with a reasonable number of program nodes.

Low-dimensional models, commonly known as reduced order models (ROMs), are an integral part of the study of the Earth's climate system. This work provides an in-depth examination of the multiple approaches used to develop low-dimensional models, combining both an educational and comprehensive review perspective. The primary focus is on climate system reduction methods, but related topics such as hyper-reduction, error analysis, and ROM application in turbulence modeling are also discussed. The chapter begins with an exploration of the intrinsic and extrinsic dimensions of complex systems, followed by a detailed exploration of reduction methods, including intrinsic dimensionality reduction techniques, extrinsic dimensionality reduction methods, and ROM enrichment methods. The potential of hyper-reduction in simplifying full-order models (FOMs) is also explored, followed by an intrinsic error analysis. The advantages of hyper-reduction are illustrated through examples of turbulent flow simplification and ROM application in weather forecasting.

Gravitational wave events that trigger neutron or neutron-star/black hole mergers can be anticipated using a neutron star's properties, such as its rotation speed. The fate following a merger, either a neutron or black hole formation, can be determined by these characteristics. Observing the resulting material explosion, called a kilonova, is challenging, but a parabolic grating on a telescope could filter key infrared signals from atomic and nuclear reactions on a timescale of days to a week post-event. The extremely fine selectivity of this tool could help astronomers gather more comprehensive data on these rare cosmic occurrences.

When delivering an X-ray beam, the radiation oncologist faces a challenge of balancing two critical factors: ensuring the beam's precision while avoiding unnecessary exposure to surrounding areas. Intercom systems play a vital role in this process by connecting the radiation oncologist with the radiation therapist, but current intercoms have significant limitations, primarily a short transmission range and substantial latency that hinders clear localization of instructions. To address these limitations, a Bluetooth Low Energy-based auditory spatialization system was designed and tested. By incorporating spatialization techniques, this system enables users to receive and deliver more accurate directional information, effectively acting as an enhanced intercom for use in a treatment room. The system was found to extend the transmission range and improve latency, yielding a performance comparable to or exceeding that of conventional intercom systems. Additionally, users were observed to provide more precise localization of directional information when using the auditory spatialization system, suggesting its potential as a valuable tool to be integrated into medical facilities, such as treatment rooms.

In compositional data analysis, we represent high-dimensional data vectors as elements of a real number space containing zero. In this framework, we apply a logarithmic closed reduction to the data vectors' components after normalizing them by their sum, effectively reducing any composition to a q-dimensional number in the real number space. In ComCo, we apply a circular transformation to the coordinates of these reduced compositions, modeling them as points on the surface of a simple geometric shape. This allows us to extend the use of well-known distance measurement tools, such as Euclidean and Mahalanoban, to measure distances between compositions. In particular, we can use these distances to determine the proximity of a composition to a cluster of compositions or to a distribution of compositions. In our investigation, we examine the geometric aspects of these distances and their relationships to known distances between compositions, as well as their differences from distances between the reduced compositions. This reveals that these reduced compositions maintain certain symmetrical properties within their geometric space. In our findings, we observed that, as the number of coordinates increases, the differences between various distance measures tend to decrease and may disappear, depending on the dimensionality of the reduced composition. This has significant implications for the use of ComCo in data analysis, particularly when dealing with data vectors that have many coordinates. ComCo allows us to perform this analysis directly on the original data vectors, avoiding any information loss that might occur during the reduction process. The current understanding of planet formation through core accretion theory is hindered by its inability to explain how planets achieve rapid and extensive growth. A new approach utilizing the collisions of planetary bodies with gaseous clouds outside the planet-forming disk is presented as a potential mechanism for the early formation of planets. In a series of numerical simulations, the dynamic interaction between nascent planets and gs disks has been analyzed under various parameter combinations. A resulting map of runaway accretion in planetary mass vs radius vs gas disk scale height shows significant overlap with known exoplanet distributions, suggesting its relevance to real-world planet formation. Furthermore, the predicted planet mass distributions derived from this model align with observed exoplanet masses, offering further evidence of its applicability.

A novel work on heuristic-driven reinforcement learning is introduced, which leverages a unique, cap-dependent mind architecture to enhance agent performance. This innovative design endows the agent with a natural capability to infer incomplete state information, identify its own knowledge gaps, remember unobscribed state components, and utilize stored insights to make informed decisions. As a result, the agent can form well-informed predictions from incomplete data, which is critical in scenarios where state information is unaccessible. To facilitate this functionality, a unique dynamic memory structure is provided, which enables the agent to track unobscribed state information and related knowledge. By integrating this multi-cased representation learning, the agent can successfully train in complex environments, even when state information is unaccessible. A series of thorough experiments were conducted and demonstrated the proposed approach's efficacy in diverse complex environments, which outperformed current state-of-the-art methods.

We examine non-resonant dark matter interactions with scalar mediators, and investigate the properties of such mediators, including spin and parity and coupling types. Our analysis is confined to cases where the mediator mass is either significantly lighter or heavier than the dark matter mass. When the mediator is very light or very heavy, and assuming the dark matter acts as its own antiparticle, we find that axial and scalar couplings to nucleons are suppressed due to non-recoiling dark matter interactions. Consequently, we deduce that nuclear recoil experiments are largely insensitive to these cases. We find that dark matter interactions with scalar mediators are only accessible when the mediator mass lies between one hundred MeV and one hundred MeV, and that within the parameter space where this occurs, there can be discrepancies between the detectability of dark matter in nuclear recoil and nuclear emission experiments.

We investigate the structure of geometric varieties associated with nilpotent algebras, where we examine each orbit within these varieties under similarity transformations and focus on their maximal abelian subalgebras. The points representing nilpotent elements in the variety of an algebra $\mathcal{A}$ form a set $\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{A})$, and our investigation involves the components of this set, with each component $\mathcal{C}$ having a similar structure, where we analyze the irreducibility, injectivity of a projection map, and the properties of polynomial functions on $\mathcal{C}$.

Given dimension constraints, dimensions of geometric varieties of nilpotent algebras are presented in our study. 

Additionally, an important open challenge is highlighted, where we need to find the largest dimension of geometric varieties for nilpotent algebras of given dimensions. 

In addition, an intriguing open question is presented, where we need to analyze similarity orbits within the geometric variety of an algebra $\mathcal{A}$, where we determine if all orbits have the same dimension, and if not, identifying the dimensions of the orbits and understanding their relationship with the algebra's structure.

Observed large-scale jets from relativistic speeds are likely to be linked with plasma disturbances in the direction of the jet and at its tip. These plasma disturbances are created and accelerated by processes such as magnetic reconnection and shock interactions with surrounding environments. The resulting radiation from the jet and its surroundings is largely produced by the interaction of the accelerated electrons with the photons from the Cosmic Microwave Background, resulting in the upscattering of these photons to higher energy levels, specifically in the GeV to TeV range, as opposed to the X-ray and GeV range associated with synchrotron and synchrotron self-compton emissions. The most prominent case of this phenomenon is observed in the jet of the quasar 3C 345, where the cosmic microwave photons are accelerated to energies of 1 to 10 TeV. The energy losses of the jet electrons due to the upscattering of CMB photons may even contribute to the observed radiation at the jet's tip and could significantly impact the energy and length of the jet.

This research introduces a novel method for image registration called SIFT-CPD, which combines the CPD algorithm with the feature correspondence established by SIFT to register medical images more effectively. Mismatched point pairs can hinder the CPD algorithm's performance, particularly in images with multiple local minima, but SIFT-CPD improves compatibility by filtering out these cases. Additionally, SIFT-CPD, like the CPD algorithm, utilizes all corresponding points, not just selected landmark points, to reduce the amount of corresponding data required for optimal results. Our experiments demonstrate that SIFT-CPD delivers impressive registrations of CT and MRI scans of brains and spinal columns, even without using landmark corresponding data.

We have obtained comprehensive optical spectroscopic data for the white dwarf binary system SDSS J082239.54$+$304857.19, capturing it at 11661 different time points across 11 years. Our dataset comprises 116 M2/M3 dwarf stars as well as M4/M5 white dwarfs, allowing us to accurately track the system at extremely short intervals of as little 9.1 minutes. Our analysis yielded a best-fit orbital period of 8.74 minutes, which aligns with our observations, as well as mass and mass ratio values of 0.370 and 0.630 respectively. Our detailed elliptical orbit solution revealed an inclination of 89.0, an argument of pericenter of 17.0, and an argument of 84.0, indicating that this particular system possesses the second largest known orbital inclination, as well as the third largest mass ratio among all systems with an entirely eclipsing orbit and white dwarf components.
