To limit the growth in the number of parameters and computational complexity of
a deep learning model, preventing overfitting while accelerating convergence and
optimizing training efficiency, we OOT-Pooling framework unifies several optimal
transport based pooling layers that can be interchangeably used with a neural
network. By formulating each pooling layer as an UOT problem and applying
iterative algorithms, such as the dual ascent method, it is possible to derive
gradient-based updates for the network weights and inputs. Due to the convexity of
the UT problem's objective function, these updates reliably enhance the
performance of the resulting pooling layers. Additionally, by utilizing
regularized UOT with an entropy term, it is possible to generate soft maximum
estimates that prevent overwriting the original input, thus maintaining its
integrity. Our UOT-Pooling framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through
extensive experiments, showcasing its ability to consistently outperform
traditional pooling layers, such as max and average pooling, in terms of
accuracy and efficiency.

We conducted an in-depth study of 166 spiral galaxies from the SDSS, focusing on the alignment of its Seyfert nuclei. By classifying the nuclei into Type 1 and Type 2 based on its spectral features, and considering the galaxy's morphological structure, we examined how these factors affect the orientation of its Seyfert nuclei. Our analysis reveals that galaxies with bulges tend to have Seyfert nuclei aligned with the bulge spiral arms, whereas bulge-less galaxies do not exhibit this alignment. We also found that Type 1 and Type 2 Seyfert nuclei exhibit different nuclear alignments in certain spiral galaxies, but not others. Furthermore, we discovered that Seyfert nuclei located in galaxy inner regions exhibit distinct angular alignments compared to those located in the outer regions, suggesting a potential relationship between environmental conditions and Seyfert nuclei evolution.

This paper examines flat general rotational surfaces in Lorentzian 3-manifolds, focusing on their geometry using the pointwise 1-type Gauss map and providing additional characterizations along with further analysis.

Prior research has highlighted the limitations of relying on ground truth depth for pre-training vision networks. In contrast, our investigation focuses on whether scene geometry prediction could be a more suitable pre-training task for such networks. Specifically, we introduce KipTraining, a pre-training approach based on predicting scene geometry from images. By leveraging the rich information inherent in scenes, KipTraining efficiently trains on a large dataset of 120,000 images and produces representations outperforming those of leading baselines. Our results also demonstrate that only minimal scene annotation is required for these representations to achieve top-tier performance on single-view image restoration.

The introduction of 2D visual tools for displaying time-series data has significantly advanced interpretability for both data creators and consumers.  TCube, a 2D tool for multi-series time data display, has been used to effectively communicate insights in complex time-series datasets, as seen in a article published in 2019. However, utilizing TCube for training other models is impeded by the requirement of aligned data, which is often difficult to obtain. To address this, a new method is presented that generates harmonized data and creates captions to support the annotation process.aligned data and associated captions facilitate the training of a model to extract meaningful information from visual visualizations, and this capability has been demonstrated to successfully train a model to extract information from visual visualizations, and this capability is shown to successfully train of vision-language model, and this is confirmed by the results of a model trained on TCube-generated data that performs better than existing models on multiple tasks.

We have calculated the SMO radius-dependent contributions to the SMO decays $B^0_s\to\mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0\to\mu^+\mu^-$ using the matching conditions imposed by the low-energy effective theory at the top quark mass scale. Our findings demonstrate that these decays are significantly influenced by SMO radius processes. Conversely, the contribution from muon mass to the decay $B^0_s\to\mu^+\mu^-$ is subdominant. Through our analysis, we derive precise predictions for the standard model long-distance contributions, yielding branching ratios of $5.77\times10^{-5}$ and $2.25\times10^{-9}$ for $B^0_s\to\mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0\to\mu^+\mu^-$, respectively. Our findings underscore the necessity of incorporating long-distance effects into theoretical calculations to accurately model the standard model predictions for these rare decays.

The Ising model on a Cayley tree, based on the free magic square group of order two, is analyzed using a symmetry approach. Using the Cayley tree as a graph, the tree's vertices and edges correspond to the group elements in a specific way, which enables the use of group theory to study the Ising model's transfer matrix. This approach results in the model having $4N$ dimension, as opposed to the traditional Ising model where it has $N$ dimension, and also leads to new insights into the model's partition function, which had previously not been explored.

We propose an alternative set of coordinates for the phase space in the 1D + 1D setting, specifically using the logarithmic transformation of momentum, to study hyperbolic equations where the loss of regularity is linked to metric degeneracy. This metric guides the dynamics on the phase space and its relationship with the loss of regularity is explored. With the new coordinates, we can rephrase the hyperbolic equation as an operator acting on a phase space function, effectively capturing the metric-induced loss of derivatives. As a testament to this approach, we rederive the primary result of Alinhac, Gressman, and Szeftel's work on $L^\infty$-norm blowup for the 1D Klein-Gordon equation, demonstrating that its proof mechanisms are comprehensible and that the method for analyzing solution behavior is interchangeable between different frameworks.

This research introduces a novel application of Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks to enhance Japanese word segmentation accuracy. Our approach integrates a conventional Hidden Markov Model (HMM)-based word segmentation system with an LSTM-based model that uses adjacent words as features. By incorporating these additional features, which can provide contextual and morphological insights, our method achieves a significant reduction in segmentation error rate, specifically a 0.2444 improvement in translation error rate on a test set of development movies from the CMU Corpus.

Over two decades, more than 17 million questions have been addressed on Stack Overflow, assisting a vast number of developers by linking to external resources. An examination of nearly 5.5 million posts on Stack Overflow, along with their associated external references, reveals the persistence of less than 2,000 resources across multiple posts. Furthermore, specific categories of educational materials, such as Coursera courses, Udemy, Stripe documentation, Python documentation, General JavaScript documentation, React documentation, Webpack documentation, ESLint documentation, Mocha documentation, and Node.js documentation, collectively account for the majority of shared resources. An analysis also demonstrates the extensive influence of top contributors, whose interventions are overwhelmingly positive, including offering detailed explanations, code illustrations, documentation references, and "MSE" references on the programming question-site, MathOverflow or, more likely, references to similar Stack Overflow questions.

The presence of a stable isothermal core within the central region of a dark matter halo, as initially proposed by recent simulations and observational studies, contradicts the expected cored and NFW corecrown theorems. This study examines the impact of such a core on the variety of galaxy rotation curves. By employing an analytical model and examining the relationship between dark and visible matter ratios, we find that assuming a fixed dark matter to visible matter ratio within the rotational support region leads to the unrealistic outcome of negligible dark matter ratios at larger radii. Consequently, we conclude that the existence of galactic rotation curves with diverse shapes necessitates the separation of dark and visible matter ratios, and we further argue that a dark matter profile with an isothermal core is more compatible with the fundamental principles of gravitational equilibrium than previously assumed.

The climate crisis demands a considerable reduction in $\text{CO}_2$ emissions by 2050, 
which requires a substantial number of individuals to adopt climate-friendly habits. 
However, cloud-point surveys reveal clouded attitudes among people regarding climate change, 
hindering effective communication and progress. 
To encourage climate change mitigation, it is essential to understand how to motivate 
individuals to take action. 
Recent climate values research offers a framework to connect personal values to climate-friendly behaviors. 
However, there is a lack of research exploring the application of these values in shaping climate-friendly behaviors. 
To address this gap, we develop ClimateValue, the world's largest dataset combining climate values and behaviors, 
with over 100,000 LinkedIn profiles, to understand the link between these values and corresponding behaviors. 
ClimateValue contains 100M user value action pairs and 30M user multiple valued action pairs, 
enabling climate value experts to train language models that predict a user's climate-friendly behavior given their values, 
generate relevant action suggestions given their values, or suggest values that explain a user's observed behavior. 
Through ablation studies, we show language models with embedded climate values outperform climate values without embedded behaviors.

NLP researchers have long been interested in developing efficient medical text mining systems, but the limited availability of training data has historically hindered their success. Recent breakthroughs in domain generalization technology have opened up new possibilities for improving performance on datasets with scarce training examples. This study presents a comprehensive evaluation of domain generalization techniques for extracting clinical symptoms from a range of training data. Experiments on the GLASC benchmark reveal that pre-training on small, related datasets can lead to improved symptom recognition performance on unseen data. Specifically, MiniCLIP exhibited exceptional generalization ability across diverse clinical texts, surpassing previous records by over 5%. As a result, mini-scale pre-training is now recognized as the most effective approach for supporting under-trained NLP models in clinical environments.

Recurring neural networks have shown excellent results in autonomous driving tasks by leveraging temporal patterns. However, their effectiveness is often hindered in scenarios that require complete state observability. To overcome this limitation, our study integrates Recurrent Neural Networks with Deep Set structures to improve self-suplearable state estimation from partially observable data. By doing so, we enhance the utilization of available information, leading to more accurateestimates, which in turn allows the RNN-based models to function effectively even when direct access to the state is limited. Our results demonstrate that this approach outperforms existing methods in a wide array of scenarios, paving the way for its application in complex tasks like developing self-sustaining driving policies.

MNNs, consisting of sparsely connected and locally interactive units, present themselves as efficient alternatives to conventional ANN models, with applications across multiple domains including pattern recognition, computer vision, and NLP. However, traditional ANN tools are unsuitable for processing VNNs, which are typically simulated using outdated and resource-intensive algorithms. As a result, training such networks using existing algorithms has often led to subpar performance compared to traditionally dense neural networks. Our innovative approach addresses these challenges by introducing a cutting-edge optimization method that enables effective training of VNNs using state-of-the-art hardware. To begin, we propose encoding neural weights and activations in a quantized format during the forward propagation process, which allows for compatible simulations on modern digital hardware. Next, we propose an optimization method inspired by the BSAM algorithm to efficiently adjust quantized weight matrices. Our optimized method yields remarkable results on four benchmark datasets, with results showing that VNNs can achieve performance on par with traditionally dense ANN models using existing algorithms.

The soft theorems for magnetic fields and the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter in the presence of a magnetic field are discussed, along with magnetic symmetry theorems and an associated conservation law. Unlike previous research that focused on spinless quark models, this work incorporates the effects of spin polarization and quark mass asymmetry, allowing for more accurate modeling of neutron star systems that are magnetars. A comparison is made between this work's results and previous research that did not consider spin polarization. Results show that the equation of state for spin-polarized matter in a magnetic field is softer than that of spinless matter, but only when the magnetic field strength exceeds the strange quark mass, due to matter asymmetry and g_s asymmetry. However, when this asymmetry is absent, a softer equation of state is obtained even for magnetic fields weaker than the strange quark mass, due to spin polarization and a lighter effective strange quark mass.

The Personal Data Alliance (PDA) acts as a secure bridge between individuals and corporations, allowing organizations to access user consented, annotated data while keeping it on user devices. Utilizing these PDA-enabled devices during off-hours efficiently increases computational output by leveraging unused time. To test PDA's performance and scalability, a large-scale personal computation network was built with 266 PDA devices and over 1000 projects, producing more than 1000 times the expected computation using personal devices off-hours, or matching the performance of a powerful supercomputer on hours basis. This article reports on the features and advancements of our PDA system, along with our network's computational results.

We present an innovative, adaptive sampling technique for accelerating numerical calculations of eigenvalues and eigenvectors of Hermitian matrices, incorporating both eigenvalue grouping and the power iteration method. By focusing computational resources on critical points of the objective function, this optimized power iteration integrates the conjugate gradient method and leverages the Chebyshev polynomial basis to accelerate convergence. Evaluation of this method shows that, compared to standard power iteration, our adaptive approach can achieve significant time savings while maintaining comparable numerical results.

We provide a detailed analysis of the measure and Hausdorff dimensions of the survivor sets for all intermediate $\beta$-transformations with non-integer $\beta$-bases. Our findings demonstrate a remarkable connection, showing that these sets are equivalent, with almost every element being a badly approximable number in a non-integer base. As a direct consequence, Hausdorff dimensions of these sets are consistent across all classes. Additionally, our research yields a precise formula to determine the measure of these sets. Our approach also enables us to address long-standing open problems regarding the measure and Hausdorff dimensions of related sets identified by Solomyak, as well as generalize some of his discoveries in new bases. Our study in variable base case reveals significant discrepancies in the resulting Hausdorff dimensions compared to previously established relationships.

We investigate SO(Nc) gauge theories with Nf quark flavors using a Su(NeF)破 Chiral symmetry effective model, focusing on the impact of chiral symmetry on gauge-invariant quark bilinear correlations for Nc = 3,4 and Nf = 2,3. Unlike U(Nf) model, Su(NeF) model includes a Wess-Zumino term and differs in its representation of flavor symmetries. In Su(NeF) model, Nf colors in the fundamental representation map to a half-integer level, breaking the correspondence seen in U(Nf) model. Using a general approach, we express anomalous Wess-Zumino terms through a universal anomaly coefficient and map color flux tubes to a dual scalar field, deriving quantum effects through an anomalous effective action. This action involves a duality transformation involving an external gauge field and reflects the influence of quark confinement and spontaneous chiral symmetry breaking on axial U(1) axions. In addition, our analysis reveals distinct features of Su(NeF) and SO(Nc) flavors from their counterparts in U(Nf) models, including a direct analogy to magnetic monopoles in Type-II string theory.

Explainability is a critical component in the practical implementation of deep learning in science. Recent attempts to tackle the opacity of deep neural networks, such as Disentangled Attribution Maps and Disentangled Attribution Curves, have shown promise in understanding model predictions. However, there is currently a lack of standardised frameworks for analyzing the efficacy of these approaches across different datasets. In this research, we explore the potential of Visual解释ability frameworks to disclose the inner workings of neural networks by applying them to two datasets: one representing the inner workings of neural networks and the other representing the inner workings of neural networks. The results of our analysis on these datasets indicate that Visual解释ability frameworks can effectively reveal the complex relationships within data, such as the inner workings of neural networks.

In the context of federated learning, there has been limited research on a method that can effectively balance functional accuracy and data privacy, particularly in the presence of malicious clients. Current approaches either guarantee accuracy at the expense of accuracy or accuracy while compromising accuracy. Furthermore, these methods often fail to address malicious clients, making them unsuitable for open malicious environments. To address these challenges, this research proposes the FLGuarantee algorithm, an innovative solution that ensures both functional accuracy and data privacy in a distributed learning framework. FLGuarantee extends the GDP guarantee, providing a more robust approach to privacy preservation. Under specific assumptions, this research establishes theoretical bounds on the functional accuracy and privacy of FLGuarantee. Experiment results indicate that FLGuarantee outperforms existing methods in terms of functional accuracy and data privacy, particularly in malicious client settings.

We developed a novel drivers testing solution that enables concurrent access to
multiple drivers, which can facilitate isolated fault detection and aid in
drivers reusability testing. To implement this solution, three key elements are
required: 1) a testbed microcontroller, 2) an abstract driver interface (ADI),
and 3) a driver abstract testbench (ADT). The testbed microcontroller emulates
driver functionality, while the ADI standardizes communication between it and the
ADT. However, there is currently no established method for implementing the ADI.
The ADT verifies the testbed microcontroller's functionality, but again, there is
no widely accepted approach for its implementation. The proposed ADI and ADT were
designed using the Pulse Lightning emulator as the testbed microcontroller and
SystemVerilog for the ADI and UVM for the ADT language-specific implementations.
Initially, specific drivers such as PWM and GPIO are implemented in both the ADT
and the testbed microcontroller, with the ADT eventually expanding its coverage
to a broader range of drivers. The integration of the implemented drivers into a
comprehensive verification environment enabled the successful testing of the
Pulse Lightning emulator.

This study introduces Timeloops, a cutting-edge call graph construction approach that can efficiently build call graphs for programs written in high-level interpreted languages like PHP and JavaScript. By combining this method with machine-call graph learning, call graphs for applications written in these interpreted languages can be built with greater accuracy and at lower costs. Notably, Timeloops excels at call graph building for call sites dynamically generated through reflection in Python, achieving a level of accuracy 3.5 times higher than the current state-of-the-art call graph building approach CallFiGurE. Moreover, both system-call filtering and程序-call graph building can be accomplished with Timeloops.

Single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) datasets contain substantial sparsity, with most measured expressions being zeros. These zeros are a combination of technical failures and biological absences. Current scRNA-seq dimensionality reduction approaches focus on the overall performance of downstream tasks, with only enhanced embedding embeddings being a common outcome. In this study, we present high-performance downstream task embeddings derived from our method, LowRank Separation Model (LRS), employing a neural variable selection algorithm to produce high-quality embeddings. Experimentation with real-world datasets revealed LRS offers significant performance gains over standard dimensionality reduction methods, with classifications in low-dimensional product spaces achieving up to 20% improvement over Euclidean spaces. Furthermore, we observed increased transparency in upstream analyses and reduced sensitivity to downstream hyperparameters with LRS.

For a long time, there has been a debate about whether supermassive black holes are efficiently displaced from the centers of galaxies by surrounding stellar masses, a process known as the "relaxation" mechanism. The efficiency of this relaxation varies significantly based on the star mass distribution, or mass function, near the black hole. We conducted numerical simulations to observe how different mass distributions impact the scattering of low-mass stars by a supermassive black hole. The simulations revealed that a power-law mass distribution leads to the preferential scattering of low-mass stars with negative energy, resulting in the less massive stars being more scattered and developing an adiabatic contraction mass profile over time. In contrast, a log-uniform mass distribution leads to a different scattering pattern, with a specific angular momentum threshold determining whether a low-mass star is more likely to be scattered or not. We also discovered that a supermassive black hole is much less likely to be displaced in the presence of these mass distributions than previously predicted by existing models. The supermassive black hole mass growth and growth history of the host galaxy are likely to be synchronized due to the influence of these mass distributions on the scattering pattern and accretion of low-mass stars by the supermassive black hole.

Model Predictive Control, especially its stochastic variant, offers significant potential for safe and reliable implementation of complex systems under uncertain conditions. However, real-world applications often involve systems with non-linear and non-Gaussian dynamics, posing a major challenge to calculating optimal solutions. As a result, many current approaches rely on approximations, but these often fall short of true optimality, making optimal feedback laws impossible to derive. In this research, we introduce a novel method for implementing stochastic Model Predictive Control that overcomes these limitations, enabling optimal systems to be achieved within a defined framework. We then extend this method to handle nonlinear and constrained systems, providing a model-free strategy that involves characterizing uncertainty for use in policy-driven state feedback. Our approach is demonstrated to be effective when applied to a real-world example of a safe firefighting drone system, showcasing its benefits over traditional methods through simulation.

The primary focus of this paper is to develop efficient commaressive ICA algorithms based on existing full-dimensionality ICA methods, achieving significant reductions in memory usage while maintaining good performance. Two key components are addressed: first, a novel approach to significant element detection in compressed sensing scenarios, utilizing an optimized search strategy within a sorted array; second, the proposed solutions for commaressive ICA require substantial computational resources, which can be mitigated by integrating fast fixed-point implementation of source separation equations and leveraging supporting experimental results. Compared to a conventional GSD algorithm, the proposed commaressive variant commences with reduced complexity under certain conditions and also outperforms another commonly used FASTICA ICA method in terms of both separation quality and memory efficiency.

We examine the difference between two types of evolutionary models that involve competition between species. The first model, known as the symmetric noisy voter model, shows various dynamic behaviors including persistence, where neither species is driven extinct. The second model, which introduces an imbalance between two species and evolves through random fluctuations, produces outcome where extinctions occur. This model exhibits complexity that spans from two possible species outcomes to ten possible patterns in the asymmetric version. A variant of this model, called the asymmetric noisy voter model, is studied through two different interaction mechanisms. These studies reveal significant patterns of symmetry breaking and complex patterns of behavior.

We investigate a vector state defined on the von Neumann algebra, represented as $M^{\\vee}$, the spatial von Neumann algebra associated with an irreducible DHR sector, $\\ve$, on a locally abelian net, $\\mathfrak{A}$, whose endomorphisms originate from charged particles. In scenarios with abelian charge, $M^{\\ve}$ typically exhibits type $\\mathrm{II}_{1}$ matrix algebras. In contrast, when non-abelian charges are involved, the structure of $M^{\\ve}$ can be either more intricate or relatively simple, depending on the state in question. In this study, we establish the conditions under which $M^{\\ve}$ takes on a simple or complex form, specifically in the context of a vacuum state and its associated local algebras, $M(x)$. Notably, for all $x \\in \\mathbb{R}^{2}$, the local algebras, $M(x)$, are shown to have a classification based on their spatial structure, containing either $\\mathrm{II}_{1}$ or $\\mathrm{II}_{\\infty}$ factor von Neumann algebras. In the context of irreducible Doplicher-Roberts sectors, we demonstrate that $M^{\\ve}$ is either a full $M_{d^{2}}(\\mathbb{C})$ or $M_{d^{2}+

A theory is developed to accurately model the dynamics of an optomechanical system that includes feedback, taking into account detection loss, and it's found that simply modeling the feedback force without considering optical output is insufficient, especially in scenarios with high coherence, as the outcome varies significantly. The developed theory is utilized to investigate entanglement generation via measurement-induced wavefunction compression, and the entanglement's resilience to thermal effects in this setting is also examined. It's found that the entanglement resulting from the combined feedback force and feedforward force, as opposed to just the feedback force, exhibits notable coherence. However, the coherence of the entanglement created by the combined effort is reduced when the feedback loop is in place, as opposed to no feedback at all, and this decrease is more pronounced with higher levels of optometrical loss, especially in cases of high entanglement generation rates.

A general method is introduced for creating subtraction terms in QCD and QED at the N$^3$LO level, specifically for the case involving a single point of 3-colinear divergence. Through the computation of loop-splitting operators, which encompass all relevant splitting functions, it becomes possible to derive splitting kernels for the corresponding counterterms, ultimately yielding master integral splitting functions. These are then integrated into splitting PDEs to obtain rapidity splitting kernels for evolved observables. This approach has been verified by calculating 3-body splitting kernels, which are crucial to the NNLO contribution of non-singlet splitting functions.

We adapt and extend two significant theorems from matroid theory: Greenberg's strong approximation theorem and Lewis's covering theorem, both for one-dimensional local rings and generally for Noetherian rings with multiple primes. Additionally, we demonstrate that our approximations remain valid under strong approximation conditions, and we illustrate how to conduct these approximations under specific ring and prime constraints.

In recent years, sundial research has experienced a significant surge, 
driven by an intriguing blend of history and astronomy.  As a result, it has 
gained widespread popularity, particularly in educational settings.  It has been 
estimated that there are over 200 sundials in various parts of the world, 
leading to the classification of sundial enthusiasts as a form of citizen 
scientists.  To date, there is no recorded evidence of sundials existing in 
Indonesia.  The primary goal of this research is to explore the feasibility of 
employing citizen scientists to document and analyze sundials in the 
archipelago.  The outcomes indicate that this approach holds promise and could 
be extended to other similar studies.

The DED2D system, comprising one source and multiple moving users, has been analyzed for simultaneous data and energy transfer. A novel framework called TFIET has been developed to maximize total data and energy delivery, and it has been reformulated as a two-stage convex problem and a series of convex optimization problems. Utilizing the properties of TFIET, the DED2D optimal trajectory and beamwidth planning have been determined, and the source's speed is either prescribed or optimally planned. Four additional strategies under specific constraints have also been proposed and compared through simulations revealing the impact of user position, trajectory, and speed on data and energy delivery performance.

The rise in automation of experimental projects has been particularly noticeable due to the heightened demand for increased telework opportunities.  This work proposes an advanced deep learning based robotic system, featuring complex moving components and fluids.  To address the challenges associated with remote and unassisted experimentation, the researchers present a novel solution for seamless automated setup establishment.  By utilizing pre-recorded video data, the system employs deep pose estimation based algorithms to track the movement of the experiment's distinct elements in real-time.  Furthermore, the authors examine multiple strategies for translating this pose estimation data into control commands and share their findings on each technique's efficiency.  When compared to other deep learning based methods, the proposed solution is found to be both more precise and efficient, as demonstrated by the success rate of automated fluid transfer tasks increasing from 31% without assistance to 64% with assistance.  The increased level of complexity results in more substantial improvements in the final precision.  The researchers attribute these positive outcomes to the reduced latency, increased sample rate utilized during recording, and the removal of human intervention for simplified pose data.

The connection between P and NP is closely tied to Asser's conjecture, which can be proven by demonstrating that its defining class, Spec, of integer sequences from bipartite graphs is in P. A new approach is presented, but it initially applies only to undirected bipartite graphs. By developing new, linear-time algorithms for checking the existence of specific, constrained connected bipartite graphs within input graphs, Spec's complexity can be significantly reduced. These innovative methods rely on novel polynomial-time verification of properties of linear equations with a limited number of variables.

We test various designs of electrostatic phase plates to see how they affect the performance of electron probes, particularly their current density and blockage factor. The type of pixel pattern, size, and spacing, as well as the overall layout, play a significant role in the effectiveness of these phase plates. The layout of the pixels can be altered without affecting the average blockage, which in turn affects current density, causing it to deviate from the expected Gaussian distribution, especially at low energies. This deviation is noticeable in the core of the probe, where the local transmission can reach up to 40% at a 10 micrometer scale, compared to less than 1% for a standard Gaussian core. The variation in local energy is directly linked to the pattern of the pixels, which affects the local probe spectrum.

We introduce a comprehensive theory grounded in categorical quantum computation to examine the fundamental nature of quantum computation, comparing it to the principles underlying universal classical and tensor network computers, who collectively exhaust the scope of efficient Turing-machine-comparable computation. By leveraging the framework, we derive simple yet insightful reasons why quantum computation stands out, Ex: its reliance on multi-controlled gates and its intrinsic connection to tunneling. Furthermore, the framework offers a comprehensive understanding of quantum circuits, including a clear distinction between universal classical and quantum computation. We also apply the framework to provide a fresh perspective on near-term quantum devices and the theoretical connection between quantum computation and error correction.

This study investigates the number of unique locations visited by a simple symmetric random walker within a d or d+1 dimensional space over n steps, as well as the frequency with which the walker visits specific sites within that area. In the count of these locations, we apply a novel method based on the intersection of the walk with hyperplanes, as represented by two-dimensional random walk paths. We use this approach along with Bessel functions to derive the asymptotic frequency with which the main path visits specific sites, as well as to address cases involving transience or recurrence in d dimensions. We also explore the application of this method to analyze the frequency with which the first time the walk visits a new dimension, for each step i from 1 to n, matches a given value.

In the context of quantum gravity, it's proposed that black holes are actually the endpoint of previous objects, as new data from the Event Horizon Telescope provides new insights. We explore an alternative model, a class of wormholes that appear as black holes with specific properties, such as a central core that behaves like a de Sitter space. This core can be interpreted as a quantum gravity remnant, much like the Planckian black hole, with its radius proportional to the Planck length. By applying the redshift effect, the large mass of the hole is transformed into the Planck length. This model, similar to the Thorne structure, allows for a simplified understanding of the hole, as it can be built from these core properties. It is worth noting that this core behaves like a vacuum with positive energy density, which, despite violating the null energy condition, has been observed to exist in de Sitter space. We examine two versions of the model, one that follows Thorne's structure and the other, featuring a Planck length core and linearly growing mass, and analyze their differences. We verify that the null energy condition is violated in both cases, as expected for traversable wormholes. We investigate two ways of averaging the energy of the wormhole, which, due to finite size, results in finite values, and present two possible interpretations of these values. We find that for an Earth-mass object, the null energy density is approximately the Planck length to the sixth power,

In doping a sheet of graphene, we use the renormalized quasiparticle velocity to determine how it affects the Fermi energy, allowing us to investigate its impact on the sheet's thermodynamic properties. Our research focuses on how this velocity influence the quasiparticle density, heat capacity and thermal conductivity, resulting in revised formulas for the heat capacity and thermal conductivity that factor in quasiparticle velocity renormalization. Our computational approach for the renormalized velocity is based on self-consistent quantum field theory, utilizing the diagrammatic method within the Moyal expansion to evaluate quantum corrections. Our results indicate that quantum corrections lower the heat capacity and thermal conductivity, with corrections increasing as doping rises. These findings are compared to experimental data on quasiparticle velocity in graphene and quantum corrected values for the heat capacity and thermal conductivity in doped graphene obtained from previous studies.

A novel end-to-end end-to-end end-to-end end-to-end end-to-end end-to-end end-to-end maskted speech synthesis system, called MaskedSpeech, is developed to improve the naturalness and expressiveness of speech by masking and reconstructing speech features. MaskedSpeech allows for increased control over the synthesis process and produces more authentic and emotionally expressive speech. Unlike traditional methods, MaskedSpeech has no training biases and can reconstruct missing speech features, making it easier to generate speech with desired characteristics. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of MaskedSpeech over existing speech synthesis systems.

High-dimensional classification is a common challenge with potentially catastrophic risks, requiring accurate selection of relevant postoperative variables and preservation of uncertainty. A novel approach is presented that integrates the Elastic-Net with Monte-Carlo Dropout, allowing us to select the optimal subset of postoperative variables and maintain model uncertainties. This method employs cross-validation and a genetic algorithm to identify the best model subset, with Elastic-Net selection applied recursively. Notably, this work is unique in its combination of Model Selection, Elastic-Net selection, and Monte-Carlo Dropout, introducing an innovative approach that differs from traditional applications of Monte-Carlo Dropout in post-training model selection. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this method in variable selection and uncertainty quantification, outperforming state-of-the-art models in calibrated risk estimation.

Deep learning based classification, in general, proves to be susceptible to two forms of attack: traditional adversarial examples and Man-in-the-Middle attacks. While both types can lead to incorrect predictions, they differ in that the former targets direct misclassification, whereas the Man-in-the-Middle attack forces an input to be re-routed to a chosen reroute target. Current defenses against adversarial examples often compromise protection against Man-in-the-Middle attacks, and vice versa. To address this, this research employs reinforcement learning to create defense mechanisms against both types of attack, utilizing a generative adversarial network to create a shared training environment that allows models to learn to reroute malicious inputs and offer protection against adversarial attacks simultaneously. Our approach, evaluated on SNET, CIFAR-10, and Tiny-ImageNet, represents the first effective defense against both Man-in-the-Middle and adversarial attacks.

Recent research has established a link between conspiracy theories and climate change denial, yet the origin of these ideas and their propagation channels remain unclear. Our study shifts the focus to the potential role of specific political entities, centering on the American Conservative media landscape. By applying a network and text-based approach to over 250 conservative media outlets, our data reveals that climate change-related conspiracy theories are predominantly promoted through interconnected clusters of outlets. Notably, these clusters are fueled by content from a small number of key opinion leaders, with Kailo TV emerging as a prominent example. Our findings indicate that these clusters are largely focused on anti-Obama and anti-China narratives, controlled or heavily influenced by Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner. Our results suggest that these conspiracy stories serve as a strategic tool to safeguard these media networks' interconnectedness and preserve their ideological goals.

Between 2012 and 2015, the LHCb experiment conducted searches for dark matter particles crossing the entire LHC run one period, resulting in the detection of significantly fewer dark matter candidates than expected, leading to the observation that any such existence would be in conflict with the standard model's predictions and existing bounds. This finding was particularly notable for the hidden $U(1)$ vector dark matter model, particularly when the dark matter particle's mass fell between 6 and 75 GeV/c$^2$, as it could be entirely disqualified by LHCb data at 95% confidence level. While LHCb's sensitivity is limited to darker matter candidates with masses below 75 GeV/c$^2$, other heavier candidates could still remain undetected, needing the assistance of other experiments like direct detection experiments and future LHC runs for detection.

In a general exangulated category $\mathcal{A}$, we determine a specific requirement that is equivalent to satisfying Serre duality. Additionally, within any exangulated category $\mathcal{E}$ containing $\mathcal{A}$ as a full subcategory with both inclusions (both incoming and outgoing) being zero mappings, we derive a criterion for realising a duality in $\mathcal{E}$ through splittable extensions. This criterion standardises when $\mathcal{E}$ is realisable as a subcategory of a certain category $\xi\mathcal{A}$, previously studied by Jasso.

Individual educational credentials and fields of study are crucial factors in determining labor market success. To address the large information gap regarding optimal educational choices, researchers employ real options valuation models to provide students with the present value of their degree or field of study. Comparing the earnings opportunities associated with various fields of study in Scandinavia, this paper employs a real options model to calculate the present value of completing a program of a specific field at a specific level. The model incorporates features such as the present and future value of earnings, the present and future value of externalities, and real options values to capture the potential to delay, abandon, or expand field-specific employment in the future. Using international survey data from international students in three Scandinavian cities, researchers estimate the international present and future values of externalities, as well as the present value of earning opportunities for various post-secondary programs. When measuring only private returns, engineering programs yield the highest payoff in Norway, followed by medicine, law, and then computer science. Conversely, when private returns are augmented with international students-per-capita, public policy programs offer the highest payoff in Norway, followed by medicine and engineering. A comparative analysis of the model is conducted with real options valuation results from a previous study, which compared returns in Canada, Mexico, and Poland. Moreover, when private returns are combined with program-specific international students-per-capita, average payoff values are similar across countries, suggesting educational programs have comparable international payoffs.
