High-resolution global illumination images are typically computed using ray tracing on high-performance GPU clusters. This process generates images that require hours of processing time. A significant bottleneck in this process is the calculation of shadows, which can be lifted with two-dimensional screen-space methods. However, these methods fail when an object is outside the view frustum or when it's repositioned. This project aims to accelerate path tracing by computing shadows on a set of specialized surfaces known as shadow casters. These surfaces employ machine learning-based compression to reduce memory requirements and are suitable for HDR global illumination images. The number and resolution of these surfaces can be dynamically adjusted to optimize performance without sacrificing visual quality. This approach shows a standard order of magnitude speedup for shadows, translating to a speedup of approximately 10 times the overall rendering pipeline.

The estimation of the covariance matrix of origin-destination (O-D) demand is a crucial component of stochastic traffic assignment. The O-D covariance estimation is based on observed link flows, but this data is typically incomplete as only a subset of origin and destination points can be accessed. Conventional methods employ full flow information for O-D covariance estimation but are受限 by the available data. With rising transportation demand, using full flow data becomes impractical, thus restricting observed data to only source and sink links. To circumvent this limitation, an approach utilizing Lasso regularization is proposed to covariance matrix estimation relying solely on source and sink link flow data. By reducing the estimation error, Lasso regularization aids in covariance matrix O-D modeling and enables stochastic user equilibrium assignment with observed source and sink link flow data.

This analysis focuses on accordions of nonlinear oscillators that are engaged in a synchronized phase, considering both a primary frequency that is consistent across the oscillators and a secondary frequency that varies randomly from oscillator to oscillator. We investigate how certain frequency properties in each oscillator interact with the synchronized phase, which is then modeled as a system where the synchronized phase evolves deterministically in response to frequency settings, with some small disturbances modeled as stochastic noise. We also consider how each oscillator's varying frequency affects the synchronized state, particularly when there are nonlinear frequency properties that are present and absent, respectively. We specifically look at two types of oscillators - one that has a simple, first-order behavior and another that has a more complex, higher-order behavior - to understand how their frequency properties and noise interact with the synchronized phase. We also look at how these factors affect the oscillators' ability to maintain the synchronized state and their resulting movement patterns, known as diffusion coefficients, which are influenced by a combination of frequency settings and stochastic noise.

Two prominent algorithms exist for creating a random uniform spanning tree within an input graph, developed respectively by Wilson and Prim, but their effectiveness heavily depends on the given graph's structure. We have designed a new, integrated algorithm combining the strengths of both approaches, resulting in significantly faster execution times when applied to certain specific graphs. By doing so, it speeds up tree generation for approximately 80% of the DUDL graph collection, an extensive database consisting of 7293 graphs.

We introduce MusicTM-Dataset, a comprehensive collection of multi-modal data that bridges the gap between music representations, facilitating cross-modal retrieval tasks. This new dataset comprises 15 sets, each containing synchronized audio and visual data, arranged across 7 branches of cross-modal retrieval challenges. We establish baseline routines for cross-modal retrieval within each branch and conduct an in-depth analysis, drawing conclusions on the effectiveness of different strategies and methods. The MusicTM-Dataset is now accessible at https://github.com/ghrbe/MusicTM-Dataset.

Visually navigating large datasets of connected data, such as Wikidata, often proves challenging due to data sparsity, relationships, and redundancy. To address this issue, we introduce Ontodia, a visual exploration tool that analyzes ontologies to reveal patterns of data usage, dependencies, and exploratory possibilities among ontology concepts. By incorporating OSModiFy, a model-based visualization explorer, users can navigate through concepts, adjust models, and gain deeper insights into their available data. OSModiFy includes various visualizations, such as dependency and exploration graphs, to facilitate navigation and analysis. Through case studies, we showcase Ontodia's utility in visualizing and examining large datasets, specifically for the Wikidata and EvoBio ontology datasets.

In the one-dimensional cubic Schrödinger equation with obstacle, both stability and instability of traveling dark solitons have been investigated. We have found that for velocities $|s|$ below a critical value, dark solitons are stable and for velocities $|s|$ above a critical value, they are unstable.

A novel, cross-platform Python library Lotse has been developed to assist decision-makers in designing guidance strategies. Built on a guidance simulation framework, Lotse streamlines the process of developing, implementing, and evaluating policies by standardizing the framework. This article details Lotse's architecture and presents use cases for its application. Specifically, Lotse utilizes functional programming principles to simplify its architecture and employs an object-oriented approach to a problem that is traditionally addressed using functional programming techniques.

Achieving a flexible, high-quality nested flux structure in the MFCQ-12 configuration is complicated by the placement of control coils. This study examines how the placement of one additional coil can improve the flexibility and shape of the flux surfaces. Through magnetic field trip time optimization and numerical simulations, it is demonstrated that relocating one coil to a non-axisymmetric wall position can significantly increase the operational window. Specifically, placing the coil at phi = 200 deg expands the adjustable range from a maximum of 40 deg to as much as 80 deg. Furthermore, the corresponding safety beta value is increased by 30%, and minor errors in the magnetic field are reduced by more than an order of magnitude.

A novel temperature-proton frequency shift technique utilizes the natural properties of protons to measure temperature in systems, showcasing applications in research reactors and other environments. By leveraging the temperature dependence of proton resonance frequency at an constant magnetic field, a shift in proton frequency occurs that can be precisely measured and translated into temperature data. This method is being tested in research reactors as a reliable and accurate primary temperature measurement system, with ongoing improvements in analysis techniques. Additionally, it may serve as a valuable research tool, providing high-resolution temperature mapping of materials in research settings.

While experiments in ultracold, mixed atomic-molecular systems are currently not complex enough for theoretical modeling, the possibility exists that future experiments could explore multiple distinct species simultaneously, each potentially forming its own condensate. Theoretically, there is no obstacle to multiple condensates co-existing, and the number of distinct condensates that can form at the same time scales linearly with the number of species for a two-body system. The purpose of this study is to investigate the conditions under which these multiple condensates can in fact form together in time, taking into account the specific requirements for a three-body system. The significant finding is that, although multiple condensates can theoretically form at the same time, the number of distinct condensates the system can support in time is actually unlimited, assuming the interaction parameters are appropriately adjusted for each new addition. This conclusion underscores the importance of specific interaction parameters in achieving simultaneous condensation in multi-component systems, even if the coupling between different species is strong.

Solar flares release energy at unprecedented rates, generating magnetic field line movements at speeds of 1-3 km per second, which induce rapid changes in the solar surface visible as magnetic transients moving at speeds of hundreds of meters per second to over 1 km per second. These transients can be observed in high-resolution images of solar sunspots and bright chromosphores, but their movement is often difficult to track in less favorable conditions due to image stitching and feature migration, resulting in underestimated movement speeds of around 800 meters per second. A case study examining a solar flare on June 7, 2020 reveals that these transients exhibit varying movement patterns, including linear progression, curvature, and branching, and their observed speeds range from hundreds of meters per second to over 1.2 km per second, often accelerating over time, and are likely influenced by the complex topography of the solar surface.

Our reinterpretation of the Madsen-Weiss theorem unveils a direct consequence: 
a connection between the topological field theory associated with closed rel. disc rel. 
point pairs, built upon Madsen-Weiss, and the tautological cohomology ring's properties. 
This revelation paves the way for a novel proof of the tautological ring's generation 
theorem, significant advances in understanding its structural composition.

This study develops a detailed analytical framework for the BDDC method, specifically for nonlinear BDDC solvers. We establish an upper limit on the condition number for the BDDC Newton solver and derive an infinite series formula. Through this research, we show that the BDDC method converges at least linearly, with performance dependent on parameters. Furthermore, we prove that, under the assumption of bounded nonlinearity and for a fixed number of subdomains, the BDDC method ultimately achieves superlinear convergence. Notably, the superlinear convergence rate is also affected by a parameter.

The success of Instagram, Facebook, and Twitter relies heavily on the users' active engagement through content creation and sharing. Grasping and leveraging users' behavior can lead to the development of new mechanisms for content processing and analysis. Our research focuses on tagging systems, exploring how users assign labels to content and the insights these systems provide about user behavior. From one user's perspective, we examine users' evolving interests and perspectives over time, and from an interplay of multiple users' interests, we delve into the dynamics of competing and overlapping interests. Our analysis reveals that users' content tagging systems evolve and adapt, and can be analyzed quantitatively and qualitatively. Our findings illustrate the value of content tagging for content-free social networks and other large-scale systems.

Acoustic metamaterials, built from microscopic rigid units, can be engineered to control sound waves in space, but thermoviscous effects impact their acoustic mass properties, a factor often overlooked in physical design. This work develops a comprehensive model of the thermoviscous-thermally-conductive interaction within chains of spherical and elastic units, leading to an analytical evaluation of the cooling effect, a non-negative outcome. Contrary to expectations, increasing viscosity, thermal conductivity, or unit spacing leads to more significant temperature drops, a trend that becomes even more pronounced in units with damped oscillations, a characteristic essential to designing acoustic materials, but potentially compromised by fluid viscosity and temperature. We examine the viscosities, thermal conductivity, and fluid temperatures that induce oscillatory behavior and offer design guidelines, showcasing the fundamental role of thermoviscous effects in crafting functional, high-performance acoustic metamaterials, with applications in creating non-diffusive sound waves and precision measurement tools.

This research focuses on resolving the global existence and uniqueness of solutions for the FENE dumbbell model with a low-frequency constraint, where the spatial dimension is two or three. Furthermore, we demonstrate enhanced regularity within certain Besov spaces, indicating how the low-frequency constraint affects solution behavior.

To efficiently utilize mobile and integrated access and backhaul (mIAB) connections,
we introduce an optimization technique that maximizes the transmission rates for a cohort of users moving in a unified group.
This involves developing an optimization method that determines the optimal movement trajectory of the group and the optimal distribution of data through the Group Backhaul Network (GN).
The optimization challenge involves vector-valued variables and non-convex functions, and is addressed through a variational mean field approach, breaking it down into smaller, manageable sub-problems, and formulating a corresponding action value function to derive an iterative algorithm for solving the sub-problems.
Analysis and three practical simulations, taking into account real-world migration patterns, demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of the proposed solution.

The effectiveness of machine learning algorithms is highly sensitive to changes in their tuning parameters. Treated as the randomized elements of these parameters, our study explores how stochastic settings interact and performance stabilize across various conditions. By analyzing several widely used machine learning techniques, including hyperopt-tune in combination with various loss functions, random forests, gradient boosting, and neural networks, we visualize the results to infer the presence of distinct optimal settings that support performance stability. These findings imply the existence of effective stochastic tuning settings that yield robust and consistent machine learning performance, and our analysis offers insight into the structure of the underlying parameter space. Ultimately, our research contributes to a broader understanding of the impact that randomized settings have on machine learning performance.

In field quanta courses, the quantization of the electromagnetic field typically begins with the Balmer series for pedagogical simplicity. However, this approach is problematic for two main reasons. Firstly, it requires prior knowledge of the Schr\"{o}dinger equation, which defeats the purpose of introducing quantization through this specific example. Secondly, it implies that matter quantization is infinite, while only the atomic energy states are infinite in number. To address these issues, we have found a hydrogen atom's ground state energy to be equivalent to the lowest frequency Balmer series transition. Based on this equivalence, we utilize the Schr\"{o}dinger equation in existing textbooks' typical electromagnetic field quantization derivations.

To address the inconsistency in reinforcement learning comparisons, we introduce a more practical environment for assessment, named RCW, which is straightforward to implement and can be easily modified to create new versions. The standard comparison of algorithms should occur within multiple instances of the same RCW environment, allowing researchers to ask, "Do these algorithms perform better overall?" by asking, "Do these algorithms succeed more frequently across many different configurations?" We designed the RCW environment based on a real-world curriculum used to develop race car controllers, demonstrating its versatility. Additionally, within our study, we showed that an existing, full-scale RCW RCW environment, representing 216 distinct setups, consistently ranks proven algorithms higher compared to a traditional single fixed environment comparison, which is often subject to significant  luck.

Liger is an innovative Java framework for high-performance parallel machine learning, developed in response to a performance bottleneck within TensorFlow. By addressing the overhead of dynamic graph construction and operation execution, Liger achieves enhanced parallel performance through the integration of a customized compiler and parallel computation pipeline. Moreover, Liger boasts seamless integration of distributed storage, load-balanced data processing using a Data Reduction System, and flexible customization options via shims. Extensive testing on large-scale computing systems has confirmed Liger's superior performance and scalability to hundreds of nodes, as well as its practical feasibility in addressing large-scale machine learning tasks at an industrial level, where we attained a 2$\times$ improvement over baseline methods and experienced up to  $\sim$ $x$8 speedup at 1000 nodes when scaling model size and data parallelism.

Building upon the recent findings of Alazzam, Titi, and Vasseur, our research explores the "Nekrasov–Vanhove" traveling waves that exist in the Navier-Stokes equations under a small perturbation of the Vanishing Viscosiy Limit, particularly near the (2,1,0)-point with a wave profile of y=f(y). It's important to note that this Couette flow is not a solution to the standard Navier-Stokes equations, but rather an essential feature of the Navier-Stokes equations under the perturbation of the Vanishing Viscosiy Limit. Our analysis builds on the essential manifold framework, which was first introduced in the context of the perturbed Navier-Stokes equations in a previous publication by the authors. We also investigate nontrivial traveling waves near the (2,1,0)-point, focusing on cases of low regularity in y, specifically with the help of 1<r<3 being not necessary in our work.

Effective control of polarization plays a crucial role in various applications, such as spintronics, nonlinear optics and communication systems, and its future is projected to have a significant impact on quantum information technologies. The emergence of 2D materials, including graphene, has opened up new possibilities for efficient polarization control due to their unique optical properties. The researchers have identified the polaritons of 2D materials as an exciting area of study for purposes of polarization control, emphasizing the need for innovative solutions for complex and highly integrated systems. One such application for precise polarization control is 2D material-based photonic circuits, which can serve as the building blocks for highly advanced devices, including those used to perform quantum logic operations. The increased density of states and strong light-matter interaction in these photonic circuits amplify the coupling between light and matter, thus requiring effective polarization control for efficient conversion and coupling of free-space light into the circuits. The researchers have developed a new method for controlling polarization using ultra-thin 2D materials, specifically ultra-thin films of WSe2 and MoS2, which not only satisfy the requirements for strong light-matter interaction but also exhibit strong ferromagnetic properties. The team utilized Ferromagnetic 2D materials, including those of WSe2 and MoSe2, to develop a new method for precise polarization control using these materials, which exhibit unique properties of spin-polarized excitons and can perform functions of waveplate and polarization analyzer without an external magnetic field.

This article provides an integrated analysis of two stochastic equations, one being the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang type equation with periodic initial conditions and driving noise in the form of space-time white noise plus a signal, and the other, a related equation with only white noise in the drive, also with periodic initial conditions. It demonstrates the possibility of solving the first equation, where the signal parameter is arbitrary, by utilizing the solution from the second equation, where the signal parameter must be precisely set at a critical value of zero, along with some crucial theoretical results that describe how the two equations interact and develop continuous paths as the remaining parameter approaches the critical value. This approach enables the establishment of strong solutions for the first equation, even when the signal parameter is not at the critical value of zero, due to a combination of two theoretical results, one being a "higher regularity gain estimate" and the other, a "loss of derivative estimate." Moreover, a related equation, a modified version of the second equation but now with driving noise in a different form (colored noise), is also studied under specific parameter constraints and with an arbitrary signal parameter.

This study examines the challenges of analyzing and visualizing COVID-19 related information using public data in South Africa. The problems encountered with local data are illustrated using case examples. The required interactive explorations to understand local COVID-19 information were identified, including rendering available data, combining sources of data, and filtering to filter noise, as documented using data stories. The limitations and issues with the South African government's released data are discussed. The study highlights the need for more detailed records of international travel, test availability, and contact tracing data, as well as the importance of visualizing available data to reduce noise from overcounting and overreporting in national totals, as demonstrated using public data analytics and visualizations with Jupyter notebooks.

Allowing a limited number of components in a subset of integers significantly alters its behavior. For instance, if a subset of integers contains a non-trivial arithmetic progression, it will also contain many arithmetic progressions with at least one component repeated a bounded number of times. This implies that, in any such subset, one can find a multiset arithmetic progression at a frequency of at least a bounded proportion. This concept is explored in the context of sumsets and products. If a set A or B contains a non-trivial arithmetic progression, it will contain multiset arithmetic progressions of the form d1 + ... + dk = d'1 + ... + d'k, where each component in the sequences represents the number of distinct values. These findings hold true for sets of integers, reals, and even transcendental numbers, with the related exponent being dependent on the number of components in the sumsequence.

We propose "Hierarchical Fusion", a novel structure for multi-modal network architecture that optimally integrates information from multiple sources. Research shows that current methods, such as early and intermediate fusion, have limitations in efficiently faking multiple modality networks. In contrast, our study introduces a more effective approach that surpasses their performance. Experimental results confirm the efficacy of this method in visual question answering tasks, specifically with the MS-COCO dataset. The code for our model is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ashwinjainhvd/ hierarchical-fusion.

The COVID-19 outbreak has led to a surge in infections and an explosion in V-shaped forecasts, which have been muddled by conflicting information. The current state of urgency for ICU beds has inspired a data-driven approach to investigate the link between COVID-19 death rates and available ICU capacity. By incorporating dynamics into the infection model, this framework predicts key epidemiological indicators, such as the number of new infections and hospitalised patients, over a range of timeframes. The inclusion of specific features - the ratio of ICU to hospitalised patients - allows for the identification of critical thresholds for ICU admission, facilitating the optimization of resource allocation. The framework is augmented by an economic cost-benefit analysis, incorporating treatment and testing costs to determine the impact of strain-reduction measures on treatment costs and future ICU requirements. Two case studies are used to illustrate its practical value and scalability.

In the analysis of the transmission eigenvalue problem for the acoustic equations, we investigate the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of the differential operator defined as:

$$\displaystyle \begin{cases} -\varDelta u - \big( \theta + 4\alpha N\beta \big) \frac{ | \varvec{x} | ^2}{1+\beta | \varvec{x} |^2} u = \lambda u, & \varvec{x} \in \mathbb{R}^N, \\
\displaystyle \frac{\partial u}{\partial \nu} - \beta \frac{\partial v}{\partial \nu} = \lambda ( \theta \nu + \beta v), & \varvec{x} \in \partial \mathbb{B}, \end{cases}$$

where $\mathbb{B}$ represents the unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^N$ and $\nu$ is the outward normal vector on the boundary of $\mathbb{B}$. Under the assumption of constant medium parameters $\theta$ and $\beta$, and for $N \geq 3$, the eigenfunctions exhibit unique localization patterns around the boundary of $\mathbb{B}$, exhibiting distinct decay rates based on the eigenvalues $\lambda$. Furthermore, the transmission eigenfunctions associated with smaller transmission eigenvalues exhibit stronger boundary localization.

This paper presents a novel utterance representation learning method by leveraging multiple tasks during pre-training, thereby enhancing the quality of the learned representations. A new framework, based on large-scale text conversion models like T5, facilitates multi-task learning by adapting W2W approaches. In this study, we focus on three key tasks: text simplification, translation, and summarization. Experimental results obtained from FALSEWORDS and SEMEVAL-2014 tasks reveal that the proposed method outperforms current benchmarks and notably surpasses a single-task baseline in semantic textual similarity. Notably, the proposed model excels particularly in handling highly similar inputs with minor variations or divergent outputs with minor discrepancies. Notably, the proposed model excels particularly on the SEMEVAL-2014 MRPC task, outperforming the established benchmark by margin of 3.6 points.

The user bundle functor, which plays a crucial role in obstructions and classifications of principal bundles, is now examined when applied to the category of simplicial groups and groups. This study determines the monadic structure within these categories, delving into its action, morphism preservation, and further properties. A detailed comparison is established between the user bundle functor monad and its restriction to user groups, an investigation facilitated by the user exact sequence and a cohomology theory. This cohomology, defined using a 3-cocycle, is explicitly calculated in low dimensions and in general dimensions for specific cases.

The number of subgroups within a given finite group G is denoted as $N_G$. 
This work presents a step towards understanding the scaling of $N_G$ in relation to the group's order, specifically in the context of $N_G$ being sublinear for 'almost all' groups of a given order n, considering an increasing sequence n -> infinity.
This result is built upon a newly introduced space of groups nG, where an increasing sequence of primes p_k, coupled with a further increasing sequence of integers m_k, defines a group for each element n = p_1^{e_1}...p_{k}^{e_k}, by taking an arbitrary tuple (e_1,\dots,e_k) and forming G as an element of nG_{p_1,\dots,p_k}.
Before reaching the stated conclusion, a topological structure is established for nG, and key continuous mappings - specifically the subgroup lattice and group multiplication mappings - are proven for elements of nG, with key properties including the sublinearity of subgroup lattices and openness of group multiplication mappings.
With these tools in hand, the desired result on sublinearity of $N_G$ is then demonstrated.
Finally, the work comments on the significance of the result and contrasts it to known examples of G, where the number of subgroups is superlinear in G's order.

The Lax pair, a system related to the Korteweg-de Vries equation, gave rise to the S^(1,0) (or y-φ) variable, a function dependent on spatial and temporal coordinates. We investigated the behavior of the first temporal and spatial derivatives of this variable by analyzing their respective n-th net points. By applying the scaling transformation, we established the convergence of these net points to the solutions of the Korteweg-de Vries equation. Consequently, we derived the numerical method for solving the Korteweg-de Vries equation, which demonstrated second-order accuracy in both space and time. Furthermore, we specifically examined the convergence of the derivative net points for a solitary wave solution, obtaining an error estimate indicating a second-order error dependence inversely proportional to the square of various parameters.

Visual Relationship Detection is a crucial task in computer vision that focuses on detecting object relationships, but the limited availability of data hinders the optimization of models. A common approach, view proposal sampling, enhances the classification ability by sampling negative proposals. However, it doesn't effectively improve the model's relationship representation. To address this issue, we propose a new strategy called Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling, which improves both the classification and the representation of relationships. By selecting negative samples based on relationship difficulty, our strategy facilitates more effective optimization. Experimental results demonstrate the benefits of our strategy, showcasing significant improvements in the model's performance. Additionally, experiments reveal the connection between view proposal sampling and BNPS, allowing for the simultaneous use of both techniques to yield substantial performance gains, specifically, we achieve 56.6 AP on the VREL++ dataset, setting a new record and outperforming the previous best approach by 2.6 AP.

To implement complex algorithms and secure protocols, it is essential to understand the origin of the remaining quantum properties within an almost-classical quantum system. We show, for the first time, that the quantum properties of a nearly-entangled two-qubit system can be extracted through a strong projective measurement performed on that system, which can be simulated by consecutively performing two strong measurements. However, performing a single weak measurement can also extract the remaining quantum properties, although it necessitates a more extensive amount of consumption. Furthermore, we find that performing consecutive weak measurements consumes less resource than performing a single strong measurement in order to extract the same quantum resource. We also explore various applications, such as resource extraction, quantum alchemy and resource-enhanced tasks in context of our research.

We present a novel social relationship learning model that leverages a graph to track temporal changes in social connections. Unlike previous gate-based graph neural networks that update node attributes over time, our model is designed to update social connections themselves as the time progresses. By employing Gated Recurrent Units, our model can determine when a social connection should be updated, similar to how recurrent GNNs update node attributes. We define and evaluate the model's performance against synthetic data generated from a simple stochastic process, and its performance compares favorably to the ground truth, as well outperforming a gate-less model.

In this work, we propose a novel approach of adaptively sampling nodes and connections in graphs to optimize neural network architectures, resulting in dynamic computation graphs that balance performance and efficiency. By applying this method to successively refined graphs, we can gradually increase complexity, giving us the flexibility to adjust models to the available computational resources at inference time. Additionally, we introduce a multi-objective optimization strategy that can simultaneously address model generalization and efficiency. Experimental outcomes on model compression and 3D molecule design demonstrate the efficacy and versatility of our framework.

This proposal outlines an implementation strategy for Multiple Constant Multiplication (MCM) circuits, building on the molecular model of computation model. By MCM, any constant multiplication $a \cdot x$ can be accurately represented as an expression $a \cdot x + b \cdot \mathit{err}(x)$, where $\mathit{err}(x)$ accounts for inaccuracies introduced during hardware implementation of inexact operations. In this implementation, the model of computation is mapped onto digital logic such that propagation rules for errors are strictly adhered to, allowing for the simultaneous calculation of the product $a \cdot x$ and its associated error term $\mathit{err}(x)$. By exploiting the separation of the error term, this strategy allows for the integration of various optimizations tailored to error-aware systems and facilitates the precision adjustment of the final result through either a direct sum or rounded value of the error term. By Tindara et al.'s analysis, the maximum possible error for any input value's rounded output is given by the sum of the absolute error term, the absolute error in approximating the inexact calculation with a linear function of the error term, and the rounding error in the final result. In general terms, the maximum possible error for any input value's rounded output is expressed as $\mathit{max\_possible\_error} = \mathit{abs\_err} + \mathit{max\_possible\_err\_approx} + \mathit{round

Recent research in quantum machine learning (QDL) has demonstrated promising potential, but current quantum neural networks (QNNs) face significant hurdles. A vital component, the quantum data encoding (QDE) method, is critical for QNN performance, yet existing QDE designs are often limited to simple data mapping or ad-hoc constructions, lacking general applicability. Moreover, optimization of QDE typically involves exhaustive searches over parametric families, which is inefficient and impractical. This study introduces a novel, data-driven quantum variational framework (qVFR) that automates QDE method development for ML problems. Our approach employs a hybrid quantum-classical variational framework, where a quantum variational fractional processor (qVFP) learns complex data patterns. By utilizing CLasso for post-processing and normalizing its outputs, our method ensures stable and accurate results. Experimental evaluations on real-world and synthetic datasets have demonstrated the superiority of qVFR over traditional QDE methods, demonstrating its potential as a universal data mapping strategy for QNNs.

The field of RF technology began in experimental physics, specifically high energy physics, but has since developed specialized RF systems for various applications, including microwave link communications and now, microwave radars, all leveraging recent advances in RF technology.

The High-Luminosity LHC and the Future Circular Collider offer potential at an energy of 100 TeV in proton-proton collisions, and a high-energy muon collider presents distinct challenges and advantages. This report provides an overview of the unique issues and potential of the muon collider, along with the possible development of a high-energy muon collider over the next few decades.

We examine the vector and scalar modes in a relativistic fluid that behaves viscosously and is distinct from equilibrium. Our analysis is centered on second-order relativistic hydrodynamics but also involves some key aspects from non-hydrodynamic modes. This approach allows us to derive universal features that are independent of specific fluid behaviors, which in turn can guide our understanding of the fluid's properties. By focusing on the differences between our findings and those from holographic methods, we are able to identify distinct fluid characteristics. Our fluid model exhibits unique properties such as non-isentropic behavior, which has significant implications for the difference between scalar and vector mode dispersion, as well as vector mode scattering. These findings are then applied to the study of jet ellipticity and sound echos, providing new insights into the study of jet trajectories and sound propagation. Our calculation reveals that this difference in sound travel times is significantly affected by the choice of fluid, allowing us to predict varied outcomes based on the fluid's properties.

The calculation of particle flux and energy radiated by primordial black holes (PBHs) is performed, incorporating their motion through dark matter. When the mass of a PBH is below $10^{15}$ g, their evaporation produces substantial low-energy flux due to the shifting of the Hawking spectrum as a result of their motion. In contrast, their high-energy flux is largely dependent on their initial position within the dark matter density profile. Ultimately, the accumulated energy radiated throughout their lifetime, under certain conditions, is found to be in disagreement with the existing limits on PBHs from gamma-ray telescopes.

This circuit evaluation approach efficiently finds the shortest reverse path through a directed graph, resulting in a simplified minimum spanning tree. By integrating the pipeline architecture of a processor, we have developed a custom reconfigurable architecture, Fast Reverse Path Tree, that significantly accelerates the computation speed and enables simultaneous processing of multiple algorithms. Experimental findings demonstrate a substantial performance improvement, up to 400 times faster than the current state-of-the-art algorithms.

This paper presents an algorithm with linear time complexity, valued CSP solving, applied to complete constraints under minimal quantitative looseness. Additionally, we expand upon recent findings from Bessy, Oudot, and Varghese (2021), revealing that a PTAS exists for valued CSPs generally, provided the crisp constraint framework is valued and valued, and characterising valued constraint frameworks where this PTAS applies in exact terms via a dual criterion.

Previous research on few-shot instance parsing has utilized specific methods such as point-to-tree or detection-to-tree approaches, but these methods rely on a substantial number of annotated trees and often produce inaccurate results when trained with a limited number of annotations. Unlike these methods, our new model, FPIO, is capable of instance parsing with a small number of annotated trees and can learn from a single annotation by directly predicting a graph of parse trees. Building on a existing parser, our model minimizes the number of annotations required and increases parsing accuracy. Experiments on the COCO dataset show that our model outperforms other few-shot parsing methods when trained with 5, 10, or 20 annotations. Moreover, our model excels in the low-number annotation scenarios, achieving comparable accuracy to the state-of-the-art approach trained with 260 annotations.

The proliferation of hyperspectral imaging technologies enables researchers to gather detailed spectral data, which can be leveraged to create labels for various objects and materials. Although SSMC serves as a benchmark for evaluating semantic segmentation, its current dataset lacks the granularity required to assess the labeling effort involved in semantic segmentation. This paper introduces an effort-dependent dataset based on SSMC, applied to the Pavia University, EMEC, and Pavia Area scenes. Each original label in this dataset is manually divided into refined sub-labels, which enhances segmentation precision. Additionally, the paper explores several approaches to automatically refine labels using spectral data, which demonstrates improved results over conventional methods. Furthermore, the paper condenses the sub-labels into two categories - good and bad quality - to evaluate the effectiveness of semi-supervised learning techniques for developing a robust model that relies on limited labeled samples.

The analysis of data from the Kepler and TESS space missions revealed complex patterns in the rotation of star KIC 9267654, which deviated from typical expectations. Although initial examination showed the star had an unusual and irregular rotation profile, further study indicated multiple distinct rotation periods - specifically, rotations every 14.14 and 25.44 days, as well a third component with a period of 2.01 days, which changed significantly between 2009 and 2021. While the cause of this phenomenon remains unclear, plausible explanations include the star having a companion object or it being affected by spot patterns on its surface that evolve over time. Although some previously reported additional stellar activity cycles were found to be inaccurate, this study confirmed the existence of an alternative period of 0.40 days, which had initially been disregarded.

This research presents a modified RAM model for computing positive integer polynomials. The model is similar to the standard RAM model, with a binary representation of integers, and it is capable of handling polynomial integers. By using the most significant bits, the model can transform a comparison instruction into an exact comparison, and it is also efficient in its addition operation, which takes time proportional to the number of bits being added. This design is justified by the model's ability to simulate a digital circuit and its relationship to a Turing machine model, and it is further validated by two important results: the model includes all standard RAM model results and it is efficient enough to include all circuit model results.

Session-based recommendation is gaining popularity due to its diverse applications, but the issue of limited data hinders its success. Current approaches rely on data augmentation to compensate for data shortcomings, but they require significant manual tuning. This work addresses this challenge by integrating self-supervised learning and graph-based representation into session-based recommendation with data augmentation. By leveraging user sessions as a distribution, our method enhances existing augmentation techniques and develops an efficient, self-sufficient data augmentation technique within the graph-based session representation. This approach leads to several benefits, including improved consistency between user sessions, simplified hyperparameter tuning, and the augmented data aligns with real user sessions. The proposed method achieves superior performance on two benchmark datasets, Dailymovie and GroupLens, when compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

This research investigates subfamilies of linear complementary code (LCD) standard arrays for groups of order p^2, focusing on p being a prime number, and presents findings for families of order p^2 and pd^2 where d is any positive integer. By doing so, it demonstrates the ability to generate large sets of standard LCD standard arrays while maintaining the capability to construct codes of varying lengths. The study begins with a detailed analysis of standard subfamilies for LCD standard arrays where the group element g is nilpotent. Subsequently, it develops conditions based on the representation theory of simple groups in order to define subfamilies of linear complementary code (LCD) standard arrays. Additionally, it examines the application of group ring elements to create families of codes with specific properties. Finally, it validates its theoretical findings through a computational example and leverages the established results to generate several codes using the software package GAP.

Infinitesimal cohomology between invariant differential forms on Lie group manifolds determines the stable cohomology of the general linear group in a stable range. Infinitesimal cohomology, however, uses a total differential that ignores the Lie bracket in group multiplication, differing from the actual differential employed in group manifold cohomology. The actual differential used in group manifold cohomology includes information from the Lie bracket. Therefore, a key question arises: Can invariant differential forms serve as a stable approximation of group manifold cohomology classes, even if they fail to represent such classes exactly? The answer lies in investigating how the discrepancy between infinitesimal and real total differential representations affects invariant differential forms. The discrepancy arises due to the interaction between differential forms and the Lie bracket during the total differential application, leading to a "bracket correction" formula. The formula expresses the discrepancy between the invariant differential form's representation of a group manifold cohomology class and its exact representation as a linear combination of wedge products of specific, real 2n-dimensional invariant differential forms represented by infinitesimal differential operators.

Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have shown remarkable success in
object categorization, but their performance typically degrades when their
state is cleared, an issue that plagues the reliability of RNNs. This study
investigates whether auxiliary variables, such as memory, can enhance the
test-time performance of RNNs by evaluating their impact on an RNN-based
object categorization model. Our findings suggest that auxiliary variables,
like the state of long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, provide little to
no additional capacity for the RNN model being optimized. This conclusion
stems from our observation that, when auxiliary variables are incorporated
into the RNN model, the optimization process significantly adapts their
states during training, rendering them an integral part of the model. As such
the RNN's performance remains unaffected when their states are cleared at
test time. This research suggests that failed RNN reliability assessments
may be attributed to optimization artifacts, rendering techniques like state
dumping and external memory unnecessary for RNN-dependent applications like
object categorization.

The skineffect, typically a feature of non-Hermitian systems, has been explored through numerical studies in specific examples. It's been observed that in one-dimensional non-Hermitian chains, such as the extended Hatano-Nelson, the skin effect is influenced significantly by correlations. Furthermore, this effect is amplified when transitioning from open boundary to antiperiodic boundary conditions. Notably, in another non-Hermitian model based on a two-subattice square lattice with unidirectional coupling, a form of symmetry breaking akin to PT symmetry was seen to give rise to the skin effect. The occurrence of the skin effect is also possible when the chemical potential is present within the non-Poincare' symmetric spectrum. The presence of the chemical potential can change the topological properties of the system and thus impact the skin effect. It has further been discovered that while the skin effect is influenced by the system's size and the chemical potential, this influence diminishes at large system sizes.

A newly proposed quaternary Golay complementary array pair based on the cyclic method is described, which significantly increases its length while maintaining low sidelobes. This method expands the maximum feasible length from GCAPs with perfect sidelobes based on cyclic construction. Mathematical justification using the z-transform shows that the proposed construction is limited to lengths that are a multiple of four. Examples of novel quaternary GCAPAs for lengths 7, 10, 13, 19, and 23 are provided. Furthermore, a proof is formulated to demonstrate the existence of biographies for FGCA pairs at these specific lengths. This approach may also be applicable to other quaternary GCAPA pairs with specified sidelobes.

Recent observations from the LHC's 13 TeV data release (95% CL) focused on anomalous interactions between the Higgs boson and vector bosons in a two-to-two process. A total of 111.7 fb^-1 of data from the CMS and ATLAS experiments was analyzed, considering two-lepton and single-lepton final states with high transverse momentum Higgs boson production and extensive forward jet activity. Statistical combinations of ATLAS and CMS results were employed in this analysis. No statistically significant deviation from the standard model was detected. A two-to-two process involving the LHC produced the Higgs boson in a high-transverse-momentum state, followed by its decay into two photons or two weakly coupled bosons, and a significant amount of forward jet activity. In particular, the analysis placed constraints on the Higgs boson's vector boson couplings in an anomalous scenario. The resulting coupling constants were found to be within the range expected from the standard model. The analysis also provided bounds on the Higgs boson's scalar couplings. The findings from the analysis placed constraints on the Higgs boson's vector boson couplings. A combination of the ATLAS and CMS results resulted in the most restrictive bounds on the Higgs boson's vector boson couplings. The findings from the analysis placed constraints on the Higgs boson's scalar couplings as well. The two-to-two process involving the LHC

Change detection using deep learning can be done in a supervised or unsupervised manner, with the unsupervised method requiring less labeled data, although it presents a challenge in design. Our new method, a hybrid approach that integrates autoencures with the differential convolutional method, is trained solely on unsupervised data, yet achieves comparable results to comparable unsupervised methods without employing change detection specific metrics in training.

Building upon the work of Besicovitch from 1954, we have refined his finding that for any given positive integer $h$, there's a constant $c(h)$ such that the maximum size of a set $A$ within the range $[1, N]$ whose complement can be represented as the sum of $h$ elements, each of which is a square, is proportional to $N$ with the proportion being $c(h)$ to the power of $1/3$. This result was first established by Gyuriak, Elekes, and Pach in 2019. Most recently, Bowen, Green, and Wolf in 2021 proved that the constant $c(h)$ is at most $N$ to the power of $-(h-1)/4$ when $h$ is greater than or equal to $4$. Our work provides a new insight and improves upon the aforementioned result to $h^{-1/2}$ and our approach is relatively straightforward, mainly relying on a well-known application of the Besicovitch-Federer covering theorem, as well as a simple bound on the number of ways in which a natural number can be represented as the sum of two squares.

Precise control of Heisenberg spin exchange interaction is vital for developing large-scale spin qubit circuits in silicon. By altering the position of a dopant in a silicon lattice, the distance between heuristically coupled spin qubits can be controlled, specifically, a phosphorus atom displaced by one silicon bond length increases the phosphorus-phosphorus distance from 0.44 to 0.55 nm, yielding an $g$ factor change of about 0.07 and a交换耦合 constant change of about 100 fJ for all studied orientations and magnetic field values, with minimal orientation dependence (<10%). However, the magnitude of the change varies significantly with magnetic field orientation relative to the crystal lattice, ranging from 100% to 15% for a 1T field, offering flexibility in experimental conditions and simplifying the implementation of controlled NOT gates. Three-dimensional structure sensing through electron spin resonance also reveals the dopant's position with high accuracy, ensuring reliable and predictable exchange interactions.

Global optimization plays a vital role in finding the optimal global solution within complex libraries where constraints may not always be present. It enables the trade-off between multiple objective functions by providing a range of feasible solutions. Global optimization has far-reaching applications in scientific research, engineering, data analysis, machine learning, and more. The key methods used in global optimization can be grouped into three main categories: evolution strategies, genetic algorithms, and evolutionary algorithms. To ensure consistency and standardization in benchmarking, the LibOPT software library was developed in C++ under the MIT open-source license, which currently includes 87 benchmarking functions and five problems, all of which can be accessed through an easy-to-use interface. This paper outlines the methodologies, development framework, and accessibility options for LibOPT, as well as its availability on GitHub at https://github.com/libopt/libopt.

We have calculated the transitivity degree in connection graphs of algebraic varieties. For complete linear projection schemes, we established an upper limit on the transitivity degree, which depends on the number of fibers and the maximum degree of the maps. We also proved that the same upper limit applies to certain types of algebraic varieties. Furthermore, we discovered the exact value of the transitivity degree in the case of certain algebraic varieties with specific properties.

The book "Quantum Mechanics and Beers" serves as an innovative supplement to primary teaching materials, featuring original content that complements and expands upon standard educational resources. It adopts an informal, accessible style to facilitate learning and exploration, covering essential topics in quantum physics, from fundamental principles to more sophisticated concepts. To cater to undergraduate and graduate students, as well as physics researchers, the text delves into advanced mathematical frameworks, including the use of tensor algebras to analyze complex quantum systems. The book's unique approach is supported by lighthearted elements, such as quantum mechanics-related jokes, illustrations, and references to popular culture, balancing the seriousness of scientific discourse.

Significant advancements in understanding and simulating the macroscopic two-photon absorption (TPA) process in semiconductors are crucial for simulating TPA behavior in various novel materials. A comprehensive examination of the basic principles underlying the TPA process is conducted, including the investigation of how it occurs, the absorption of multiple photons, the emergence of charge carriers, the evolution of the wave function, the evolution of the density matrix, the carrier relaxation time, the recombination of carriers, the generation of free carriers, the absorption of TPA, the changes in the linear refractive index, the absorption coefficient of TTA, the changes in the linear refractive index of TTA, and the changes in the imaginary part of the dielectric constant of TTA.

Misogynistic content in online spaces has grown in prominence, prompting a need for reliable methods to identify and mitigate it. Prior research has found that large language models (LLMs) possess an inherent capacity to detect text associated with misogyny. However, the root of this capability remains unclear, with speculation suggesting either latched correlations or transfer of knowledge from pre-training. To investigate this, we analyze the misogyny detection abilities of LLMs, focusing on their most influential layers and tokens, which tend to emerge towards the later layers and often relate to contextual keywords like 'women'. Our results indicate that these models rely on key content keywords to make detections, supporting the theory that they utilize both their parameterized knowledge and input content. Furthermore, the performance of our most advanced models approaches, and in a few cases, surpasses, the state of the art, achieved through human annotation or machine learning, with our current record standing at an F1 score of 0.876.

This research focuses on the existence and uniqueness of solutions to a novel backward stochastic differential equation that includes past values in its generator. The generator is assumed to be dependent on a delayed time interval and possibly unbounded in a local sense. The analysis builds on key concepts from a stochastic differential equation that accounts for initial path information. The results are particularly relevant to the study of backward stochastic differential equations with delays, which often come from the random horizon optimal stopping problems associated with a geometric Brownian motion.

Reinforcement learning achieves exceptional performance in robotics control, yet its operational limits are largely unknown and difficult to predict. To address this issue, we developed a planning-based learning method that incorporates lower bounds on likelihood noise within the dynamics model, thereby enhancing the robustness of the resulting control policies. By integrating this constraint into the learning process, our approach significantly reduces the risk of encountering unrealistic outcomes, thereby enhancing the overall system robustness. Empirical testing within a learned dynamics framework, specifically using Soft Actor-Critic, demonstrates the robustness benefits of our constraint-enforcing method, specifically its ability to accurately estimate operational limits and remain resilient to perturbations in the environment. Furthermore, our constraint facilitates more precise estimation of operational limits and yields robust planners capable of consistently meeting task objectives, resulting in improved reliability and functionality.

A recent approach to solving the Kuser N file L demand problem, known as coded caching, has garnered significant interest due to its ability to reduce traffic load. In this paper, we introduce a novel strategy to design coding schemes for this problem. Our strategy establishes a connection between coding schemes and a class of upper triangular zero-one matrices with specific properties, referred to as combinatorial objects. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that various existing coding schemes fall under this framework. Leveraging this approach, we derive new, outperforming schemes by modifying these matrices while preserving key properties. As an example, we propose an innovative caching scheme that surpasses the existing best standard in terms of transmission efficiency.

This study proposes a constructive and predicative framework for reasoning about the meaning of programming languages. Our approach builds on the SCOTT model, an interpretation of predicative dependent type theory introduced by Miquel. By applying higher-order abstract syntax, we achieve a predicative and consistent model while maintaining the ability to discuss specific languages with rich type systems, similar to those found in Coq or Lean. Our work specifically examines the Scott model for predicative dependent type theory with features such as hax and universe polymorphism.

A detailed examination of the coefficients of degenerate Eisenstein series for Hecke
groups is provided in this paper. It involves analyzing certain symmetries related
to Weyl group components and involves central values of these series. This analysis
enables us to establish combinatorial formulas for Hecke operators that act on the
degenerate Eisenstein series. Ultimately, we obtain explicit series expressions
for Hecke operators acting on these specific Eisenstein series.

Current conflict resolution methods for mobile robots primarily rely on local distance thresholds, disregarding the robot's spatial layout. This research proposes a novel approach that integrates the specific geometry of a mobile robot's arm to predict potential collisions more accurately. The proposed strategy is being tested on a robotic arm in an environment with static and dynamic obstacles, employing a combination of A* path planning and dynamic threshold conflict resolution techniques. The project's challenges, including collision detection and avoidance, are addressed through the development of customized algorithms, adapted from existing path planning and collision avoidance methods. By leveraging the robot's unique spatial configuration, the proposed solution achieves more reliable and efficient collision avoidance, demonstrated by simulation results using the Gazebo simulator and ROS framework.

To some extent, NLP can be seen as a response to the inherent ambiguity in human language, which often necessitates translation or interpretation.  However, NLP's goals extend beyond mere translation of spoken and written words to also encompass the synthesis of natural language.  This capability has significant applications beyond simple translation, particularly in fields such as law and medicine where clear and accurate communication can mean the difference between life and death.

The sensitivity of Ramsey interferometry in complex systems has long been a limiting factor, but this constraint can be overcome with the implementation of nonlinear complex-valued quantum gates known as Hadamard gates, which lead to an exponential improvement in the system's phase estimation capabilities, particularly in the presence of technical noise as experienced in Bose-Einstein condensates, effectively doubling the rate at which the system overcomes noise-related limitations known as the Heisenberg limitation with regard to the system's population size, a notable enhancement from the conventional linear approach, which achieves only a scaling that is inversely proportional to the system's population and is limited to quadratic improvements in the system's phase estimation capabilities.

This paper deals with several new value-distribution theories for non-linear differential equations, focusing on the interactions between the images of meromorphic mappings and specific geometric entities, such as hypersurfaces and hyperplanes, within complex projective spaces.

This paper presents an innovative approach that integrates signature-based Gröbner basis algorithms into the calculation of polynomial system solutions. By leveraging this method, we efficiently pre-process the Gröbner basis to accelerate the computation of solution sets, achieving faster evaluation and arithmetic verification rates. We also accelerate the calculation of multiple solutions through the use of the Newton form and a binary interpolation strategy. Experimental results confirm the enhancement of solution-set computation times, and our finding that the chosen signature type has no significant impact on the Gröbner basis size allows us to list the algorithm's solution-computation prerequisites.

A statistical model for describing the rapidity distribution of photons from Cu+Cu collisions is employed. Utilizing the rapidity density of photons from Cu+Cu collisions and the mid-rapidity particle yield in Au+Au collisions, the model is able to determine the rapidity density of baryons. Consequently, ratios of various rapidity densities are calculated: $\overline{{d^2N(p_\gamma)/dy}/d^2N(p)/dy_{\rm Cu}}$, the rapidity density of photons per baryon; the rapidity density of mesons per baryon; the average number of pions per baryon; and the ratio of average pions per baryon in Cu+Cu compared to Au+Au. Consistent with the scaling behavior observed for other particles, the model indicates that the photon-based quantity aligns with the established data, using a size correction factor.

The function exco_2(n,H) represents the maximum number of edges in a 4-uniform hypergraph with n vertices that lacks subgraphs similar to H. Research shows that for certain H sets like {K_4^3,K_4^-}, exco__2(n,H) has specific properties, namely that it's o(n^2) and o(n^(3/2)), respectively. This note provides a correction to part of the research related to K_4^- and presents new findings that maximize the edge bound for another set like {K_4^3,K_4^-_2}.

Rendering geometric shapes like arcs and ellipses poses significant challenges
due to their complex nature. One particular challenge is accurately depicting
arc joins, especially when lines converge or diverge. Traditionally, this has
been approached by approximating arcs with polygonal shapes. Our research
introduces a more effective method by integrating a vertex-based approach
directly into the circular arc renderer, enabling precise and efficient
rendering of arc joins. Our solution outperforms prior polygonal approximations
not only in performance metrics of approximately 0.3% improvement in mean
absolute error with the WAG method) but also in providing a more natural
visualization of arc joins compared to the primary workflow.

This study develops a quasi-interpolation formula based on the novel radius-based function, which maintains convexity and monotonicity, by leveraging its connection to the Lagrange interpolation method and carefully choosing modified basis functions. The effectiveness of this formula is enhanced through the use of optimized parameters and numerical examples that verify its efficiency.

The TeV gamma-ray and positron excesses observed in the galactic center region may be attributed to pulsar halos within 100 parsecs of the galactic center. By calculating the pulsar halos' contribution to gamma-rays using the empirical formula for electron distribution, the calculated gamma-ray emission aligns precisely with observed patterns. By analyzing the contributions of pulsar halos to the galactic gamma-ray emission, the calculated results fit both the gamma-ray and cosmic positron excess observations. Consequently, the hypothesis of pulsar halos is a viable explanation for the observed cosmic positron excess and diffuse TeV gamma-ray emission. By comparing the calculated gamma-ray emission to previous simulations, the maximum effective electron distribution can be determined. By analyzing the pulsar population forecast for the next decade, the actual and anticipated pulsar populations can be compared. The findings indicate that distinguishing the gamma-ray emission caused by pulsar halos from other potential sources will be feasible within the next decade. Therefore, the hypothesis of pulsar halos is a viable explanation for the observed cosmic positron excess and diffuse TeV gamma-ray emission, and it will be further verified through future gamma-ray observations.

This study presents a novel method of enhancing ASONet, previously introduced by Zhang et al., for super pixel delimitation masks as data augmentation for Neural Networks. It employs a region-based approach to create varied pixelated masks, which preserve semantic information while maintaining class attributes, allowing for more comprehensive training and better convolutional neural performance. Complementary training of the network in the original image format alongside these augmented masks has been found to yield significant performance improvements. Computationally, this method offers improvements over traditional pixel-based mask augmentation, particularly for images with numerous classes, by reducing computational demands by up to 80% for 1000-class images. ASOPNet, a modified version of the model, has demonstrated superior performance over the original ASONet, with an 8% increase in accuracy for 10-class images and a 20% increase for 1000-class images when trained with the augmented masks.

This work provides a quantitative evaluation of climate change communication across various platforms, allowing for straightforward comparison of their effectiveness. Initially, we analyze PNAS, Scholarly Communications across multiple channels, and Wikipedia to assess their impact on disseminating climate change messages. We then compare the effectiveness of these avenues with that of policy Papers, general interest science articles, and economic literature. Our findings indicate that policy papers attract more attention from climate change advocates than academic climate change research, and that they reach a broader audience, extending beyond the primary research academic community. However, we also observe that scientific research, general interest science articles, and economic literature maintain a higher level of engagement from climate change advocates compared to policy PNAS, general interest science journals, and economic literature, where the engagement from climate change advocates is relatively lower compared to other segments.

Soft robotic systems are increasingly being studied, but predicting and controlling the dynamics of soft materials remains difficult due to the complexity of their mathematical expressions. Utilizing Koopman operator theory, this research transforms soft robotic systems into linear hybrid models through a combination of physical and data-driven methods. The integration of the two approaches enhances both physical and numerical understanding of the systems. Extensive experiments using a soft robotic actuator validate the new model's accuracy, demonstrating its effectiveness in simplifying the control and optimization of complex soft robotic systems.

Optimization is crucial for machine learning, and the choice of method is a significant decision for researchers. This note discusses an alternative to the Random Karman-Mahavani Method, highlighting its limitations and proposing Natural Gradient Descent, based on Fisher information, as a more efficient option. FG, an implementation of SGD, takes into account the geometry of the parameter space for a faster convergence rate.

Recent findings from the Euclid High Level Working Group 6 (HiWG6) catalog, a collection of high-precision optical data, reveal the spectral characteristics of distant active galactic nuclei (AGNs) up to a redshift of 3. The spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of these HiWG6 AGNs reveal typical broad-peak features, with spectral breaks in the observed light curve. Using machine learning algorithms on the spectral data, we found a strong correlation between machine-learning predicted distances and the traditional measurement, with an improved accuracy at higher redshifts. The application of this measurement to the Euclid catalog indicates that typical Si II absorption, often found in supernovae, is present in most AGNs. Furthermore, we found that features related to this absorption are stronger when the host of a potential supernova exhibits lower star-formation rates.

The time of death prediction for lung cancer patients is of significant value to clinicians. This study introduces a new prediction model, Lite-ProSENet, which is based on the powerful signal encoding capabilities of Transformers but in a more efficient and streamlined manner. By combining a lightweight encoder with a decoder that processes temporal information, the model can achieve high accuracy in predicting survival times while reducing the calculation complexity and data requirements. With this architecture, Lite-ProSENet delivers state-of-the-art performance with an AUC of 0.816, surpassing current methods while demanding fewer computational resources and cleaning less data. Additionally, the model exhibits robust generalization capabilities, effectively reducing the need for exhaustive data annotation.

In various fields, understanding the internal states of agents is crucial for identifying decision-making mechanisms. Current approaches are often opaque despite producing high accuracy, so there is a need for methods that prioritize interpretable state representation. Our solution is LINGUA, a generative language model that creates text-based state representations and agents' decision rationales in complex environments. Utilizing Reinforcement Learning with Natural Language, LINGUA enhances its Rationaling能力和State Representation, resulting in better performance compared to existing models, such as LRL, and enabling more effective communication with users and fellow agents.

Cosmological parameters are inferred from the power spectrum of the cosmic microwave background (CMB), but this is limited by systematic effects, particularly from foreground contamination, which becomes more significant at certain wavelengths. These impacts are more pronounced at higher multipoles ($\ell$), where they surpass those at lower multipoles and even affect the estimation of noise properties. We investigate the effect of foreground contamination on the CMB power spectrum and the associated uncertainty at full angular scales, utilizing the Planck and WMAP data. We model the various components and calculate the power spectrum, comparing it with the observational results. We analyze the spectral index distribution and find that the power spectrum accurately covers the range from $\ell = 2$ to $2200$. We apply Bayesian inference to estimate the cosmological parameters based on the empirical power spectrum and our theoretical model. We employ two noise bias models - one ideal and one more realistic - to assess their influence on parameter estimation. We demonstrate that our results are sensitive to noise model assumptions, particularly at the highest multipoles. However, when we limit our analysis to the range $2 < \ell < 1500$, our estimated parameters are highly accurate, with values nearly identical to previous planck results, with minimal deviations less than $0.01\sigma$.

This article builds on the work of Kujawa and Muth on tensor product irreducibility for highest weight modules over certain Lie algebras and U(h)-free modules. Our expansion allows us to analyze tensor products involving both highest weight modules and U(h)-free modules, utilizing minimal one-dimensional modules as a key tool. The resulting isomorphism criteria are expressed in terms of isomorphism between specific modules.

Neural networks, including Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models, have excelled in NLP tasks, including sentiment classification. However, due to the abbreviated and unconventional nature of tweets, which frequently omit standard grammar and punctuation, the application of these techniques to sentiment classification presents challenges. To address these challenges, we developed a novel approach that incorporates a bag-of-words feature extraction method combined with a hybrid word embedding strategy. Our proposed approach utilizes recurrent neural networks to classify the sentiment of tweets. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, achieving a high accuracy of 91.44% in identifying the sentiment of tweets.

In this study, we examine the role specifications, focusing on their impact on dialogue systems, particularly the AI conversational partners, and the substantial differences in interactions based on assigned roles. We start by examining the existing principles of role-based systems, then explore how role specifications affect these systems, before applying this understanding to develop effective role specifications for AI conversational partners.

Current research on the background of gravitational waves focuses heavily on high-frequency ranges but often overlooks another type of background, known as "memory background," which behaves differently and dominates at lower frequencies. We have created a detailed model to analyze this memory background, taking into account the evolution of memgrams - a concept that maps the population of gravitational wave sources over time. Our model reveals that the memory background can be estimated based on the rate of non-memory background, allowing for a more broad understanding of the memory background, especially at frequencies above the most sensitive frequency range observed so far. We have also found that future detectors, such as Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer, will have significant exposure to both the memory and non-memory backgrounds, with a memory-to-non-memory ratio of approximately 0.1 and 10 respectively. We have further noted the potential for distinguishing the memory background from the non-memory background through a unique 'saw-tooth' signature left by individual wave events, which may allow for a more accurate estimation of the memory background.

We present a all-encompassing theory of supersymmetry breaking via gauge interactions that can also explain neutrino origin at a PeV scale. This massive scale fits well within the limitations imposed by proton decay, a consequence of having only two right-handed neutrinos. A complicated series of reactions involving the breaking of electroweak symmetry result in supersymmetric features that can be identified, including specific lepton asymmetries and a supersymmetry-related signal known as the scotogenic signal.
