We focus on the study of G2-instantons with symmetry from the SU(2) group.
It's discovered that the class of abelian instantons is expansive, providing additional insight into the first order rigidity of these instantons, specifically in the context of G2-invariant fields.
Furthermore, we establish the existence of a family of G2-invariant ASD ASD connections, extending the known relationship between G2-instantons and ASD connections.
This relationship was previously identified as a local diffeomorphism, but our findings show it is merely an immersion.

To compare the normality of operators, we establish the relationship of normality levels and determine the conditions for $\Phi_{\varphi, \psi}$ and $\mathcal{C}_{\varphi}$ to be $C$-normal when the source space is the space of holomorphic functions on the unit disk, equipped with a specific norm.

The study primarily focuses on the largest $p$-core $p'$-partitions that exhibit the property of being $p$-neutral. Notably, the sequence of the lengths of these $p$-core $p'$-partitions that don't exceed a certain limit can be determined accurately using the principles of largest $p$-partitions that comply with specific constraints and the concept of congruence within a group of numbers that are relatively prime to $p$.

Machine learning models for point clouds are becoming increasingly prevalent but are also more susceptible to geometric adversarial attacks due to the structureless nature of point clouds. Current methods for defending against such attacks either rely on modifying the model or inflating its margins, but these approaches have limitations in terms of their range of applicability and optimality. To address these challenges, we introduce the Threshold-Propagation Framework (TPC), a method that relies on interval arithmetic to certify and optimize a wide range of 3D models against the most demanding geometric attacks. By doing so, we provide the first time and accuracy certifications against these attacks and demonstrate the ability to boost certified accuracy while maintaining optimal models. Experiments on the MNIST-pc, ShapeNet, and AutoEncNet datasets confirm that TPC can increase certified accuracy by up to 10% without compromising a model's test-time performance.

We assess interference in a network of AFS FMCW radar systems, where each node transmits multiple radar signals per packet, as seen in applications like intelligent vehicles and monitoring systems. Interference in this type of radar can lead to decreased performance, including lower throughput and larger delays. To address this, we apply Poisson approximation to assess interference probabilities and network throughput. Next, we examine the impact of key parameters, such as chirp density per packet, target range, and power settings on overall network performance. We evaluate the effectiveness of an intelligent scheduling technique, incorporating interference awareness and backoff strategies, in enhancing network throughput and minimizing delays. Notably, our research shows that adopting a higher number of chirps per packet can lead to significantly higher network throughput compared to traditional methods using fewer chirps.

To investigate the Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interferometry, particularly the detection of entangled two-photon absorption in non-linear materials, a theoretical framework is established. This allows for the calculation of reduced density matrices for the output photons based on known statistical states of the input photons, resulting in general expressions for the visibility of the HOM interferogram. This visibility can serve as a reliable indicator for entangled two-photon absorption. The proposed formula encompasses the visibility derived by Li et al. and demonstrates that even in the absence of the visibility, entangled two-photon absorption may occur. This new understanding may guide researchers in discovering novel applications of the HOM interferometry.

We have developed a highly flexible and versatile T-equivariant elliptic cohomology spectrum, denoted as Ell_X, for any elliptic curve X, which generalizes the previously established work of Mount, Stojanoski, and Strickland, who constructed a T-equivariant version of elliptic cohomology specifically for a fixed isomorphism between two elliptic curves. Our approach utilizes the technique of adding additional invertible elements to a cohomology theory, applied in this instance to the function field of X, and we have shown that this results in a cohomology theory with a rich and nuanced structure that captures the full range of symmetries inherent in the geometry of X. This approach allows us to define and study the cohomology theory of any elliptic curve, which can be thought of as a generalized version of equivariant K-theory with complex structures. Our methods are expected to be applicable to other cohomology theories and may lead to a deeper and more profound understanding of their properties and relationships.

A novel approach to knowledge graph completion is presented, which leverages node- and edge-type encodings in a knowledge graph specific to temporal events. The proposed method innovates by incorporating cyclic patterns in time encoding, facilitating an effective representation of the cyclic nature of time. Furthermore, it introduces a time encoding scheme such that the differences and relationships between time points can be accurately represented and the future occurrence of time points can be extrapolated. In the context of temporal knowledge graph representation, a knowledge graph embedding framework is adopted, which incorporates future time point extrapolation based on the above-mentioned scheme. Experimental findings in diverse real-world scenarios indicate that the knowledge graph is more effective and the proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art time-based knowledge graph embedding methods.

We present a new classification for ground sound made audible through impact, focusing on its distinct high-frequency characteristics. This sonic phenomenon, distinct from the prevalent geometric acoustic models, manifests in three high-frequency impact sounds produced when objects hit three diverse surfaces: concrete, wood flooring, and carpet. We identify the precise threshold for detecting this sound and developed an algorithm to efficiently identify impacts from multiple objects with minimal misclassifications. Moreover, we developed a compact model that can accurately localize impacts, pinpointing the object involved with over 90% accuracy and determining the object's identity with over 90 classes accurate, allowing it to replace more complex state-of-the-art models in this area.

Our investigation into practical bell nonlocality uses reveals that even slight deviations from ideal correlations in quantum information technologies can significantly impact their relevance. This report delves into a specific case of imperfect measurement settings, demonstrating that real-world applications of bell nonlocality are feasible and beneficial.

Systems with highly degenerate flat bands, which allow for exceptionally fast electron transport, can be engineered through specific principles. While these principles have traditionally relied on symmetries, utilizing degenerate orbital sets, or arranging atoms on sub-lattice structures, recent research has uncovered a novel approach. It has been demonstrated that introducing randomness into the arrangement of orbitals within a two-dimensional system can result in undisturbed, degenerate, flat bands. The positions of these degenerate states are influenced by continuous parameters, which can be altered without losing degeneracy. The effectiveness of this method has been validated through exact diagonalization and Gutzwiller approximation calculations. The simplicity and generalizability of this method has significant implications for designing materials with novel properties.

Research on two-dimensional (2D) materials has gained momentum in the fields of theoretical and applied physics, with the discovery of novel 2D compounds such as TMDs, graphene, and BCN. Our study reveals the electronic and vibrational properties of BCN and compares it to its doped variants. Utilizing the FP2K code, our research reveals that hydrogen's presence significantly enhances electron-phonon interactions, resulting in higher superconducting transition temperatures. Furthermore, our findings indicate that replacing hydrogen with deuterium or tunneling electrons through it can lead to the onset of superconductivity in BCN and doped borophene.

This note explores the flattened parts of a partition, denoted as $f_{n,k}$ (where $1\leq k\leq n$), which count the number of partitions of an $n$-element set into $k$ subsets, such that at most $2$ elements belong to each subset within. We examine these values within the context of a flattened version of the Gaussian binomial coefficient. We also establish a connection between $f_{n,k}$ and the standard parts of a partition, denoted as $p_{n,k}$ (which count the number of ways $n$ elements can be partitioned into $k$ non-empty subsets), through the examination of the ratio $\frac{p_{n,k}}{f_{n,k}}$. We demonstrate the monotonicity of this ratio with respect to $k$ and present explicit upper bounds.

We examine dynamical systems arising from linear actions of finitely generated nilpotent groups, modified by periodic components, on the space of character mappings from a fixed finitely generated abelian subgroup to the unit circle. The use of a "unit circle" metric distinguishes this study from previous work on affine toroidal dynamics, revealing significant differences in the two dynamical behaviors. We present two key findings: (1) the periodic component's impact on the dynamics is constrained to a specific condition for achieving chaos; (2) the group's non-commutative properties cause actions on the space of characters to diverge from similar actions on a torus.

Evaluating the functional safety of automotive driving systems is both intricate and time-consuming. Recent advancements in formal verification, specifically model checking, offer a chance to optimize this process. To streamline safety evaluation, we introduce a method that allows model checking to verify the functional safety of automotive driving systems while considering their functional limitations. This is efficiently achieved through the development of abstract models that can be supplemented with safety constraints, enabling the checking of whether these restrictions can be adhered to without compromising safety.

The complexity of nonlinear systems in diverse applications, such as modeling natural phenomena and engineering processes, requires advanced analytical frameworks. Dynamic systems are often simplified with constant parameters but frequently involve time-varying parameters or changeable structures. This paper explores the potential of the Koopman operator framework for analyzing dynamic systems with varying parameters or structures. Focusing on finite-rank operators, we demonstrate that certain systems with changing structures or parameters can be expressed using finite-rank operators and thus fall into the coherent space of a linear dynamic system. Building on existing research into linearization through Koopman operators and its applications, we examine the feasibility and limitations of this approach for capturing essential dynamics in non-stationary systems.

In the early 18th century, King Frederick I of Prussia, who was also a patron of the sciences, commissioned mathematicians to write a comprehensive analysis of the philosopher Leibniz's conceptual framework of infinity. As a result of this inquiry, the mathematicians responded with a 48-page response, now known as the Demonstratio mathematica, in which they dissected and sometimes contradicted Leibniz's distinguished views. They posited that bounded and unbounded infinities were fundamentally distinct, contrarily to Leibniz's supposition, who believed them to be equivalent but limited or unlimited, respectively. Furthermore, the mathematicians argued that concepts of unbounded quantities inherently contained the potential to actually become infinite, a notion rejected by Leibniz. Notably, these responses aligned with the thinking of the prominent Prussian scientist Euler, who was at the time still in his early twenties. Interestingly, these responses failed to make a favorable impression on Leibniz, who criticized the Prussian scientist's approach as misleading the court. Furthermore, the Demonstratio mathematica did not influence early Prussian thinking about calculus, the concept of a function, or infinity, as later documented in the pioneering scientific works of the early 18th century.

The cosmo_pt model, introduced in 2019, is designed for separating foregrounds from the cosmic microwave background and is simultaneously fitting for cosmological parameters and separating sources. In this study, the influence of foreground removal on accurate cosmological estimations and source separation is examined using the Planck satellite data and the South Pole Telescope data sets. Foregrounds are removed from the Planck data in four stages with increasing intensity, starting from a basic level and up to the most aggressive removal. For each stage, parameters and noise are estimated with the Commander algorithm, and these results are compared with the full-sky data. Ultimately, up to three levels of foreground removal yield parameters consistent with the full-sky data, while up to four levels are found to produce a clean cosmic microwave background map free from residual foreground interference. In contrast, fitting for parameters with the full-sky data and removing foregrounds leads to divergent results, indicating a potential bias in our understanding of the cosmos.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be infinite-dimensional vector spaces with possibly different underlying fields. Suppose the linear map from $s \in \ell^1(\mathbb{R}, X)$ to $T(s) \in \ell^1(\mathbb{R}, Y)$ is defined by $(T(s))_n = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} A_n^{(k)} s_{n-k}$, where $A_n^{(k)}$ are bounded operators from $X$ to $Y$. It has been proven that if $Y$ is a Hilbert space and there exist $b, c > 0$ and $d \in [0, 1)$ such that $\sup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \|A_n\| < d$ and $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \|A_n^{(k)}\| < c$, then $T$ maps any sequence of vectors in $X$ to a sequence of vectors in $Y$ that contains a linearly independent subset.

Recommender systems that are built on document models have the potential to address the issue of accuracy degradation in systems that rely on user-item interactions only, especially in scenarios with very few data points. This is particularly relevant for building recommender systems in domains like science that often have extremely sparse data. One effective approach to leveraging document models is to combine them with user profiles, which can be on a par with or even exceed the quality of individual user profiles. To meet this need, a new method called DSPAR was developed to create sparse and domain-aware document-based recommender systems. It combines the benefits of document and user profiles while enabling the sharing of user document interactions across multiple domains. The proposed framework employs a new representation for user profiles that is based on latent topic information and uses an adversarial training approach to ensure consistency in the information it provides. The effectiveness of this method was demonstrated through the creation of multiple datasets and extensive experiments, the results of which indicate significant performance improvements over multiple baseline models.

Recently, the concept of conditional freeness was reexamined in the context of random matrix theory by Bai and Sun. Their work focused on understanding how conditional freeness affects asymptotic behavior, particularly in relation to eigenvalue distributions. This paper broadens their findings by investigating the implications of conditional freeness on Stieltjes transforms and associated eigenvalue/differential transforms.

System monitoring is essential for ensuring the reliable operation of real-time systems, but accurately detecting and analyzing faults often requires precise synchronization between the monitor and the subject system. However, when there is timing uncertainty, current monitoring tools fail to operate effectively, leading to either missed faults or excessive system intrusion. Existing solutions either rely on complex algorithms or simplistic assumptions, neither of which fully addresses the issue. This research presents a new type of adaptive monitoring that falls within the scope of real-time and safe computing. It develops adaptive energy-based specifiers that can operate within uncertain timing constraints by incorporating timing intervals and a scheduling system. Additionally, it creates an efficient algorithm to convert these specifiers into standard logical forms, enabling standard monitoring. This approach is implemented in practice with the use of the CHYPETES real-time system and an adaptive algorithm called CYPRULES that enables the flexible and efficient monitoring of the system with minimal disruption.

Researchers have detected the $D_s^{*+}$ meson decaying into a $p$ and $K^0_S$ with an intermediate $a_0(980)$ resonance. An analysis of $6.98\,\text{fb}^{-1}$ proton-proton collisions at $13\,\text{TeV}$ by the LHCb experiment found the $a_0(980)$ resonance with a branching fraction of $(1.46\, \pm\, 0.12\, \pm\, 0.19)\times 10^{-4}$. Additionally, the average lifetime of the $K_0^*(892)$ was first measured when it was reconstructed via its decay into $a_0(980)\pi^+$; the result was $\Gamma = 161\, \pm\, 16\, \pm\, 13\,\text{MeV}$, consistent with the central value $\Gamma = 164\,\text{MeV}$ from Particle Data Group tables.

We've developed two sets of stabilization parameters for the Very Large Telescope Interferometer's core correlator, GRAVITY, which are essential for maintaining precision in the system's wavefront stability. By leveraging on-board cameras, we've been able to refine these parameters, allowing us to improve the core correlator's performance. As a result, the custom-configured link operates more reliably and efficiently than the default settings. Two additional cameras, monitoring the reference path, enable the derivation of supplementary stabilization parameters. These parameters supplement those acquired from the science target and successfully enhance the core correlator's performance. Our analysis has demonstrated that the custom-stabilization parameters have allowed the GRAVITY instrument to achieve its maximum theoretical precision, thereby maximizing the core correlator's potential and selecting the optimal data analysis method for each observation.

A core objective in cluster analysis is the $k$-center problem which necessitates finding $k$ centers that minimize the maximum distance between each point and its nearest center. Its variation, the $k$-center problem with restricted capacity, involves selecting at most $k$ centers out of a set of $k$ centers, such that each center has a certain capacity. 

We investigate the complexity of solving this problem under restricted capacity when the data has a certain property, where its structure can be represented as a collection of regions with certain characteristics. We prove that with restricted capacity, finding a minimum $k$-center cluster is a challenging task, even when limiting ourselves to choosing only one center from each available set of its $k$-center. 

We demonstrate this difficulty by reducing a well-known NP-complete problem under polynomial time mapping to this data structure. As a result, we conclude that even when limiting ourselves to choosing only one center from each available set of its $k$-center, finding a minimum $k$-center cluster is a well-known NP-complete problem when the structure of its regions has a certain property, where it has only one region, is convex, has an intersection property, has a union property, etc.

We consider the equation f^qLH(A, B, n) = p, where the composite operator consists of the product of the nth-order linear differential expression, composed of derivative terms and polynomial coefficients, and the q-th power of the function f. This leads to the conclusion that for the Brück conjecture in this context, its composite version holds for the case when the hyper order of the entire function f is less than 1/2, and it also confirms the conjecture for the special case when E(f) = E(p) is less than or equal to 1, and it proves that the equation has only constant solutions under the condition when the hyper order of the function f is less than or equal to 1/2, for the case when the expression consists of just two terms.

This research presents a modified version of solving a polynomial linear system, using a probabilistic and efficient method that can handle errors, especially in cases where the errors are significant or random. By leveraging the ability to handle one error per column, the study develops a strategy to handle multiple errors without significantly increasing the number of errors introduced. As a result, the number of evaluations can be reduced to approximately $n\ell + m\log_2(n)$ for scenarios with one error per column, where $n$ and $m$ represent the dimensions of the polynomial linear system.

In this study, we propose the controlled quantum engineering of a three-level V-type atom interacting with a cavity field to create entangled photon pairs at will. By adjusting the cavity decay rate and atom-position, we can quantum correlate photons in a controlled manner, leading to a trade-off between the emission of correlated photons in matching and opposing optical modes. The process of photon pair emission in the cavity can be modeled using a two-dimensional effective Hamiltonian, where we introduce an artificial magnetic field by shifting the cavity mode frequency. This causes the effective Hamiltonian to behave as if it were a Zeeman system in a magnetic field, enabling the controlled release of entangled photons in the desired state.

High-energy-density behaviors of five alkali elements (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs) were investigated through ab initio simulations, with a focus on their compressed states, velocity, and phase transitions. This research demonstrated that these elements obey corresponding states principles, with similar equations of state, shock velocities, and distinct post-main sequence ionization patterns. Equations of state were formulated and found to align with validated data from previous studies, including Jupiter's core compression, particularly in the compression of hydrogen.

Within a quantum field theory where local parity is broken, the effective action for a vector meson is explored, followed by an examination of the vector meson's polarization in a Chern-Simons medium with zero temperature. The presence of the Chern-Simons term results in the acquisition of mass by the vector meson, whose magnitude grows linearly with the medium's chemical potential and can be understood through a generalised Landau-Pomeranchuk theorem in this medium. The Chern-Simons interaction also breaks gauge invariance, which is restored by the simultaneous acquisition of mass in a gauge-invariant manner. The theory, however, becomes non-renormalizable at an energy scale proportional to the chemical potential, indicating a fundamental shift in the system at lower energy scales and a plausible scenario for the confinement of new particle types within this range.

This paper addresses size estimation in a specific type of network by presenting a distributed algorithm that operates independently of the network's structure. The algorithm, when applied to a finite undirected network, utilizes a data packet, randomly injected into the network, to generate a size estimate. Analytical methods, including both exact formulas and simplified approximations, are developed to evaluate the estimate's accuracy. Additionally, the study extends the research to assess the size estimate accuracy for a random network model.

A novel approach to resolving the Hamiltonian constraint in relativistic cosmology is presented, varying from standard methods by not immediately solving for the conformal factor, instead treating it (and its gradient) as independent variables. This strategy mandates a separate treatment of the conformal degree of freedom, resulting in an evolved conformal constraint that, when paired with a suitable initial treatment, ensures the constraint's satisfaction at later times. We apply this approach within 1+logular slicing, presenting an efficient implementation of the Hamiltonian constraint solution that minimizes the conformal factor's outer product norm.

The main chamber of the JUNo (Joint autonoMous/neutrino/nuclеus/Oscillations) experiment, currently under construction at the former CNGS site in Lingao, Guangdong, China, is filled with 20 million water-Cherenkov detectors, each 20 cm in diameter and renowned for their exceptionally high light yield.  A crucial part of the experiment's data analysis will be accurately reconstructing vertex positions from neutrino interactions.  Due to the experiment's large detector scale of several thousand tons, even small systematic errors in position forecasting can significantly impact resolution.  Current simulation tools, such as G4NeuLand, provide a starting point, but further refinement is required for full functionality.  A newly versatile Monte Carlo tool, vMC, has been created to enhance position forecasting accuracy and may eventually supersede G4NeuLand within the JUNo experiment.

In the study of multivariate time series forecasting, identifying the linkages among various series is a crucial step. Consequently, most current models, which utilize series information, are focused on improving prediction accuracy. However, these models often overlook the relationship between series, which is critical for tasks such as forecasting. Additionally, recent models based on new optimization techniques still face practical challenges, including extended running times and potential data loss. Building on the success of the Transformer, which uses a global self-attention mechanism to capture long-term dependencies, its variations, such as Informer, have sought to make attention mechanisms more efficient. Informer initially showed great promise in forecasting tasks, using only a subset of encoded keys and values, which led to reduced computational costs. However, this method still has limitations, as it focuses on long-term dependencies while excluding shorter-term dependencies, which are present in some time series. Also, its use of linear projections in encoding may negatively impact the key-value and query vectors. Also, the way it calculates masks may not sufficiently reduce the model's parameters. Also, it often overestimates the length of these masks, which may negatively impact both the model's accuracy and computational efficiency. Also, it relies heavily on the number of key and value heads used in the model, which significantly affects the model's size. To address these issues, we introduce the Enhanced Informer (EInformer), which overcomes the limitations associated with the original Informer. Specifically, our method replaces the use

ADC designers need models that accurately represent the atmosphere's scattering of light. However, some complex models, like MODTRAN, calculate the scattering process directly from molecular data, which can be unnecessary and unnecessary for many applications. The effect of Rayleigh scattering is well-established and known for over a century; using modern multi-term Rayleigh scattering models without also accounting for the classical Regime of Scattering can lead to unnecessary overcomplication. A study examined various atmospheric models and found two unsuitable options, MODTRAN and RASCAL2, due to their reliance on a detailed, term-by-term calculation of radiative transfer. The problem is exacerbated by the fact that many atmospheric models currently in use, like MODTRAN and RASCAL2, also rely on a cumbersome combination of Rayleigh and Mie scattering principles. This can be unnecessary and inefficient for many applications. A simpler approach to ADC design involves using a simplified, regime-based scattering method for rays that pass through the clear sky, which combines classical Rayleigh scattering with a simplified, simplified version of a more complex, complex scattering calculation. The clear-sky algorithm performed comparably to a full atmospheric simulation in most cases, with the most significant difference between the two occurring when the clear-sky algorithm underestimated the scattering of the sun's light in the blue range.

Predicting multiple categories often faces a performance plateau when using multiple-labels as information, unlike two-way classification where it is more effective. To address this challenge, we developed a method called Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble, which leverages label information to improve multi-class performance without extra training overhead. In PILE, we create pair-wise labels from the top-k predicted labels and use them in an iterative process. First, label information is encoded, then pair-wise labels are derived, optimized, and the model's main task performance is enhanced. By applying PILE to multiple NLP benchmarks, we showed its consistency in enhancing multiple-choice performance with minimal gains in other areas, and our results indicate traditional label aggregation methods can be outperformed by PILE without external labels.

We investigate a network of sensors to detect dark matter, specifically focusing on the noise introduced by ultralight bosonic particles known as "scallops." Our analysis shows that the detection performance significantly improves with multiple sensors compared to using a single sensor, and the optimal gain in output quality is achieved by optimally combining the inputs from all sensors, especially when devices have independent noise sources.

The complexity of recovering sparse vectors from underdetermined linear measurements is highlighted in the context of the basis pursuit problem. The paper focuses on the role of the spectrum of the analysis matrix's central section, particularly in terms of how it affects the sparsity level and how it impacts the feasibility of basis pursuit for achieving optimal sparse representations. An analysis of the basis pursuit problem leads to a connection with an optimization problem that helps establish upper bounds on the basis pursuit error. The study also explores the relationship between these bounds and the condition number of the analysis matrix, and in the context of Gaussian measurements, it quantifies the basis pursuit under特定 assumptions on the condition number and sparsity. The paper further explores the effect of nonlinearity in the central section on the basis pursuit performance and compares it to linear transformations, and in doing so, it finds that certain nonlinearity types such as sign, principal component, andhashed activations have different impacts on the basis pursuit error reduction.

This paper presents P4Test, a comprehensive test suite for programmable switch compilers, aiming to address the research community's growing interest in this area. Due to the limited number of open-source compiler backends, thoroughly evaluating a new compiler is particularly challenging. P4Test facilitates comprehensive compiler assessment by serving as a convenient benchmark and tool for P4 testing, especially in situations where a compiler's correctness is in question. P4Test consists of an extensive collection of hand-written test programs and automated scripts for benchmarking on multiple programmable switch compiler backends. The results from running these tests on a range of real-world compiler backends reveal insightful insights into compiler performance, enabling researchers to efficiently compare their compilersP4Test is accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/p4-testing/P4Test.

The study compares the solution of the vector transport equation with and without the pressure-velocity coupling, utilizing a mesh with two dimensions, a time-stepping method, and a P1/P0 element formulation. The results demonstrate that incorporating the pressure-velocity coupling through a mixed finite element method improves the overall solution quality, especially in capturing flow features on coarse nonconforming meshes, in contrast to methods that do not account for the pressure-velocity coupling.

Machine learning, particularly in its distributed forms, faces challenges of ensuring the privacy and fairness of sensitive data.  To tackle these issues, advanced approaches such as federated learning and differential privacy are employed.  These efforts to protect and fair machine learning also raise opportunities for exploring efficiency and performance enhancements.  This document serves as an introduction to these topics, with a focus on distributed privacy and fair machine learning.  It is part of a larger collection of survey papers that address various aspects of this intersection.

A LHCb experiment analyzed proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV energy, which was recorded over a 2.5 million $B^+_{c}$ decay events. The analysis focused on an excited state of $B^+_{c}$ in the range of 1.2-1.4 TeV, which is the result of the $B^+_{c}$ decaying into $B^+K$. The analysis found two excited states, which were denoted as $B^+_{c}(2S)$ and $B^+_{c}(3S)$; furthermore, the research introduced a new state $B^+_{c}(1D)$. The study also made comparisons with theoretical models and established predictions for relative spin-coupling.

Runge-Kutta - Nyström methods, a combination of Hamiltonian problems solver techniques, can be seen as combining Runge-Kutta methods for general problems and sigma methods for Hamiltonian problems. This paper focuses on continuous-stage Runge-Kutta methods for Hamiltonian problems, developing specific conditions for one-step CHAM methods when applied to Hamiltonian systems with momentary gradient structure. These methods have distinct properties, namely, preserving the Hamiltonian, symplectic, and ductile for that type of system.

This research introduces a cutting-edge technique for efficiently training generative deep neural networks by leveraging local critic training. By substantially reducing the range of interactions considered in gradient calculations, this method dramatically improves training speed without sacrificing model accuracy. We successfully applied this technique to deep convolutional and recurrent neural networks, obtaining comparable results to state-of-the-art alternatives while achieving notable gains in training efficiency. Additionally, we discovered that this method facilitates local structure learning for generators, specifically for convolving neurons. This finding leads to the development of a novel, efficient U convolutional network that outperforms existing non-symmetric models.

We examine how weak dissipation affects the boundaries of Wada basins in a two-dimensional chaotic system known as the T\"{e}nnessee game. The Tennessee game is created by iteratively drawing dissymmetric arcs that connect three curved fixed points, which are also the boundaries of its four interlinked escape basins. By modeling the generation of these arcs as a subset of a more comprehensive family of arc-shaped sets, which include random stick-bending processes, we analyze the influence of dissipation on the topological structure that governs the Tennessee game. Numerical results indicate that even a minimal level of dissipation leads to all basins sharing the same boundary, which displays intricate scaling behavior across different lengths. This boundary is found to be topologically equivalent to a type of space often seen in fractal structures. Moreover, we observe that the dissipation-induced modification of the boundary significantly impacts the probability of particles escaping through one of the basins, resulting in a nonequilibrium distribution of escape probabilities. The nonequilibrium weights of the basins are influenced by dissipation through a universal mechanism, resulting in the baseline escape probabilities maintaining the same topological properties across different levels of dissipation.

The muon g-2 collaboration has identified the parameter space for the new physics model $E_63$ as potentially explaining the muon g-2 anomaly based on current data. The muon e-2 collaboration's future projects, specifically the muon-muon collider and E-Mu2E, are well-positioned to further investigate the parameter space identified by the muon g-2 collaboration. The muon-muon collider can detect signals related to the boson $S$, while the $E$-$\mu$2E experiment can detect signals related to the boson $A$.

The capacity to comprehend complex video content through detailed analysis of key areas and their evolution over time is greatly enhanced by this proposed method, Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN). By leveraging two distinct attention mechanisms, a single-step focus on attention spans across channels and spaces, a multi-step process extends time-wise to identify evolving important regions and relationships between adjacent frames. A forward-backward attention fusion step further enables the model to comprehend attention maps, yielding improved capabilities. By combining these mechanisms, HAN excels in understanding action contents, particularly when dealing with complex videos featuring multiple actions and with extended duration. Extensive testing on commonly used action content datasets has demonstrated the effectiveness of HAN, achieving the best performance compared to existing deep learning architectures for action content comprehension.

We have investigated the outcome of scattering an electromagnetic wave off both near-extremal and non-extremal four-dimensional black holes. Our analysis indicates that scattered waves off near-extremal black holes maintain their electromagnetic character, whereas scattered waves off non-extremal black holes transform into scalar fields. Interestingly, this scalar field has a long-reaching power-law decay profile, which could potentially pose an obstacle in fully verifying the AdS/CFT duality for this system. However, using quantum information theory to track how the scattered waves affect the black hole's entropy, we found that near-extremal and extremal black holes preserve their entropy, whereas non-extremal black holes lose entropy. This supports the hypothesis that near-extremal black holes share similar mathematical and physical properties with extremal black holes.

Star formation is a critical area of study due to its far-reaching effects on the cosmos, making it the most influential process after the Big Bang, as it ultimately makes the cosmos habitable and enables the presence of water - key to life as we know it - in the universe, thus making life in the universe a real possibility. This article, which is a part of CosmoLife meeting special issue, focuses on the findings of our recent research into star and planet formation, as well as the cosmos, as it relates to the potential for life in the universe. This research has explored star formation across various wavelengths, from the ultraviolet to the millimeter, as it occurs at different distances from the Earth, as it builds and destroys molecules essential for life, as it creates and destroys planets, as it makes the cosmos habitable, as it knows not to make the earth too close to a star, as it knows the cosmos needs life, as it knows the cosmos to be a place for living things, as it makes the cosmos a place for life to know the cosmos, as it knows the cosmos to be a place for living things, as it makes the cosmos a place for life to know the cosmos, as it makes the cosmos a place for living things, as it makes the cosmos a place for living things, as it makes the cosmos a place for living things.

When calculating the entropy of a probabilistic distribution using importance sampling from another distribution, we face a challenge if the target distribution doesn't have a direct way to be evaluated. Focusing on this issue, we derive efficient estimators for entropy and related quantities like Fisher information and relative Fisher information, and prove their asymptotic normality. Our research also reveals the link between the relative Fisher information and the Kullback-Leibler divergence. In addition, we establish the asymptotic efficiency of our estimators for sample sizes based on the relative Fisher information. Our methods are supported through experiments on both synthetic and real-world data, and the code for their replication is available online.

This research centers on applying Borel measures and their dynamic properties to model and analyze complex semiconductor manufacturing systems. By utilizing these measures, researchers can assess the flow of products through various stages of the manufacturing process and identify key statistical properties such as expected values, variances, and temporal patterns. The dynamic properties offered by Borel measures enable researchers to investigate the flow of products across different time frames and identify patterns within these flows. The application of Borel measures also enables researchers to analyze the flow of subsets of products through the manufacturing process, facilitating comparisons between different product types and identification of common trends.

Network security is a pressing concern in the age of internet-of-things, making it essential to develop resources that are both user-friendly and efficient in detecting attacks. Existing classifiers, although effective, are often impractical for use on attackers' devices due to their demand for memory. Our proposed tool, NBcoded, overcomes this limitation by moving encoding and classification processes off the attacker's device, thereby enabling deployment on a wide range of devices with memory constraints. By moving these processes off-device, NBcoded also boosts performance, thereby resource allowing the attacker's device to focus on packet collection and streaming. Thorough testing of NBcoded on multiple attack vectors, including botnet and malware, demonstrates its success in safely encoding and classifying data, as well as in resource conservation and scalability for attack attribution.

For specific classes of groups within metabelian categories, we've determined the optimal growth gap, varying according to whether they are finitely represented, torsion-free, or a combination of these properties. Our findings indicate a maximum growth gap of 4 for finitely represented metabelian groups, 7 when they are torsion-free, and up to 25 when they are both torsion-free and finitely represented. Notably, we found finitely represented torsion-free groups in the commutator subgroups of solvable groups of degree 6 that exhibit a growth gap of 7 relative to $\mathbb{N}^k$, as well as new groups within the Commd($G^5\backslash\backslash G^7$) category, produced from PSL(2,5), displaying a growth gap of 7 relative to (Z^3)^k.

A new method is proposed to differentiate biological entities from non-biological objects based on their movement, specifically using the traits of motion to identify life. By modeling entity movement as a Markov process, our method raises the question: can a Markov structure be established for all biological entities, and are the characteristics of biological motion distinct from those of non-biological motion. After collecting trajectory data for biological entities, artificial cells, and inanimate objects, applying the three-clusterness validation, statistical comparison, and principal component analysis revealed that the trajectory data can indeed be organized into three distinct clusters. Notably, principal component analysis showed that the first component accounts for 97% of total variance and separates the clusters effectively, validating that the motion traits of biological entities are distinguishable from those of non-biological entities. As a result, our method demonstrates feasibility and provides insight into both the definition and exploration of synthetic life.

Solving complex partitioning issues in power networks and data mining applications poses significant challenges, especially with large datasets and numerous constraints, even with the latest high-performance computers. Emerging quantum computing technology offers the possibility of more efficient solutions to these complex optimization problems through quantum algorithms,, particularly the quantum evolutionary algorithm, which could outperform classical methods despite current quantum computers being less powerful. To effectively utilize this algorithm in standard optimization settings, it requires adaptation to account for the unique characteristics of quantum computing, such as solution representation, evaluation, and operator design. In this research, we apply and refine this algorithm to solve a real-world power network partitioning problem, taking into account the specific limitations and features of near-term quantum algorithms. In comprehensive tests, this algorithm consistently demonstrates superior performance compared to other advanced classical optimization algorithms, especially in efficiently locating suitable starting solutions and exploring solution relationships, while also matching it in solution quality and overall efficiency with 100 target partitioning problems. Additionally, even smaller quantum computing systems can rival powerful classical supercomputers in performance, especially relevant for scenarios involving a large number of problems or those that need to be solved repeatedly. As such, this near-term hybrid quantum approach shows promise in solving extremely complex optimization problems that even the most sophisticated classical algorithms struggle with.

Computer modeling of a falling object typically includes standard physics, like air resistance and elasticity, but recent research adds two new components - random fluctuations from numerical errors and the impact of numerical errors on the object's motion. 

Computer modeling simulates a falling object through a series of calculations, where each step involves measuring the object's position, velocity, and other properties. These measurements are often inaccurate, which can create small errors, like noise, in the simulated object's behavior. 

Researchers have found that by running a computer model of a simple falling object and tracking its behavior over time, they can observe patterns of change and movement that match the expected results of a statistical model. 

The proposed model applies to a basic computer model of a falling object and can be extended to more complex scenarios, like simulating a skydiver or a satellite. 

By understanding the potential impact of numerical errors on a computer model, researchers can gain a deeper insight into the statistical behavior of complex systems and their state of equilibrium.

We investigate the possibility that localized extra dimensions explain the lightness of the $\mu$ term and the missing particle puzzle. Interactions between standard model particles and the radiation zone allow the lightness of the extra dimension and a large supersymmetric mass spectrum to coexist. However, if higgsinos and a specific gaugino are the primary constituents of the neutral dark matter, their non-standard production methods could lead to detectable signals at the LHC. Since the dark matter particle's mass is usually determined by supersymmetric equivalence, there could be a connection between the gauge localization and the mass of this particle. While this scenario presents challenges for direct detection, it seems compatible with all current constraints.

A key requirement for developing practical quantum networks is the existence of high-power on-chip single-photon sources. The increase in quantum information applications using chips with microresonators and waveguide circuits requires an even more efficient solution. However, the presence of interface losses has historically limited the efficiency of such systems to less than 50%. To overcome this limitation, we developed a novel design for a microcavity that features a conical shape, coupled with a beam splitter and an input waveguide. The curved surfaces within this design redirect and recapture photons back into the circuit, thereby eliminating scattering loss. The use of finite-difference time-domain simulations and 24-nm thick silicon devices has validated this design's potential, resulting in a record-breaking 96.2% extraction efficiency for photons from a silicon microcavity. The incorporation of a box-like structure further boosts this efficiency to 99.2%. The combination of this design with an integrated waveguide has enabled the development of a compact and efficient source for photons on-chip, resulting in a footprint of just 12 x 65 micrometers. The incorporation of an atomic paritron system has also verified the accuracy of our simulation-based design process. This study investigates the effects of damping on longitudinal sound waves within a "soft potential" framework, but with a crucial modification: the interaction between space and time is decoupled. This approach is applicable to a variety of materials, including fluids with an extended understanding of dynamics, solids with potential issues in the crystal structure, and materials displaying anomalous diffusion of sound. When considering low-frequency and high-frequency ranges, the modified model predicts specific thresholds for the damping of sound waves: $\omega^2$ and $\omega^{4/3}$, respectively, distinct from the standard $\omega^{5/3}$ threshold found in traditional models.

The accuracy of predictions for inclusive processes involving a photon and multiple jets is limited by two factors: higher-order corrections and uncertainties in parton distribution functions. To overcome this limitation, a new method is developed that combines the calculation of matrix elements for multiple partons with probability distributions for multi-parton PDFs. This method effectively removes the constraints of traditional factorization, allowing for a more precise understanding of the process. A framework is established to interpret multi-parton contributions to PDFs and interpret their effects on factorized distributions. Numerical demonstrations using TMDFactorizer show that including multi-parton contributions results in improvements of 10-20% in precision for 10-30 GeV range of the probed scale.

We've developed a robust theoretical framework that connects the spatial distribution of light within a disordered system to its eigenmodes. These eigenmodes, which are determined by random parameters, can be reconfigured by changing specific aspects, ultimately allowing for the creation of any desired intensity pattern. Our work demonstrates the possibility of generating complex patterns, such as micrometer-scale images and customized optical waveguides, simply by adjusting the parameters influencing these disordered systems.

Multi-objective optimization, long a staple in evolutionary computation,
often falls short of its potential due to a common understanding: 
multimodal optimization, in which various species thrive, excels at finding
unique, high-value solutions. In contrast, it typically focuses on generating
numerous solutions of similar value. We introduce a unified framework for
both types of optimization, introducing a multi-fitness selection process.
We test this new approach using five benchmark functions, discovering it
outperforms existing methods in reaching optimal solution accuracy.

This project aims to investigate the stable matching problem, with a focus on larger groups of agents, where each agent's preferences are represented by a ranking of goods. Given the computational challenges associated with this type of input, we examine specific scenarios in which agents' preferences are numerically assigned to goods. Our research targets two key questions: determining the feasibility of identifying a stable matching that corresponds to the population's preferences (related to the utilitarian welfare problem) or finding a stable matching close to this best possible match (related to the ordinal welfare problem). Additionally, we delve into the inverse problem, which involves identifying the ideal stable matching and then finding the population's preferences. Our analysis focuses on the computational difficulties and complexities of these problems, specifically in the context of agents with binary valuations, and we also consider the scenario in which agents have more nuanced preferences (richer valuations).

In systems exhibiting valley Hall transport, vertical electric current is forbidden; however, this state can be influenced through various mechanisms. For instance, the application of strain with uneven distribution and magnetic fields in a plane both facilitate implicit valley Hall current. Our research focuses on examining dark current in MoTe2 monolayers under combined plane magnetic and strain conditions. These investigations reveal that the application of in-plane magnetic fields amplifies the valley Hall current, an effect that is particularly pronounced when the strain is non-uniform. Additionally, the valley Hall current is enhanced by the interaction between magnetic fields and electron-phonon effects, the latter of which introduce valley decoherence via scattering with acoustic phonons. Notably, the valley Hall current is robust against these effects, and can be effectively managed, thus making MoTe2 an ideal candidate for developing valley-based devices, including valley Hall electronics and spin valves.
This note aims to extend the concept of stabilizers, stabilizer groups, and the cloud center, originally proposed by Burdzy and Tsukamoto in 2021.

A high-frequency series-fed circularly polarized antenna, with a hose-like structure, is designed, analyzed and simulated for the L band design space. This series-fed antenna, with a diameter of 17.5 cm, terminates in a patch that gives it an average gain of 9.5 dBi within a 12.5 % bandwidth (1485-1545 MHz). During the process of analysis and optimization, the antenna developed a novel half power beamwidth range of 30-45 degrees. Due to its capability for ground-based polar reversal via rotation, the antenna exhibits high cross-polarization isolation and can achieve a 10-dB axial ratio less than 10 degrees. Although the antenna's gain and beamwidth are suitable for L band applications, its relatively low frequency limits its performance in G band and higher.

Reinforcement learning's potential to develop customized quantum error correction strategies has prompted our investigation into using it for decoding. We applied this approach to probabilistic Lattice Kite codes, a type of spatial code that has previously been analyzed using system-specific decoding algorithms. We compared the performance of our reinforcement learning-based decoder with the existing algorithm and existing machine learning decoders. We discovered that the performance of our decoder is robust and comparable, even without fine-tuning, whereas the other machine learning decoder required extensive hyperparameter optimization to achieve similar results. To further demonstrate the versatility of our approach, we explored multiple error propagation scenarios in probabilistic Lattice Kite codes and found that the performance of our decoder is comparable to the optimal performance of the reference decoder.

Quantum systems with complex interactions can offer significant advantages in sensing by becoming entangled. However, achieving these benefits often requires very low temperatures, which can be an impractical requirement. Research has shown that the level of quantum entanglement can be preserved across different quantum systems, even without lower temperature requirements. Furthermore, the development of a specific approach to quantum metrology leverages this property by utilizing individual events in non-constant quantum systems to enhance its sensing capabilities. This method is particularly effective when applied to a system involving coupled superconducting circuits, which can produce collective states of many particles and utilize their varying dynamics for precise measurements. Notably, this quantum jump metrology approach not only offers better than classical sensing capabilities, but it also surpasses sensing methods based on constant quantum systems. Notably, this advantage can be achieved without requiring very low temperature requirements, which is often the case for quantum sensing.

This study presents the yield of 11 hadrons measured as a function of momentum fraction $x_T$, defined as $2p_{\rm T}/\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$, in Au+Au, Pb+Pb, and A+C collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 200$ GeV and 2.76 TeV, and 2.76 TeV, respectively. All results were normalized with respect to proton-proton and proton-proton effective cross sections at the same momentum fraction. The ratio of A+C to proton-proton effective cross sections follows the same trend as Au+Au and shows a decrease with decreasing momentum fraction $x_T$. Furthermore, the presence of a systematic $x_T$-dependent enhancement in the Pb+Pb and A+C collisions has been identified. The trends observed in A+C collisions are influenced by the use of a non-fully-on-shell $u$-quark as a projectile in the experimental setup.

We demonstrate the ability of digital-analog quantum computing to simulate the Fermi-Hubbard model with high efficiency by emulating continuous-time Hamiltonian simulations with continuous parameter variation. Our approach involves creating an analog of the Fermi-Hubbard model's Hamiltonian on the Google's Sycamore quantum processor, achieving this through a combination of hardware-controlled microwave pulses and software-defined entangling operations. As a result, we can accurately simulate ground-state preparation and prepare fermionic wavefunctions with minimal computational overhead, thereby enabling reliable estimation of observable quantities, such as energy. Our approach has also been successfully applied to conduct finite-temperature simulations by adapting the Hamiltonian to include a finite beta value. Our research has significant implications, as it illustrates the feasibility of quantum simulations with both increased efficiency and resilience against quantum processor errors.

A novel, adaptive algorithm called Bonsai efficiently builds robust features from data, making them ideal for feeding into pre-trained models. By iteratively building a decision tree, it extracts informative representations at each node. Resulting trees generalize well and often require no. Our method is particularly valuable in training transfer models, as the same tree can be used across multiple tasks. Moreover, Bonsai's accuracy is linked to that of A* with Adaptive Heuristics. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method with experiments on 19 datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance in visual classification, visual recognition, and face authentication.

We developed an algorithm based on weighted-mutation assisted genetic techniques to optimize the clarity of light that passes through complex scattering environments. The traditional approach to resolving such phenomena, known as adaptive optics, often relies on gradually enhancing the precision of the light's focus by correcting its deviations using a mirror that can be adjusted in real-time. Our algorithm, however, rapidly achieves high standards of focus by identifying and implementing optimal adjustments. The effectiveness of our approach was validated through computer simulations that demonstrated a significant improvement in contrast, approximately four times better than the conventional method, which in turn allows for more accurate imaging and reduced access times.

The size of testing samples plays a crucial role in generating accurate value function estimates, which can significantly influence policy learning outcomes. However, excessive testing samples can lead to computational inefficiencies, as many value function methods rely on parallel evaluations. To address this issue, we propose a new technique, Parallel-Free Estimation (PFE), which allows value function estimates to achieve high accuracy with a minimal number of testing samples. As a result of this approach, experiments have shown that PFE consistently outperforms traditional methods, such as Actor-Critic, in terms of both sample efficiency and computational complexity while minimizing the reliance on parallel samples for evaluation.

A novel category of CMOS sensors, which are monolithic and feature a single thick charge-collection layer, has been introduced for the detection of low-energy neutrons using nuclear recoil and gamma rays. To optimize charge collection in this new design, we analyzed the impact of a thick charge-collection layer on the collection of charges. Through simulation and experimental testing of the BC-EMOS sensor, we found that increasing the active sensor thickness significantly enhances neutron sensitivity, particularly when combined with a sufficiently thick field collection electrode. To minimize energy dispersion by recoil nuclei, we determine that a collection electrode between 50% and 70% of the total sensor thickness yields the optimal performance. EMOS monolithic sensors have shown a substantial improvement in neutron discrimination capability over AMIC, achieving collection thresholds approximately 5-10 times lower than the ionization threshold for silicon. Moreover, collection thresholds significantly below 5 eV have potential applications for ultra-low threshold dual-phase xenon detectors, significantly expanding detection capabilities in dark matter searches.

A novel detection technique for exoplanets in ground-based imaging systems has been proposed, called Difference Image Composition at Low Resampling. This method enhances the sensitivity of the planet search by minimizing the resampling of telescope data, thereby reducing the effect of planetary noise and increasing the study area efficiency. The effectiveness of this method was tested using actual astronomical data from ALFOSC, demonstrating its accuracy and suitability for extracting exoplanets in various system configurations. This method can be applied to various imaging systems and helps in reducing the computational noise in the analysis.

Predicting corporate yield spreads plays a vital role in forecasting stock market returns and the business cycle, and the spreads' quadratic relationship with systemic risk underscores the importance of accurate short-term predictions. A substantial obstacle in improving prediction precision is the increasing interest rates, which can severely distort model performance, especially with the potential for negative interest rates in the future. We develop a novel framework using factor models to predict forward rate curves from large multivariate time series data, incorporating the factors' contributions to market risk and a dynamic process for curve evolution. This framework enables multistep forecasting of yield spreads without the need to assume a specific distribution for the curves, effectively addressing the issue of negative interest rates. We improve the model's performance through multistep forecasting and the selection of relevant corporate bond factors, yielding highly accurate out-of-sample predictions that surpass existing benchmarks across various factor adjustments and correlations to market risk and portfolio-specific characteristics.

The DUNE Near Detector's design and positioning within a 14-kiloton liquid argon time-projection chamber enable a comprehensive investigation of neutrino oscillations, including a detailed analysis of sterile neutrinos, despite not being the primary focus of the experiment.  By combining 3D imaging capabilities with a customized event reconstruction, researchers can simulate nuclear de-excitations resulting from nucleon interactions induced by neutrinos.  This simulation will facilitate an enhanced search for sterile neutrinos, particularly in a dedicated search where it's possible to clearly distinguish between events involving de-excitation and those that do not.  By focusing on nuclear de-excitations occurring within the first 3 nanoseconds after a nucleon interaction, researchers could set significant limits or discover a 3-eV neutrino mass limit, or develop a mass measurement with statistical uncertainties of approximately 0.3 eV.  Furthermore, nucleon interaction rates can be accurately quantified, providing reliable normalisation factors, with the capability to achieve precision in the range of 1-5%.  These factors can be applied to an improved search for nucleon-induced nuclear reactions, such as neutron decay events, thereby enhancing the sensitivity in cases of neutron production via inverted ordering or radioactive neutrinoless double beta decay.

Proposed cluster-robust estimators for linear models with fixed factors offer enhanced inference under weak assumptions, particularly in small samples and scenarios with multiple clusters. Our results indicate that these estimators are more accurate than the conventional panel lemma, Hall and Scott Marshall estimators, and especially, they outperform newly introduced cluster-robust estimators by Scott Marshall and Andrews in such cases. The estimators employ novel representations, boosting their accuracy to $O_p(n^{1/2})$ with a single cluster and $O_p(g(n))$ with multiple clusters, where $g(n)$ represents the count of the smallest clusters. The estimators are adaptable to various estimators, including M-estimators and limited dependent variables, and the results can be implemented using existing software with a simple adjustment.

A computational approach with a two-step integration process, tailored for complex fluid dynamics involving multiple phases, is developed and implemented. This method combines a solver for incompressible multi-phase flows with the original code of an industrial software package. A multi-scale time-stepping integration algorithm, or MTSA, is applied to simulate interactions between small and large particles with greater efficiency. By applying MTSA to particle-laden flows, we demonstrate significant improvements in computational efficiency, reducing wall-clock time by a factor of 10, while maintaining synchronization accuracy of four orders of magnitude. A corresponding fluid-dynamics error, stemming from numerical approximations, stands at three orders of magnitude below the synchronization accuracy.

The thermodynamic properties of thermal states in quantum field theory lead to significant problems during black hole evaporation due to the lack of consistent particle definition in curved spacetime. In studies of de Sitter space, it becomes clear that there is no unique particle definition, which poses challenges in exploring the thermodynamic behavior of the vacuum state by comparing it to Minkowski space. To address this issue, we investigate whether particle definition can be introduced in de Sitter space and find that, while an adiabatic particle definition is feasible for frequencies below the de Sitter curvature scale, it is not applicable for higher frequencies. As a result, we identify two distinct regions for particle definition: one with a time-dependent, adiabatic definition, and another, high-frequency region affected by the horizon, which lacks a consistent particle definition and is dominated by geometric effects. To circumvent the information loss problem, we explore introducing an external time-dependent mode function as particle definition and find that, although this approach can describe Hawking radiation, it cannot simultaneously preserve the empty space properties, which is consistent with the equivalence principle and suggests that the cost of defining particles for Hawking radiation results in the distortion of flat space properties.

Using the BJL model for the dipole cross-section, which incorporates the saturation scale's dependence on size and the nuclear color charge density, we examine predictions for color flux tube length and nuclear broadening. The BJL model is enhanced with power and Gaussian models to reflect the free quark contribution, and these enhanced scales are used to simulate A p collisions. The simulations are carried out for A=6, 12, 56, and 238, and for collisions with free nucleons and various nuclei.

We demonstrate that the equation $7^{m} = a^3 + b^5$ has a solution for any $7^m$, with $a$ and $b$ being positive integers. This is achieved by showing that there is at least one instance where the equation's $m$ value is the highest possible. Building on this, Bugeaud and Mignotte conjectured that in such instances, at least one of the integers $a$ or $b$ is not the $7$th power of another positive integer. However, in a recent study, it was found that there are infinite instances where both $a$ and $b$ are not the $7$th power of any positive integer.

The presence of air that has been drawn into a liquid jet, which occurs during the liquid's motion through a channel, significantly influences its behavior. Although this phenomenon is crucial for applications in atomic force microscopy, previous studies have not been included in the theoretical framework that describes the liquid jet's motion. We apply a novel approach, which has been used in aerodynamics to model skin friction, to take into account the air that has been drawn into the liquid. Our results reveal that the air that has been entrained into the liquid jet causes it to oscillate in response to disturbances, which is consistent with the known effect on liquid jets at high speeds.

A growing number of applications are leveraging non-volatile memory, given its ability to maintain data integrity in the event of system crashes. To make the most of this feature, an algorithm-based understanding is essential, which can be adapted and applied based on specific requirements, such as crash resilience or data optimization. In this study, an investigation was conducted into how to automatically incorporate this algorithm-based knowledge using a technique known as control-flow transplantation, an approach based on control-flow sensitivity. However, while the current method shows promise, it falls short in accurately representing control flow during loop unrolling and memory copy operations, resulting in excessive control flow extraction. As a result, our research presents an approach to resolve these limitations by identifying and removing these issues, which not only improves performance but also accelerates execution time compared to other methods. Additionally, our study found that non-volatile loop unrolling and memory copy optimizations can significantly contribute control flow, resulting in execution speeds up to 7.67 times and 12.1 times faster, respectively, while still maintaining control flow precision.

Networks of documents can now be easily accessed and linked via the internet, but their complexity demands advanced techniques for comprehension. Traditional statistical techniques, such as topic modeling, fall short in handling network structures. A new technique, the hierarchical document topic model, better suits analysis of network structures. We developed an efficient sampling algorithm for this model and a fast Gibbs sampler. Extensive testing on synthetic and real-world data confirmed the model's method finding capabilities, variable discovery, fast convergence, and ability to capture network structure in a few layers. The model's results revealed key topics and structure of real-world networks, outperforming other techniques. A browser interface was created to facilitate visualization and comprehension of network structures.

An in-depth analysis of three-body escapes was conducted, involving extensive numerical simulations and accompanying animations. This study examined the statistical properties of three-body systems, revealing that their properties align with prior research and satisfy self-similarity, a principle that signifies the presence of inherent order.

Our research focused on the distribution of residual energies from "spectator" particles and found that it converges to a Cauchy-Lorentz pattern, a finding that is also present in gravitational three-body systems. This outcome supports the hypothesis that non-gravitational three-body systems exhibit universal behavior.

Our analysis of "runaway" particles showed that their velocity distributions follow power-laws with varying exponents, which are influenced by the specific system under consideration. Additionally, the proportion of "runaway" particles that achieve unbound orbits was found to be negligible.

To understand the acceleration of "runaway" particles, the concept of maximum multiplicative nesting was introduced, which can be applied to various system parameters. This framework enables the derivation of theoretical predictions for velocity distributions, which are then validated through direct measurements of these distributions.

Measurements of $\psi(2S)$ and $J/\psi$ mesons have been made in separate rapidity ranges and at various transverse momentum levels, using $p+p$ and $p+\mathrm{Ar}$ collisions. The data, collected with the ALICE detector, were obtained from high-energy collisions, including those of $2.76\,\mathrm{GeV}/\mathrm{c}$ per nucleon and $15.8\,\mathrm{GeV}/\mathrm{c}$ per nucleon. The results, reported as nuclear modification factors, show that at lower transverse momenta the $\psi(2S)$ is more strongly suppressed and more rapidly recovered with increasing momentum than the $J/\psi$. This suggests that $\psi(2S)$ suppression is an average of events with varying degrees of medium interaction, whereas $J/\psi$ suppression result from events with intense medium interaction. Additionally, at higher transverse momenta, $J/\psi$ exhibits less media interaction and both particles show comparable nuclear modification, indicating similar media impact and energy loss for both at higher momenta.

This study presents a term structure in continuous logic, establishing that any equivalence relation can be faithfully represented within an equivalent complete metric space. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this concept applies within the framework of metric spaces, confirming that any equivalence relation may have a faithful term representation, which in turn can be translated into an equivalent relation defined by a function. We also explore the implications of these findings on the terms and relations of the original structure.

One effective technique for identifying and addressing significant changes in complex systems relies on change patterns. While these patterns are extensively used in software engineering, they are largely confined to the management of code modifications. This study presents a new application of change patterns in system management, focusing on system refactoring through an approach that combines singular value decomposition with a quantitative metric for measuring system complexity. By comparing the Ranks of SVD results from established and altered system matrices, the concept of refactoring patterns is introduced. These patterns assist managers and developers in determining the necessary adjustments to restore a modified system to its original state. Two case studies involving academic institutions validate the effectiveness of this approach. Notably, a positive correlation between Complex Network metrics and system complexity values is found, with Higher values of patterns' ranks indicating greater complexity in managing changes.

Deep sequential models like recurrent neural networks and convolutional networks can model complex patterns, but they struggle with long sequences of data without extensive pre-training. Pre-training often isn't an option in many real-world scenarios. New methods combining these models for image time-series analysis have emerged, but they still fall short. To overcome the limitations, this paper explores attention-based enhancements for sequential models, demonstrating an improvement in handling long sequences without extensive training. Experiments on image time-series classification show that combining attention with sequential models yields comparable results to recurrent neural networks and significantly outperforms standard convolutional networks on large datasets. Additionally, the proposed attention models are more efficient in terms of training and inference time. Code and data are available on GitHub.

We conducted an analysis of data collected by the XMM-Newton satellite, focusing on observations of Cassiopeia A, a supernova remnant, that took place between 1997 and 2014. Obtaining a total exposure of 260 ks, this analysis allowed us to map the high-energy X-ray emission within the shell of CSHA A, demonstrating that it is uniformly distributed and not confined to any particular area. Calculating the overall count rate in the energy range of 2.5 to 12 keV, this analysis yielded a count of 2426, with an associated statistical uncertainty of just 1 percent. Comparing the overall count rate to previous measurements, this analysis confirms that the high-energy X-ray emission from Cassiopeia A has remained stable and at a constant level over the past 3,000 years. Another significant finding from this analysis is that the X-ray emission within Cassiopeia A is linearly polarized, with a estimated degree of polarization of 11 percent, within the margin of statistical error. The polarization pattern within this analysis is aligned with the radial direction, matching the orientation of magnetic fields detected in radio observations, providing support for a scattering origin for the high-energy X-ray emission, with the primary unabsorbed emission being an unpolarized free-free process.
